Here is an extract from an interesting lecture, delivered by Sir Andrew the other day, to the Students of the London Hospital: "Tea is a blessed beverage. Ido not know what I should do without it. But there is tea and tea, and one svf the teas I have in my mind is the representation of all that is physiologically wicked. Igo about town a good deal holding consulta- tions here and there, and about five o'clock, when I get into a place, the lady of the boosts will say to me : • Sir Andrew, you look tired, do let me give you a cup of tea.' I say • thank you very much. But the tea has stood for half-an-hour, and she remarks, • I know you do you not like it strong, Sir Andrew. and she then pours about a tablespoonful of the tea into a cup and tills thecup up with water. Now I call it positivecruelty to give tea like that to anybody. and I hope you, gentlemen, will always set your face against it. Tea, to be useful, should be first of an Black China Tea the Indian Tea which is being cultivated has become so powerful. in its effects upon the nervons system that a cop of it taken early in the morning, as many do, so disorders the nervous system that those who take it actually get into a state of tea intoxication, and it produces a form of nervous disturbance, which is most painful to witness. If you want to have, either for yourselves or lor your patients, tea which will not injure and which will refresh. get Black China Tea, putting In the right measure—the old fashioned teaspooeful for each person and one for the blessed pot. Then pour on briskly boiling water, and within eve minutes you most pour It off again, or it will become wicked instead of good." Such is Sir Andrew Clarke's opinion and advise. A few words of warning, however, are necessary to those who have for gotten what this old fashioned ea is like. PLEASANT PARAGRAPHS.

A sane:wan and comic writer cannot possibly be said to be over weak or feeble in his joke; for he is always pun-gent. DID you ever know a young lady who would admit the bosomest of her bosom friends to be "very pretty ?" HIGHLY COMPLIMENTARY. —BPOWII—" You never 'found me out in lie; did ye, Smith ?" Smith—" No, Brown, I've invariably found you at home in 'em." WE are twitted with being a mercenary nation, and one of shopkers. There is no doubt the most Important shareholders in the country are the plough-share holders. Musanoom growing has been recommended for agriculturalists. As it is, agriculture is in such a state to-day that there is mush-room for improve- ment. PEOPLE who would inflict chastisement upon inanimate things are often called fools for their , pains ; and yet how often we hear of sensible ' people putting their hats on "the rack." RIDDLE-ICULOPSNESS. Why should one na- turally expect to receive civility from a parish clerk ?—Why, because, don't you see? he is sure to be well versed in the amen-ities of life. A CONSIDERATION.—G.O.M.—" You'll keep 'em quiet, Parney, my boy; won't you, for my sake ?" Parnell—" Oh, ah, it's all very well say, Keep 'ern quiet;' but what'll my friends in America say?" REAL RARE RIDDLE. —Why must an Alderman of the city of London, when he is unable to satis factorily accomplish his "forty winks" after dinner, be necessarily in a miserable frame of mind ?—Why, because, you see, he is—ahem 1— un-nappy. SIGNS OF THE END OF THE SEASON. —Trix (to Prudentia, elder sister)—" Prue, dear, aren't you pretty nearly sick of lawn tennis? Why do we do it ?" Prudentia—" Well—you don't understand— but it's about the only game we can play—with men." Trix—" Bother men 1" SIB HENRY Tnomrsoa holds that artificial teeth are an evil in those of advanced years, because they enable such persons to masticate flesh. When the teeth fail naturally, it is Nature's design that the individual should subsist on vegetable diet. "I AM afraid all these children are a great deal of trouble to you," said a minister to a mother who had children of all ages about her and who was far from strong. "Oh, no, sir," she said, "children aren't trouble; they're only fatigue." SIR GEORGE WARRENDER was once obliged to put off a dinner-party in consequence of the death of a relative, and sat down to a haunch of venison by himself. While eating, he said to his butler, "John, this will make a capital hash to-morrow." "Yes, Sir George, U you leave off now 1" "GRANDMA, have you seem the coinage 4he Government are now making—three pieces to a penny ?" asked a young Hopeful bone for the holidays. "No," said the old lady, with much interest; "what are they like?" "Two farthings and a halfpenny," answered the graceless youngster. He raised his hat to one, and the other said, "Do you know that gentleman ? " "Oh, yes," the other replied. "Lila mother was my mother's only child." What relation was the gentleman to the lady? The moral in obvious. A fellow with ears like • that should fold them over the top of his head. ONCE a careless man went to the cellar and stuck the candle in what he thought was a keg of black sand. He sat near it drinking wine until the candle burned low. Nearer and nearer it got to the black ,and, nearer and nearer, until the blaze reached the black sand—and, as it was nothing but black sand, nothing happened. Why, her bonnets make me Look like a fright!" MISS CLARA : "Do you think, Mr. Featherly, that Miss Smith, whom we met last evening, is a very plain person?" Doesn't iverybody know that they get a round hole an' pour a lot ov iron round it 1" (hr a Sunday lately a Presbyterian congregation, worshipping in an ancient pile, were somewhat tickled to observe their precentor cease singing In the middle of a verse' and hear him give out the following line for the special edification of someone in his immediate vicinity:—" I say, Betsy, woman, you're singing the wrang tune," and then resume his avocation with as solemn a countenance as if nothing particular had occurred. LINENDRAPERS' shops in the country are some- times the scenes of ludicrous conversations. The other day a young lady stepped into one and in- quired of a very good-looking assistant, "Sir, have you any mouse-coloured ladies' gloves?" " Mouse- coloured ladies, miss?" "Yes, a sort of grey; just the colour of your drawers there," meaning the shop drawers, which were paiuted grey. •My drawers, Miss!" ejaculated the young man—" my drawers, Miss! why, I don't wear any 1" The young lady was carried home on a shutter. "My uncle has just voluntarily sent me a cheque for 25 dohs." "Where is the bad luck about that?" "You see I was just going to borrow nO dole. from him, and now I can't in decency do it. The old scoundrel has headed me off. I've been fleeced out of 25 dols. by the old villain." A YOUNG MAN dropped into the office of a Dakota • itwyer and said, "What is a habeas corpus?" We are authorised to state that a post-card con- taining answers to a series of questions submitted by the Fabian Society and purporting to bear the signature of Mr. Gladstone was not despatched by Mr. Gladstone. The signature, if resembling his, is a forgery. .

Mr. Isaac Holden, M.P. for West Yorks, who cele- brated his eighty-fifth birthday last Saturday, is a veritabl6 Parliamentary evergreen. He is a small wiry man with keen blue eyes, and of erect stature. He has scarcely a grey hair, and looks well under sixty and somewhat juniur to his son-in-law, Mr. Illingworth, M.P., who is in his sixty-seventh year.

Mr. Holden has had a chequered experience in public life. He eat as a Raaical in Parliament from 1865 to 1868. Then again, after a lapse of fourteen years and three unsuccessful contests, he re-entered the Bouso in 1882, and has sat con- tinuously ever since, and will,his numerous friends hope, remain in Parliament to promote Radical measures for many years to come.

A "round robin" is being circulated on the Con- servative side of the House of Commons pointing out to Mr. Balfour the inconvenience of the uncer- tainty as to the date of the dissolution, and in- timating that the signatories are not able to pledge themselves to remain in attendance at Westminster through the month of July. The communication is being extensively signed.

Our proximity to the General Election is shown by the activity of the Tory agents in London. Ly- ing leaflets are being scattered broadcast. Little complaint need be made against these falsehoods. ' They are of the thorough kind which defeat their own object. He must be a numskull who would believe the Tories have passed all the legislation for the good of the working classes or that that party has a monopoly of political virtues.

The acquiescence of the Government in Mr. Bryce's resolution on the subject of access to moun- tains was understood at the time to be given in order to shield Ministerial candidates in Scotland from the awkwardness of being heckled on this point. No steps have yet been taken to give effect to the unanimous opinion of the House expressed on that occasion. Mr. Bryce will take an early op- portunity of reminding the Government of the pledge implied in theit acceptance of the resolution.

"Wild, wicked, and wanton," was how Mr. Her- bert Gladstone, on Monday night, in Hackney characterised Lord Salisbury's seditious speech. If Ulster, acting on the Premier's suggestion, rebelled, Mr. Gladstone remarked that they would be pre- pared to" take the usual course.' "Thanks to a systematic policy of Coercion in Ireland there are plenty of prisons, and rebellious Orangemen could he put into the cells occupied by distinguished Nationalists." Mr. Gladstone thinks that if Ulster fights against Home Rule she will be much more I foolish than he takes her to be.

Lord Deerhurst has just left Englend for a new and prolonged " trek " in darkest Mashonaland. During his last flying visit to this country his lord- ship was engaged in .the preparation of a book of African travels which should be interesting when it appears. He has "done" Mexico and other un- imaginable places, roughing it with the roughest in the goldfields of N. Australia. He is of the purely .Saxon type, middle-sized, no hair on the face, and a frame suggesting the ideal of toughness and " staying" powers.

An interesting feature of the book will be Lord Deerhurst's contact with Lord Randolph Churchill in his amateur African adventures. His account of the member for Paddington's exploits will prove very entertaining. Here is an extract from Lord Deerhurst's diary :—" Oct. 5. I went to see Ran- dolph to-day. I think him an extremely rude man, but I am told it is only his manner, and that I am treated better than most men. I wonder that some of the men don't go for him. He has got himself into very hot water over here, and is very unpop- ular. 7 Oct. Randolph sales are on, and lam very busy buying things. At one of his sales he put up some tea which he said was given him by the Queen. The Boers at once took on, and it was sold for some- thing like .24 per lb. His sales lasted four days, and pecuniarily, I should say, were a success, but they made him more unpopular than before owing to his tremendous stinginess. He stood there, bullying the auctioneer, and allowing no one to have a say except himself, and he.insulted nearly everyone he came across."

During the Duke of Connaught' s stay in London, in order to hold the second Levee of the season, he will stay in the suite of apartments in Buckingham Palace which has been granted to him by the Queen for the term of her life. These rooms are on the south side of the palace, and look out on Bucking- ham gate. The Palace gardens are now one blaze of tulips of every colour. The trees are all out, and so big are the gardens, and so dense the foliage, that the lake in the centre seems as if it were in the heart of the country instead of in the centre of the capital.

Mr, G. H. Hibbs, the Premier of New South Wales, who will be in London a few weeks hence, has been overhauling the accounts of his predeces- sor, Sir Henry Parkes. He reports the discovery of "unauthorised expenditure" to the amount of £641,930, amongst which there is a curious little item of £48.5 for a bust of Lord Salisbury. What the Sydney people want to know is why Sir Henry Nikes was in such a hurry to saddle the country l with a bust of the Tory Premier that he could not wait to get the item sanctioned by Parliament? This sort of toadying is a lamentable anti-climax to the career of a man who was a Birmingham Char- tist in his early manhood.

The Irish Industrial Village promises to be one of the most. popular attractions of the Exposition at Chicago. It will realise to the American public the actualities of cottage labour ani hand indus- tries, as carried on in the remote country and con- gested districts of Ireland, in a way not otherwise possible; for it is intended to send over the very peasants with their simple looms and dye pots, their" sprigging" frames and lace pillows, and to show how deftly Irish fingers can work with the most primitive of appliances. A committee has been formed, consisting of Lady Aberdeen, Mrs. Ernest Hart, and Mr. Peter White to carry this practical and picturesque idea into effect.

There was a sense of the fitness of things in the selection of the Duke of Connaught to open the Horticultural Exhibition on Saturday. The special 'tabbies of his Royal Highness are military tactics and gardening. In the intervals which the Duke spends at his Surrey home—Bagshot House—he occupies himself chiefly with his garden, and, fur- nished with scissors, gloves, and other needful im- plements, affords his neighbours an edifying example of an English country gentleman, busily weeding, planting, and pruning the plants in his domain. By the way, the uncles of the late Duke of Clarence are not only wearing severely black suits and neckties, but deep mourning borders to their pocket-handkerchiefs.

-- CuHord Hall, Lord Cadogan's Suffolk property, near Bury St. Edmunds, where young Lord Chelsea took his bride on Monday, is a comfortable house just three hundred years old, for It was built by Sir Nicflolas Bacon, the first baronet of England, and half brother to Sir Francis, in 1591. The estate was at one time the chief country residence of Marquis Cornwallis, the widow of one of whose ancestors married a son of Sir Nicholas Bacon. The park is very charming, and the little church is of some interest, and was built by Sir Stephen Fox, from whom are descended the Earls et Ilchester. Lord Cadogan has added a fine new wing, which possesses every modern luxury and comfort, but hardly adds to the beauty of the old Elizabethan mansion. --

Dr. Herber Evans, in his address as President oi the Congregational Union on Tuesday, dealt with a subject now rapidly coming to the front—the unity of the Free Churches. The subject is discussed in • the Nonconformist Press, a Free Church Congress is to be held in Manchester soon, and there is a general desire for closer unity and more concerted action. Dr. Evans said that "a growing sense of the evils arising from our division is one of the most promising signs of the times. The problems of do- mestic, social, and national morality call for con- certed action." Union is desirable for these things, and also for promoting Christian brotherhood. Unio. n is alio needed for political purposes, to con- solidate the forces against disestablishment and to remove the other injustices which Dissenters suffer under existing laws.
The Queen has forwarded LS to Mrs. Isaac James, of Tredegar, who recently gave birth to triplets.

A HEARTLESS MOTHER'S CRUELTY TO [ATA, RIGHTS RESEII.VED.I HER CHILDREN. THE CURSE OF THE CALLERLEYS. At the Warrington Borough Magistrates' Court on Monday, before the Mayor (Alderman Greenall) and By LILLIAS WASSERMAN, Aldermen Francomb and Harrison, Mary Burke, wife of William Burke, of Gee-street, was charged Author of "Some Fisher Folk," "Judith," "Where with wilfully neglecting her three children on the the North Wind Blows," &c., &c. 25th of January last, by not providing them with proper food and clothing. Mr. B. Shearer proseeuted on behalf of the Board of Guardians, and said they did not intend to take any further proceedings of this description as there was now an officer appointed for the purpose for the district, but this was not an ordinary Union case. The defendant absconded on the 28th of January after the offence, and about three weeks ago came to him with an order for the workhouse, and had been there since.—P.C. Bell said en the 25th of January he found in the defendant's house a little boy, her son, aged 5 years, with nothing but a dirty shirt and an old waistcoat on, a little girl aged 5, with nothing but an old petticoat on, and no shoes or stockings, and a little boy about 6 months old lying in a cradle wrapped in an old blanket, with nothing else on. The little girl said their mother had gone away and left them, and their father was at work. There was nothing in the house, for the children to eat and not even tea or sugar. In one room there was a heap of flocks, and two bed ticks, and in another room an old mattress, but no clothing. He reported the mat- ter to Mr. Shearer.—Mr. Shearer deposed to visiting the house and finding one of the children quite naked ; and undoubtedly suffering very much: The next day when he visited them the father had clothed the children. The defendant had pawned their clothes.—The defend- ant stated that she was brutally treated by her husband, and gave him a very bad character, and Inspector Spinks deposed to taking her home for admission when she complained he had locked her out, and he said she had gone out of her own accord. She charged him then with keeping her several nights in the back yard and he did not deo), it. He said "the children are all right now, and I wan't nothing more to do with her." tie was a steady hard-working man.—Mr. Shearer gave the same testimony as to the husband's character.—The defendant was sent to prison for a month's hard labour.

CHAPTER XL THE TEMPTATION OF JACK BREAMISH. Silvia Callerley's sad voice and frightened looks, ever since the night upon which the Bonny Bess was lost, had haunted Jack Brea.mish persis- tently. What a melancholy change had come over her in little more than a year's time ! He recalled with delight and yet with sadness the impression she had made upon him at their first meeting. She had come to him with the sunshine and the flowers, and had seemed exquisitely in harmony with them and with the pleasant spring time. A pretty, dimpled, childish creature, brimful of mirth and gladness. He went over that meeting many a time • dwell- ing upon all its details; and remembering the most trifling incident, in a way that would certainly have filled her with surprise, had she ever become cognisant of it. Her helpless terror, as she sat on a big stone in the middle of Yarrop Burn, with the water swirl- ing by, and how she cried much in the same sort of fashion as a child might have done. Strange now was it to remember that his first 'sensation upon noticing her there was one of vexation, because her presence might spoil his best fishing ground, and because the pool where he had fondly reckoned to catch a big trout napping, was ruffled and dis- turbed. Little knew he then what lay before him, and what an important position in his life she would monopolise. All the big trout in Yarrop Burn might swim in peace, and small heed would he now pay to them if Silvia Callerley were by. With surprise, he recalled the fact that on that occasion he had positively held her in his arms and carried her to the shore. And this without the slightest feeling or emotion whatever, while now— why now the very memory of the fact sent a thrill of fearful, half guilty delight through his sensee. Quite as emotionless had he been when he de- manded a kiss for payment. What wondrous dignity and hauteur the little creature had de- veloped at this impertinent proposition, and how proudly she had insisted upon his respect and deference for Lady Callerley. Then he smiled as he remembered how—recog- nising his foolishness, and his utter absence of any intent to insult—she had thawed again, and talked so sweetly that his heart went out to her at once, and he thought of her in much the same way as though she really was the sister he had always longed for. How tender, and gracious and sym- pathetic she was then; a revelation to him of what womanhood really meant. Up to that time he had known little of women, nothing of ladies, save in the one instance of his handsome sister-ii-law; an instance which had not an elevating or beneficial influence upon his ideas of the sex. His poverty had shut him out from most of the houses where he might have met young society; his poverty, and the fact that‘his great personal attractions made him what we now-a-days call a "detrimental." Be- sides Madam had taken care to warn prudent mothers of his taste for low company, and his care- less habits. So " Good-for-nothing-Jack Bres.mish " was left pretty much to himself and the fisher-folk: a state of things he had grown accustomed to, and never thought of grumbling at. It caused him,, however, to be all the more sus- ceptible to Silvia's charm of manner; and it is per- chance some excuse for the state of mind into which he had gradually drifted. There is nothing so con- ducive to the passion of love as solitude, leisure, and the concentration of interest upon one person of the opposite sex.. Homceopathy may be practised with marvellous success, even upon the most ob- stinate cases of this capricious disease. But Jack never even spoke to another woman ; and as he was at the age when one must love somebody, the re- sult was exactly what might have been expected and foreseen. To himself, however, it must in justice be stated, that it was totally unexpected and surprising, and his disgust at his own feelings was only equalled by the anger he felt at Sir Lancelot's conduct towards Silvia. What did the latter mean by speaking to his wife in a hitter contemptuous fashion, such as one might use to an enemy It wail unfortunate that Jack should have been close enough to them to hear what passed between the married pair on the night of the wreck ; when Silvia went up to Sir Lancelot, and timidly faltered out her thanks for the preser- vation of Teddy's life. How differently would he, Jack Breamish, have taeated that sweet creature had fate given her to him for wife?. This daring thought leapt into his mind with a suddenness which prevented it receiv- ing the instant repulse ths.t.it ought to have met with. Silvia, his wife ! It was bewildering, intoxicating, delightful. It is never safe to dwell upon the possibility of any- thing becoming right, which at the actual time of thinking about it, is wrong.. There is an ener- vating influence arising from such thoughts that tends to soften the moral fibre, and to weaken the powers of resistance. when, temptation comes

for what might have been: The young - felloW "Was vefy simple. He was all unversed in the deep in- trieacies and subtleties of the un-tender passion. That love should ever be cruel, that it should appear not infrequently under the guise of hatred, that it should punish itself and consume itself in the fire raging within, before it woult abate an iota of its pride; these were things lie had not sufficiently studied humanity to understand. His heart began to beat more quickly at Silvia's words. She loved—who was it that she loved? This question went on repeating itself to him in an idiotic monotonous fashion, and so loudly that it prevented him hearing anything else for a few minutes. Then he awoke to the fact that Silvia was mill speaking. " Death is not always cruel. No, it is life that is cruel—cruel and mysterious, and hard to under- stand! You say Ailsie is to be pitied, and I tell you this, there are those living who envy her— envy her—because she has had her husband's whole heart, she has been loved—loved—" Silvia's voice sunk as she came to an end, and the last words 'loved—loved,' were moaned out with a soft, lingering, melancholy cadence, full of pathos. By this time they hai reached Yarrop burn; and S ' llvia weak and shaken by the excitement under which she was labouring, sat down to rest upon a big stone by the edge of the water. .Despondency followed close upon excitement, and after a mnute or so her head drooped and fell forward into her hands, held up to cover and hide I the face, wet with tell tale tears. Meanwhile a wild tumult raged within Jack's breast. She loved. Who was it that she loved? Ho threw himself upon his knees by her side, and put his trembling arm around her. He tried to speak, but it was a minute or two before he could command his voice, and even thee it sounded hoarse and unnatural. "And you, . Silvia,—clear—Cousin Silvia—you have been—you are loved too !" There must have been something strange in his tone, for it pierced even through Silvia's pre- occupied mind, though fortunately she did not recognise its full signilicance. Jack was fond of her, and Jack was sorry for her. She had betrayed herself, but there could surely be no harm in trust- ing him? She took her hands away from her face, and Jack could see the tears- upon it quite plainly. "Oh, if I could only believe it? You say so to please me, because you are kind-hearted, and be- cause you sae that the want of Lancelot's love is killing me." I He who was kneeling by her side, started when she said this, and in a very gentle fashion withdrew his arm. She looked up at him. Oh, no, I do not mean that, Cousin <Tack, clear Cousin -Jack! Ido not mean that.you would ever say what you do not really believe. But I love him so—oh, you do not understand how dearly I love him. I did not recognise it until he was offended, because I said horrid things to him, and he turned from me in anger. And. now—now I believe I shall die unless he loves me! Tell me how to make him care for me—do now, there's a- dear cousin !" With one of her sudden changes, Lady Callerley had in the last sentence thrown aside her deeper and- more tragic mood, and the "do now' was coaxing and childish in the extreme. By this time Jack Breamish was completely master of himself. The temptation—the one great temptation of his life—had luckily been withdrawn before he yielded to it irrevocably. Now that the mad fit was over, he was sick, sorry, ashamed.; God forgive him! He was not good enough even to be near her, and yet, in her innocence and; un- happiness, she appealed to him for advice and. for help. He groaned in spirit at the irony of fate, bat fortunately managed to show no traces of- his troubled mind.. Silvia wondered slightly at his exceeding pallor, but when he caught her glance, he smiled, and the effect of sadness and pain was gone at once. It cost him much to summon that poor smile, but the effort did him good. "What a question to ask me, Cousin Silvia !" he replied, in a light and flippant tone, "What should a bachelor know of the troubles and perplexities of married life—at least a bachelor of my sort, who is—is shut out from any—any—well—any chance of that-kind of happiness ?" He tried to say who has never been in love," but the lie stuck in his throat. "Dear Lady Callerley, he will love you, he mast love-you, even. if he does- not do so already; of which fact I an/ by no means certain. Some people are by nature undemonstrative ; and the Callerleys, as you know, are a strange race. They are so proud, so reserved, so fearful of misconstruction; that they appear cold when in reality possessed by very deep and iutense feelings. They can hide fiery passions beneath a calm exterior "—here Jack was painfully cognisant of his handsome sister-in. law's peculiarities of temper—" and doubtless your hurhand thinks it better so to hide the great affec- tionr he has for-you from the world, while hoping that you yourself know and trust him too com- pletely ever to- doubt it!" Lady Callerley laughed a trifle scornfully, though sheovas grateful. fee' the kindness prompting this pomible explanation. You talk, like a book, cousin! I only wish ' that I could think as you do. But then you see you do .not know all the circumstances, and I cannot I very well explain—it is too humiliating !" ilvia meant here that Sir Lancelot had married her out of pity; and to save her from poverty, an idea which galled and stung whenever it recurred to her, as of, course it did with a frequeney and persistence only found in unpleasant subjects. " Expla n nothing, please explain nothing tarther, ' licoke in Jack with haste. He was keenly conscious of his false poeition, and felt as though he could beat no- more. His heart was sore o and' his head waa,throbbing, poor fellow! Oh, to be able to rush away alone—anywhere— anywhere—so- that he need not longer keep up this ghastly farce of uninterested adviser and com- forter. He was too. young to play the part properly, and ;it came hard to him to dissemble. He had to toy over and over again to himself these words, "-!t is for Silvia, it is all for Silvia. She must not be made more, unhappy." "It wilt be sure to come right in the end, dear Lady Callerlee 1. Believe me, and have patience. He will love you yet 1" He railed her hand to his lips ; made some excuse to leave her, and was gone before Silvia could answer. Jack Breamiih had reached the limits. of I his endurance.

along. One day Lady Callerley and Jack met, while both were engaged upon the same errand of mercy, namely, visiting the bereave& Just at this time the village, was a scene of per- petual wailing and desolation. The sea had begun to give spits dead; and from house after house the bread winners were carried to their last resting places bathe old churchyard of Callerley, where still the ocean could croon lullabies to them, in its remorseful moods. For the sea has moods and passions and rages and rernorses like a sentient creature, to the people who live by and upon it. It may not rejoice with those who rejoice, but they hold that of a certainty it mourns with these who MOUTIL Mourning and feasting go hand in hand. It would ill become those left to withhold the right of a " menseful funeral" to those gone before. However poor the cottage may be, some semblance to a feast must seeds take place within.% its walls, when the last sad rites have been paid ; when the coffin has been carried out, and a dirge sung over its melancholy journey. It was at the door of old, Carr 's house that Silvia and. Jack chanced upon each other. Thither had poor Bill's body been carried, so that proper honour should, be paid to it; and the young widow Ailsie was very determined that everythhig about the funeral should be done decently and in order. It comforted her stimewhat for the loss she hall sustained that people should say it was the grandest funeral ever held in Breamish ; and that Mr. Wynne himself should honour it by being present, and that Lady Callerley came down to condole with her on the following day.. "You have been to see Ailsie, then ?" said Jack, as he greeted Silvia solemnly, and they walked on side by side. "She is to be pitied, poor little lass. They were true lovers undoubtedly, and they, had been married so short a time that they, bad ,not grov matter of fact over their happiness.," This was an awkward speech, but Jack also recognised the awkwardness of it too late. "She is to be pitied. Ali, yes I" said Silvia, thoughtfully, "to be pitied because she has lost the husband she loved—the husband who loved her 1 But how if she had never known the happiness she mourns for--how if she had never been one, heart and soul, with him who is gone?" Jack watched hen closely as she spoke, and could see clearly enough that it was of ho hypothetical, case she was thinking. She had half forgotten the. fact of his Fesinee ; and pursued,, as though alone, her sad train of thought. "Death 1 Is that the worst that can befall true lovers? No, no, there are partings far sadder and infinitely more irremediable than those brought about by death. If love is true it must be immor- tal, and if one had ever really known it, one would care nothing for the short separation life would mean. It would merely be a sleep and then,—and then .when one awoke, it would be still together through all eternity." These words were a great surprise to Jack. it did not seem possible that this was little Silvia Callerley, the childish creature who had been in his thoughts. Through the sadness of the speech thrilled an intensity, a passion, utterly at variance with all he had hitherto known of her. A beautiful, cap- ricious, wayward, yet affectionate girl he had judged her. But these words—they were the heart hot utterances a a woman. A woman who had lived and suffered--ay, and loved also. Who was it that she loved? Her husband? Jack remembered the looks and words he had seen and heard pass between them, and could scarcely credit the possibility of Sir Lancelot having inspired any very warm affection in his wife's bosom ; spite of the piteous cry of "(ionic back. Lancelot! that—might only_ke regret
CHAPTER XIX A SUPPER AT THE HALL,

When things were at the worst with the Breamish household, and when horses mid dbogs had been sold in order to stave off the most pressing of his creditors, the squire fell in for a legacy from a distant relative ; a legacy of suffieient importance to set him on his feet once more. He • might --had he been a wise man—have lived comfortably upon the increased income derived from),this windfall; but unfortunately there are persons upon whom experience has no educating Influence whatever, and the poor squire was of these; wherefore in place of paying off, his debts, and taking care of the rest of ,his capital; or using it judiciously for the sorely needed repairs on his estate, he began throwing money to right and to left, in the reckless manner peculiarly his own. His stables were partly re-built, and stocked with expensive cattle; new men were hired as grooms and stable helpers, and old hangers on had their wages raised. To be sure this last extravagance was more than excusable, since some of the poor fellows had been paid nothing for a considerable time; and certainly deserved a recompense for their leniency. Under the influenoe of this unexpected prosperity the mercurial spirits of Squire Brearnish rose to the highest point. Ever open-handed and generous, he appeared to, fancy that his newly-replenished purse was incap- able of exhaustion. He was now able to indulge to their fullest ex- tent his sporting tendencies "I mean to have the best stud in the north, and nothing less will content me, by Jupiter 1" he would declare to his head groom, walking restlessly about the stables and yard, and discussing with gusto the points of his several horses; and the groom, while inwardly scoffing at such an insane ambition—for the wideawake little man, having been trained in a great Yorkshire racing stable, knew what an un- attainable ideal this would prove—would nod his head, and swear that the squire was in the right of it in this resolve. If his master chose to ruin him- self over the business it was useless to try and dis- suade. Besides there would be the more pickings for a shrewd, capable man, who had the manage- ment of things. And what of Madam, and her clear head and capacity for business matters? She had become so one idead in her mad and vin- dictive hatred of Lady Callerley that nothing else

AN IRISH STORY. Some years ago when Ireland was in a more dis- turbed state than it is at present, and murders, agrarian outrages, and other crimes were more eommon, a Mr. Scott, who resided in the western part of Tipperary, was entertaining a number of friends at dinner. Amongst the guests was one named Hunt, who had the reputation of being a man of more than ordinary courage, his claims to the character being the fact that be stood six feet two inches in his stockings, that he always travelled alone and armed to the teeth and was loud in speech as to his being ready for all comers. His host, Scott, was a small but compact man, who was loved by rich and poor, gentle and simple. Ile always had a joke for his acquaintances. After dinner the conversation turned on the state of the country, and how much worse their own county was than any other. "Come, Hunt," said Scott, "tell us if it be true that you carry a small armoury in your driving seat?" " Not exactly an armoury, Scott," replied Hunt, "but I do carry a brace of pistols or two in my dog cart. I think I should be prepared in case of necessity ; and,should I be attacked,shall use them without the slightest eompunction." " Why, my dear fellow, you don't expect they will attack you ?" exclaimed Scott in pretended astonishment. " Well, perhaps not ; but it is better to be pre- pared for these fellows. Look at poor Waller's case; they were not satisfied with one there. The ruffians killed the whole family.: " Yes, indeed, that is true,' replied Scott. " But, Hunt, though I don't make bets usually, I'll lay you fifty pounds, and Bassett shall hold the stakes that the first man who attempts to rob you of your money or your pistols, when you are travelling in this armed-to-the-teeth style succeeds. What say you, is it a bet ?" "Really, my dear Scott, it is a strange wager, returned Hunt, but I'll take it." The money was deposited in Hassett's hands, his eyes twinkling with merry humour. "What are you up to ? ? said he to Scott, as the latter placed his stakes in Ilassett's hands. "Never mind," replied Scott. The subject then dropped, and the entertainment went on in real Irish style. Shortly afterwards, Scott excused himself for a few motnentsrand had a short consultation with his head groom. "Saddie Grapeshot," was his last order before returning to his guest," and take him down to the fir clumps." On rejoining his friends, Scott found that Bunt, who had a long distance to go to reach his home, was preparing for a start, and bad ordered his dog- cart; and, after finishing his punch,he rose to wish his friends " Good night." Hunt left the house, and was soon heard :outside looking to his pistols and other weapons of his "armoury." This done, he started in his dog-cart, and drove down the rather long and dreary avenue leading from Scott's house. It was very dark, so, that he could not see many yards before him. Suddenly he noticed a man on horseback riding towards him. What or who could it be ?- Probably' the police patrol. He was, however, soon' in-

formed. "Stop !" exclaimed the horseman, in a rich brogue, tiding up to Hunt, and levelling a pistol at his bead. " Stop !or I'll put daylight through yet big carcase !" Hunt pulled up all in a flutter, and began feeling for a pistol, his nervousness showing bow muck use it would be when he tound it. "bibo !" cried out the highwayman, "are yo don't kepe them hands ov yer's off that pistol-case,. rfiailow the brains of yer's out this minnit. Come, Misther Hunt, I want any small silver or gould ye may have; ye may keep the notes. Come, sir, git down, an bout& yer horse's head while I takes thins; quick Misther Hunt, tbe patherole 'll be round soon ; down wid ye 1"' Trembling with fear, he did as he was desired, and gave up his money and his watch to the robber, while he permitted the latter to search his dog-oart for arms. But what was the unfortunate Hunt's astonish- ment when he saw the thief deliberately take out the pistols and coolly fire them off, one by one in quick succession. Hunt was completely duLb- founded at this audacity. The fellow would alarm the neighbourhood, and very likely bring down the constabulary or military, who were at no great distance. Nor was he mistaken, for Scott's guests, ' hearing the rapid discharge of firearms, after call- ing in vain for their host, seized every imaginable ' weapon they could find in the hall and rushed down the avenue, there to behold the rather extra- ordinary scene formed by Haut, the robber, and ' their horses. Hunt could not understand the robber's quietly remaining to be arrested, and naturally supposed he must have some assistance at hand. But the mystery was soon solved,as the highway- I man, bursting into a hearty fit of laughter, ex- ' claimed, " Bassett, my boy, hand over the cash; I've won my bet. See! I've cleaned out Hunt with this ? " So saying, Scott, for it was he, held up the key of the hall door. The burst of laughter that followed this dis- sovery was only equalled by the ebagrin of the un- fortunate victim. At first Hunt was furious,but his courageous character had suffered 80 severely that his anger only caused more merriment. "Come," said Scott, " you are my prisoner, and you must return with me. Everything is iair in war or love, and I had a right to take my own means to win my bet." The others joined their host in making peace,and Hunt was brought back to the house, but his repu- tation for bravery was gone for ever.

Rven little Lance was shamefully neglected; and the pooe boy; finding both parents absorbed and unapproachable, would have fared badly, had it not been for the Watchful care and tenderness of Uncle Jack! Poor Lance! He missed exceedingly his bright, companion and playfellow, Lady Callerley. ' Nature took a strange revenge for the crimes his mother had committed-by instilling within Silvia's mind a feeling of dislike and repulsion towards innocent little Lance. Ever since her baby's death Lady Callerley could not bear the boy to come near or to touch her. it was an unateoUntable , and one ot *bleb she was rather ashamed ; but axe very sen- sitive to adverse or the opposite influences, axild Lance knew, without a single word being spoken en either side, that her liking for him had vanished. Be was a right loyal little fellow, and he still wor- RlZshipped Silvia, and thought her the most delightful beautiful creature the world held; so he bore the pain of her aversion in silence and uncomplain- ingly, and was still ready to love and serve her whenever and wherever she chose. He knew of nothing he had done to change her feeling or to offend her in any way; but since the sight of him annoyed her so, he kept persistently away from Seaton-Callerley, inventing all manner of excuses, rather than tell the truth, and say, "Silvia does not care for me any longer; so, as I love her dearly, I must not vex her with my presence !" Many a night he puzzled his poor little brain to try and find out the reason of the change; but all in vain. He used to look up at the picture of the angel that he fancied resembled his pretty lady, as though it might help him if it would! But the angel only smiled its placid, inhuman, super-celestial smile, and continued unmoved by his pathetic looks of appeal; until at length he fell asleep, out of sheer weariness and wonderment of spirit. Uncle Jack was unhappy in those days also, and was exceedingly glad to have the lad's company. It comforted him somewhat and eased the pain at his heart, when the young creature clung about him with adoring affection and trust. Many a long day these two passed together, and they did each other no end of good; being both affectionate, and inno- cent, and simple natured. Well would it have been for Jack lireamish had the squire done the right thing by him, and doim it at once. If he could have had his commission now and gone off to join his regiment—since he was too old. to enter the navy save as a Volunteer—a service which he would have infinitely preferred—in the active round of duties and drill he might have found solace ; and at any rate would most certainly have escaped much mischief. But the Squire,.beins of a dilatory, disposition, kept putting off this his bounden duty; from day to .day; while his intentions towards Jack were ever of the kindest and best. When at last it was settled, andthe young fellow was to go, the Squire—who had never honoured him before in any such fashion—must needs honour him now with a farewell supper. To this festivity all the choice spirits of the neighbourhood were invited. Riddel of Thornyrigg, the hardest and most daring rider in the county; Will Forster of Whin- ton, with his baritone voice and his boisterous laugh; Tom Scott, the mad sqirire of Black-end Foot; these and a dozen other rollicking roystering swains, promised a lively meeting. Why the Squire should have invited Sir Lancelot Callerley to meet them, or for what reason Sir Lancelot should have accepted such invitation was inexplicable to most of these men. Teddy Wynne was to be there, of course. Teddy was the source of unbounded merriment to these rough riding North-countrymen. Nothing like him had ever been met with in those, parts before. He had made himself exceedingly pleasant to Squire Breamish, who swore that "if Lady Caller- ley was a pocket Venus, by Jove-, her brother was most certainly a pocket Apollo, or whatever that fellow's name was who played.= the Jew's harp, and bewitched the women-folk." If Teddy did not play on the Jew's harp, he could at all events whistle like a laveroek, and produce some wonderful music out of a coffee-pot, playing upon the spout as on a flute, and he could also sing the newest convivial songs, and tell stories of the raciest description, anent many leaders of fashion- able society, known only by name hereabouts, if known at all? But Sir Lancelot's gloomy visage—for gloomy it undoubtedly was at this time—was a decided set off against Teddy's good company, and probably the squire "simply invited the farmer out of cour- tesy, half-hoping for a refusal. If so, he was doomed to disappointment. The truth is, Sir Lancelot's jealousy was all aglow and eager for fuel to feed its flame; and sought the said fuel with a persistence worthy of a better cause. Jack Breamish never went to Seaton-Callerley in those days. He knew his own weakness, and was afraid, with an hoisest and-wholesome fear. A much better thing it xe as for him to shun tempta- tion than to daily with it; and poor Jack, when once he recognised what the right was, alway tried to do it. Surely then, with) such a state of things Sir Lancelot Callerley might have been content? This, however, waii far from being the case. With the curious ingenuity of all self-torturers he managed to twist 'the fact of Jack's prolonged absence into a reason greater for suspicion. Evidently sometlning must have happened to drive him from the; presence of Silvia. lie would not shun her society, unless—unless what? This was a quest:ion which the baronet could not answer; but it wonried, and perplexed, and annoyed him beyond measure. kVECL Silvia's !innocent wonder at Jack's pro- longed absence dill not tend to reassure him. It might be all parti and parcel of the plot which he knew existed against his happiness. They were both deceiving ham, his wife and her lover. He was sure of it. So ihe bided his time, and watched them narrowly. When the fun at Breamish 'Hall begen to wax 1 fast and furious, Sir Lancelet sat in the midst of the revellers, cal; and sober and self-contained to all appearance; but in reality madder than the maddest there. Teddy Wynne was in good form, full of life and merriment; but Teddy could not drink glass for glass against these hard-drinking squires ; and sub- sided very soon into the depths of an arm-chair, and an uneasy slumber, disturbed by restless dreams, wherein he was first falling overboard from the deck of the Bonny Bess, and being fished up by Cuddy Widdringten, whop insisted upon him marry- ing Old Nanny by way of gratitude for the afore- said rescue; and upon his refusal threw him back into the boiling ocean, and right into the jaws of a shark; which mid shark wore a blue jersey and a sou'-wester, and bore a strong resemblance to the man who had once talked of making a meal off the little dandy—without pepper or salt. But the songs and the merriment went on with- out Teddy, and the glasses were filled and emptied again and again. "Come Jack, give us a toast! Thou art the slyest dog over thy love affairs; andyet a comely lad, with the blood running warm in his veins, as it must needs do at thy age, is surely not without a sweetheart? Out with her name, Jack, fir be , she high, or be she low, she'll serve as an exmse I for another bumper !" Thus urged Will Fortter, when all the ordinary healths had been done justice l!' to; and felling back in his chair-, he roared en; a Bacchanalian verse "A reason fair is everywhere, , While lives a comely lass; r , For Phillis neat, or Chloe sweet We'll fill a brimming glass." z [ The great, slightly hoarse baritone rang through the room, and was followed by a burst of applause. ,The sentiment was exactly suited to the audience, and went home to their hearts at once. • Now Jack Breamish had been drinking deeply , 1 all the evening, and as—spite of popular rumour 1 , which, crediting him with all the sins invention could furnish, did not . fail to add drunkenness to the list—he was usually extremely moderate in his potations, he had lost his head a little. The fact is that thelad, acutely conscious 'of an ache in the region of the heart, . a narcotic. By this; time the took the liquor as Painwashaeldtake-cen and a pleasant feeling of exhilaration its place. Had he been (rite sober be wheounlodwndeveis acted with such Imprudence as prl ahyaevde. Rather than have spokencrlight y of the woman he he would have con- worshipped aml held .sa ed ; rid yet her name rose sented to be cut to pieces to his lips, and he had spoken°. it out before he could lo cheek thepu imlse. oks upon a star cannot notice a ot He who twinkling candle," he cried, with the exaggerate gallantry of speechi then in vogue, but which said d g llantry was n this case an expression of real "so far as I am concerned there is but ding ette ; woman in the world. I give you therefore the sweetest and the fairest of ladies, Silvia, Lady Weil*"

tnimediately. opposite the speaker Sir Lanceiot was seated; and as the name passed poor Jack's foolish, babbling lips, the baronet started and half rose from his seat ; his dark eyes flashing fire. A thrill of suspense ran through those hard drinkers. Through all the country side was the Callerley temper known and dreaded, although the cpresent head of the house had not as yet prove:d his nertge bir any public display of it. . But Callerley was more of a man of the world than any of his predecessors. . He gave a quick and comprehensive glance around. ;They were all watching him breathlessly, 'expecting a storm. Recogaising the awkwardness of the situation, he controlled -himself by a great and sudden effort, though the veins on his forehead swelled like whip- cord, and his dark cheek was suffused with crim- son from, the blood which had mounted to his head. Nevertheless as he took up a decanter, and filled his glass to the brim, not a quiver or shake in the. hand betrayed emotion. . • "I am highly honoured, gentlemen" he'saul. a calm, monotonous voice, " Here's to the health of Silvia, Lady Callerley—my wife I." There were sighs and gasps, as of relief, from' those assembled; and then with one accord they rose to their feet and drank the toast right glee- fully. There were some there, however, who noted that Callerley grew even more silent after this incident, and that his eyes seemed glued to the face of young Breamish. A handsome face it was, too, and a win- some one, with a look of rofinemeiat it did not lose even under the wine flush fast overspreading it. What was he thinking of, this Sir Lancelot Callerley, most uneonvivial of revellers, as he sat there, like a mute at a funeral, and allowed the bottle to pass him again and again, without replen- ishing his empty wine glass? Was he comparing his own dark solemn visage, with that of the bright and sunny young Antinons across the table, and wondering which was the more likely to win a fair lady's favour? Who knows? At anyrate one thing is certain, that when those who were sober enough to rise from the table, left behind them those who lay ingloriously defeated; Jack Brearnish had drunk a treat deal more than was• good for him; and Sir n celot Callerley, on the contrary, was perfectly sober. In these degenerate clays it ,is difficult to under- stand that the worth of a man was then appraised in the same way as the size of. a cask, and that the • proportion of liquors which could be poured ino either increased their value; that it was then eon' sidered inhospitable to allow • a guest to leave thocii table solzer, and that even sensible, strong-inindel man were I;.fraid of exposing themselves to ridieudes by a confession of their real inclinations tewa+rhe ttemPerance, and therefore- wallowed in ":- Mire like the rest of the swine. Verily, great is Sur tyranny of fashion, even in the matter of sirnht:sB aok Breamish was not tipsy enough to BOY Rua, the and encouter his fair sister- in- s frown and cold looks in the morning ; gathering himself together as best he could, he 5% nO off en foot—in default of the horse which he did , ;wry possess—for his lonely three-mile walk uPhi' to the old farm-house where he had his little room , under the tiles. (To be continued), tb...

div.p: FOOTBALL FATALITY AT ST. HELENS,

Mr. Brighouse, county coroner, held an inquest tt at St. Helens Town Hall, on Saturday, on the body of William Ellaty, aged 14 years, son of John P.llaby, night watchman at Messrs. Pilkington's glasaworks, and who lives at 24, Raglan-st. The father stated that he had on several occasions warned his boy not to play football as it was dan- gerous, but he played on Good Friday with other boys near the Grammar School, and received a twist of the ankle. On the following day he was playing again, and got a kick on the ankle. It was not until Sunday that he complained of pain, and he was taken to DT. Davis, af the Medical Aid Association, on Monday. The boy grew worse, and Dr. Davis attended him at home until the 23rd, when he was removed to the Providence Hospi- tal„ where he died on Thursday.—William Gaskell'a b", • 13 years of age said they were playing on the Satur- day. Deceased' was dribbling the ball down, and wit- Was trying to kick it off, when they came into can- tact. Deceased afterwards said he had been kicked on the ankle, but he evidently did nOt attach much im- Portance to it as he went on playing.—The parents stated that during the boy's illness he said it was as ac- aident, and did not blame anyone.—Dr. Davis, who had made a post-mortem examination, said the twist of the ankle had nothing to do with death. The vittence 0 the kick cn the Saturday had caused inflammation of 1116 lining of the bone, accute suppuration, with entire areakdown of the tissue of tha lower leg,and subswient bloodpoisonieg„ from which he died.—The jury returned verdict in accordance with the medical evidence, add- lag that death was due to accident, and no one was to " mama.

Ratepayers o' Nyowton, Caunt yo see yore done, Wile thoose Earlesteawn messsrs Grin becose they'n won? Wile these chaps are botchin', Waint yo—caunt yo stir, Till th' owd Tax collector Knocks at yore front dur'? • • ' rtrit4 Will yo pay a shillin' Tax laid on lth' peaund, •• An' like Angels' whispers, l':01 Never make a seaund ? Will yo turn yore faces • - Cowardly to th' all, Wile yer brass is squander'd On that Public Hall? Public Hall! nay, rayther Blunderin' Job sublime! Proof o' waste an' folly Beet to th' eend o' Time! Public Hall!! Lord help us! It's a public scoff: An', like ev'ry nuisance. Wants to be " ta'n off I" It wud be a godsend, If, by gradely means, It cud be securely Blown to smithereens! Then its perpetrators Wudn't look such foos ! Wudn't sarve for ages Critics to amuse. Then, this staring folly,— This darned "suit o' close,"— Wudn't, throo God's mercy, Stink i' ey'ry nose Then, eawr Gas and Sewage Met be treated fair; An' we'd save eawr taxes, Ilevin' lots to spare But thoose Earlesteawn members, Blind ez bats er moles, • Waint be sed, until we'n Poo'd urn ovver th' coals ! Or, wen th' Reck'nin' Day cum.% An', wi' one wild sheaut, We con seek these bunglers, And—well—purr um cant! Then, eawr childre's childre, Ey'ry time they meet, Shall proneaunce this verdict— " Serve the Blunderers rest !" TIIM liyowto., God bless o'. May 13, 1891

CROWNING THE MAY QUEEN AT IIAYDOCK. The second annual festival in connection with the coronation of the Queen of the May, 'took place at Haydock on Saturday in favourable weather. The lay was extremely tine,but the strong breeze which blew along the route taken by the procession, ren- dered matters very unpleasant, owing to the clouds of dust which prevailed. The running of the steam trams also greatly interfered with the order of the procession, as many diversions had to be made in order to avoid accidents. The organisation on the field was very badly carried out in consequence of the large ,crowd of spectators breaking through the fence, and crowding the space set apart for the coronation and subsequent festivities. As a result, the comfort of the children and of many of the spectators was completely spoiled, and the festivities came to an abrupt termination after the May pole dance. It wedd be well in future if the Committee took steps to provide against such a contingency. The procession, avhich was of fair dimensions, started from a field near the Wagon and Horses hotel, about half-past two, in the following order :—Marshal, on herse back, Mr. S. Pimb- Haydock Brass Band. May Pole dancers, 'Buffalo Bill on horse back, Soldiers, Flower girls, ex- Qiraen, Miss Nellie Cunliffe -, Red Riding Hoods, Hospital nurses. Lurry with Britannia in centre, the four corners being occupied with representatives of Scotland, Ireland, Wales, and United States. Darby and Joan, servants, bakers, milkmaids in cart, engaged its dispensing milk, butchers, colliers, hewing large blocks of coal, lady cricketers, washerwomen on lorry, Zperforming the duties of wringing and ma,ngling clothes, Joiners, negro minstrels, 'newspaper boys, sword bearer Master H. Pilling, sceptre hearer Master W. Dollin, crown bearer Master R. A. Foster. Queen, Miss May Greenall, aged seven. The queen was very nicely at- tired, and bore her great honour with benoming dignity. She was seated in a brougham, drawn by a pair of horses, accompanied by her maids of honour. Misses Mary Mclntyre, May Sefton, Bertha Arnold, and Jessie Isherwood, and her pages were Arthur H. Marsh and Herbert Twist, both of whom were attired in suits of prune velvet. The line of march tvas 'from the field to the Toll bar and back as far as ale Ram's Head hotel, where a turn was made for the field. Cn arrival at the field "Ally Sloper " amused the spectators by taking copious draughts of " Ensweetened." The coronation was then proceeded with, the queen being crowned while seated on a gorgeously made throne, by Miss Nellie Cunliffe, the ex-queen, the band afterwards playing the ." National Anthem." The effect, however, was spoiled by the break- ing in. The plaiting of the maypole ribbons was I then proceeded with and gone through with excellent 'precision, the dancers having beee trained by Mr. John Ralphs. The ladies' cricket match had be be abandoned. Prizes were awarded for the best turnouts of horses, as follows:—l. Messrs R. Evans and Co., (W. Carter driver) ; 2, John Cawley ; 3, Wm. Balharry. • Pony races for the " May Queen "steeplechase took place and the awards were as follows : 1, Kay's " Jock, " 2, McEwon's, "Madame D'Albany." 3, Mer- cer' "Romping Girl," but a protest was lodged against the winner. Dancing should have been indulged in un- til dusk, but owing to the disorganised state of the field this part of the programme wasnot carried out.
MIT FESTIVAL AT GOLBORNE.
A PICTURESQUE SCENE.

The advent of the annual May Festival at Gol- borne, on Saturday, was the occasion, the weather being most propitious, of the usual thronging of pleasure seekers by ordinary and special trains to witness the modern revival of the antique spectacle and ceremonies so picturesquely associated in the mind with the merry England of pre-Puritan times. In front of the residences of the parents of the ex- Queen of the May aid the Queen elect there were artistic floral disp'ays,and flags were exhibited here and there at convenient points of vantage through- out the main streets. There was, indeed, a general air of holiday mirthfulness about the place, which showed that the ideal of the old-time merry England was meant to be approximated to so far as that part of it was concerned, and so far as modern conditions would admit, for the afternoon at least. The children who were to take part in the festivities assembled, between two and three o'clock, in the Recreation Ground, where the usual coronation and other ceremonies were to take place, and a most diversified and motley pageant they con- stituted. There were natty little flower girls with baskets of flowers daintily hung on their arms; there were hospital nurses with their white aprons and mob caps looking, as they tripped lightly over the green. the impersonation of neat-handed Phil- lises for nursing services.; there were little Red Rid- ing Roods in numbers which would have made bounteous meals for an army of rapacious wolves of the kind described in the nursery legend. A num- ber of the latter children, too young to walk, had to be conveyed to the field in lurries, and a cur- ious sight they presented huddled together, in their red cloaks and caps,and with their heads just above the sides of the carts, looking like so many beds ef animated poppies being driven about the field. Boy soldiers in blue uniform with red military facings and with miniature martial equipments, in the way of toy swords and guns, were so numerous that it was evident that there had been small difficulty in recruiting them for the occa- sion. There were sailors, too, to be seen, but in such small numbers as to suggest that the maritime instinct was not very strong in Golborne. In full keeping with the new usage among working-men of dedicating May Day to industrial demonstrations, there were hosts of juveniles to be seen in various parts of the field repre- senting various descriptions of trades and indus- tries. There were bakers with their paper caps, and snow white aprons, butchers with aprons and cleavers, blacksmiths, joiners, shoemakers, and others ; and there were colliers with blackened. faces, and cerrying picks and safety lamps. Then there were little girls in picturesque costumes as gipsy dancers; and there were others arrayed as lady hunters and mounted on fine-looking steeds. The grotesque element was by no means wanting. There were troops of littletoy negroes, and there was a repre- sentative of Ally Sloper, riding on a donkey cart, the [juveniles finding rare diversion in his nasal longitude and antics. In another conveyance appeared a lively representative of Mother Hubbard, and old women with long pipes, represented by young women whose light- hearted merry laughter at themselves and each other but ill accorded with their get-up, were scattered about the field. A real Donnybrook-Fair looking Irish- man, with battered hat, shillelagh, and long pipe, was to be seen promenading about the field ; and everywhere as one wandered about one came across some quaint, fantastic, or picturesque looking indivi- duality; adult or juvenile. A striking feature in the pageant, or revel, as it might be called, was a lurry on which on a raised dais stood a young girl ,(Miss Sarah Ellen Cook) representing Britannia, about her being children who represented Ireland, Scotland, and Wales. A little girl in Highland costume took the part of Cale- donia.; another girl standing by her typifying Wales by wearing the well-known tall conical hat so dear to the female denizens of the Cambrian hills. A little boy in front of the lurry carried proudly a green flag, with the Irish harp in yellow ppen it. The ex-Queen Miss Elizabeth Tither, and the Queen-elect, Miss Francis Eckersley, daughter of the late Mr. Ellers Eckers- ley, formerly of the Railway Hotel, Golborne, were being driven about the field in carriages the beheld of all beholders, the latter young lady arrayed in a silk turquoise dress, trimmed with swan's down, and wearing a tulle veil and silk sleeves and stockings to match. Two mounted members of Lord GF.rrad's yeomanry cavalry from Ashton rode immediately front of her carriage and two more came behind. She was also attended by pages and escorted by her sceptre and sword bearers, Masters Robert John Price, and William Parr, and beefeaters, Masters Ellis Eckersley and Tons Underwood. The maids of honour follewed in another carriage. The field was almost encircled with an array of caravans, shooting booths, and other attractions, so that on its outskirts it presented all the appearance of an animated fair. The children were marshalled in , procession in the field, and proceeded by way of Grundy I Legh, Peter, Heath, High, and Churchastreets, to the Smithies,then returned to the recreation ground, by way of Bridge-st., entering the ground at Caupce s Court. The Golborne band, the Ashton-lane Brown band, and the Firs-lane band,also the Hindley Green rnorris dancers were present in the field and in the procession, and enhanced mush the enjoyableness of the affair with excellent music and artistic dances. A maypole had been erected in the centre of the field, and on the proces- sion returning there was some pleasing dancing by the Elindley Greer, Morris dancers and a troop of little girl gipsy dancers ;" and then came the maypole dances, under the conductorship of Mr. John Dearden, by a number of children dressed in white, the May Queen watching the festivities from her throne erected clo-e 'The coronation procession to the foot of the throne and the crowning of the May Queen by the ex-queen afterwards took place, and the National Anthem was then struck up by the Firs-lane band. Morris arid gipsy " dancing, to the strains of the Golborne band, subsequently took place, and some extraordinary feats • of strength were exhibited by Ajax "the conotierer of Sampson." after which the bands played for dancing • till dusk. The names of the committee by whom the festivities were carried out and who deserve every credit for their management were :—Messrs. E. Last (chair- man). J. Unsworth, T. Mort, J. Bate, J. Helsel!, J. Byrom, .T. Wakefield, sen., J. Wakefield, jun., W. Rat- tershY, J. Clayton, P. Cook. and G. D. l'itt, Dr. Dobb, M.C., Mr. Alfred Caunce, treasurer ; and Mr. Joseph Sankey, secretary. The children who took part in the proceedings must have numbered not far from a thousand, whilst the visitors equalled this number thrice
ARCHDEACON'S VISITATION AT

WARRINGTON PARISEI CIiI7RCM At Warrington Parish Church, on Wednesday, the wc,rdens and sidesnaen appointed in Warrington and district at the recent vestry meetings were sworn in to their offices. A short service was con- ducted by the Rector (the Rev. P. W. Willis) and afterwards Archdeacen Taylor delivered his charge. In the course of it he said that a careful perusal of the 47 questions in the Articles of Inquiry would give a fair idea of the duties of churchwardens, but 'he recommended them to procure a copy of the very valuable pamphlet art "Church wardens and their Duties," by Chancellor Espin. In general, they were the proper guardiansand keepers of the parish church, its goods, its furniture, itscrnaments and utensils, &c. It was also their duty to observe and report whether the services of the church were duly performed by the minister, but they bad no right to in- terfere with him in the performance of his duties, whether they approved or disapproved of them. Their office was simply in this respect one of observation and complaint, if complaint was necessray. Archdeacon Taylor said there seemed to be some misapprehension as to what was the proper habit or dress for the officiating minister, but hisludgment was, and he gave it with a full sense of the responsibility for what he said, that the surplice, hood, and tippet, the last-named being per- mitted by the 58th canon, and prescribed by the 74th, were the only canonical and lawful habits of the church in performing Divine service; nothing more and nothing less. As to the services themselves, it was the minister's province to decide, subject to revision, whether certain portions of the service—certain of the psalms; or creeds, or Litany—were to be said or sung. The minister was to judge that; also by whom they were to be said or sung other than the general congregation, and whether there was to be isstrunaental music or not, and by whom to be played, had also been decided to be within the direct jurisdiction of the minister. If the wardens had a complaint to make, they 'could make it in the proper way. Many said there was no authority for hymns, but he did not believe it. In the Act of Queen Eiizabeth, 1559, and ever since in the usage cf the Church, would be found an authurisation for hymns. By an Act in 1872, permission was given to the clergyinaa to divide or separate the morning prayer, Litany, and the Lord's Supper, and to use these three services either together or in varied order. By the same Act it was declared lawful for a minister to deliver a sermon or a lecture and have no service preceding it except a collect with or without the Lordzs Prayer. No one could now:justly complain of the inelasticity of the Book of Common Prayer or want of variety. If there was want of variety, it was not the fault of the law.
