div.p: 11IL
THE EXAMINER. SATURDAY, MAY 14, 1892.

ACCIDEN'T HOSPICAL.—The number of cases in the Accident Hospital in November was 8. No deaths. The number in hospital during December was 12. There was one death And an inquest in consequence. BIRTHS.—The births during November and December were 194. or 3'1'54 per thousand of population. SMALLPDX —There has not been a case of smallpox for some years in this town. TYPHOID FEVER.—Twenty-one cases of typhoid fever have been notified during November and December, 1891.. Many of these cases have arisen from bad drainage and defective closets, and wkm reperted the Local Authority took immediate steps to remedy existing defects. From these cases there were two deaths.

SCAVENGING —The Highway and Health departments o this Board are carried out in a highly efficient and satisfactory manner. OFFENSIVE TRADES.--Tbs escape of sulphuretted hydro- gen from some oc the works has been occasionally highly offensive. When notified of the nuisance the 'United Alkali Company took Steps to remedy it, although not always acknowledging that the escape was from their works. lam pleased to report that thereexiste a greater desire on the part of the United Alkali Company to pre- vent any recurrence of this nuisance.

div.head: YEAR'S DISEASE IN WIDNES.
div.p: A YEAR'S DISEASE IN WIDNES.
MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORTS.

dEn consequence of his 'resignation, Dr. Cooper presented his report for the first ten months of 1891. The deaths registered during that period numbered 570, and, calculating on a population of 31,000 to the middle of 1891, this gives a death rate of 18.38 per thousand of population for that portion of the year. ZYMOTICB.—The deaths registered from the eight prin- cipal zymotic diseases during the ten months numbered 52, or 1.67 per thousand of population, and were as follows :—Measles 14, scarlatina 3, diphtheria 0, whoop- ing cough 19, typhus fever 0, typhoid or enteric fever diarrhosa and dysentery B,,continued fever 1, membran- ous croup 1 ; total 52.

AGES AT DEATH.—Deaths of persons under 1 year 161, over 1 and under 5 103, over 5 and under 15 29, over 15 and under 25 32, over 25 and under 60 167, over 80 and under 78 ; total 570. Nimmons DISEASES HOSPITAL.— The number of cases treated in thelnfectious Diseases Hospital during the first ten months of 1291 was 48; of these only seven ended fatally. Acorns:4'r 110SPITAL—The number of cases treated in the Accident Hospital was 53, of these nine ended fatally. Biwrus.—The number of births registered during the ten months was 1,013 0r.32.67 per thousand of popula- tion. INougsrs.-27 inquests were held during the period under observation.

A/neer-ca.—A wide-spread epidemic of measles began at the end of July. Ila,pp ily the disease was of a mild type, only n deaths being recorded as due to measles since the commencement of the epidemic, although 750 cases were notified as having occurred during the 10 months ending 31st Ootcrber. SCARLATINA.—There was a slight epidemic of this disease in the early part of the year, 16 cases having been notified in the month of February, but happily it was stamped out by removing the patients to the hos- pital in as many instances as possible, and only three deaths were registered as due to scarlatina during the 10 months, as against nMe in MO and 32 in 1889. ENTERIC OR TYPHOID FEVER.-42 cases of this disease have been notified during the 10 months, the greater number in September and October; of these only six proved fatal ; 22 cases were removed to the Infectious Diseases Hospital. WHOOPING Cottnir.-If., deaths from this malady occurred during the first six months of the year ; as the disease was not notified I cannot give the number of cases.

DIARAMBA AND DYSENTERY.—The number of fatal cases of these diseases registered in 1889 was 34, and in 18-20. 26; I am glad to be in a position to state that dur- ing the first ten months of this year the number has fallen to eight, which is very satisfactory, and is due,in my opinion, to better sanitation and more care in scav- enging. SCAVENGING.—The seays-iging continues to be carried out satisfactorily by means of the Board's own staff and plant. _

I WATER SUPPLY.—The water supply continues satisfac- tory in every respect. Puaz.ie Woxas.—No extension of main sewerage has taken place during the period of observation, but four gushing tanks have been fixed in various parts of the township in order that the main sewers may be kept thoroughly free from obstruction. Seven streets and a large number of back passages are being paved and sewered, and will be adopted as soon as the work is completed. .

OFFENSIVE TF.ADES.—The nuisance arising from the Chance-Claus Process is still the cause of complaint, alt though the United Alkali Company have done a grea deal to mitigate the offensive smell, notwithstanding which there is room for further improvement. ALKALI WASTE.—The AlkatiWaste deposits are beinz dealt with in a more satisfactory manner than formerly. Dr. O'Keeffe's report for the months of November and December 1891, stated that the deaths registered during that period numbered 93, and calculating on a popula- tion of 31,000, this gives a death rate of 18 per thousand of population for that portion of the year. ZTKOTICS.—The deaths registered from zymotic dis- eases during November and December were as follows : Measles 5; scarlet fever 2; typhoid fever 2; total 9; or 1.74 per thousand. INFECTIOUS DISKSSES HOSPITAL—The cases treated in the Infectious Diseases Hospital during November and December 1891 were 14, of these 4 died in November.

div.head: WIDNES FIRE BRIGADE.
div.p: WIDNES FIRE BRIGADE.

-- Air. I. Carr superintendent of the Widnes Fire Brigade, submitted his annual report to the Local Board on Tuesday. The total number of tires that have occurred during the year within the rateable district (exclusive of chimney fires) is five, outside the rateable district one.

The Brigade has had three calls—on one occasion their services were not required, at the remaining two the fires were extinguished by the brigade. In three other eases the fires were put out by the per- sons living in the house, together with neighbours, without calling for other help. The estimated total loss from fires is £lOB. The estimated value of property at risk is .E 3,750. The Brigade appliances have been kept clean and in ' good repair. The total number of street hydrants is 195. During the past year the new fire station and I cottages have been completed., and the foreman and nine firemen took possession in January last, making ten men now residing on the premises. Five new mem- bers have been enrolled during the year. bringing the brigade, for the first tirae since its formation, up to its full strength, i.e. three officers and twelve firemen. The majority of the members are employed by the Board in the Gas and Water department, who have been given preference on account of their knowledge of the street mains, hydrants, and valves. The condition of the brigade, as regards effieiency and discipline, is fairly good, at all events, there is considerable improvement upon last year, which may be said to be mostly due to the greater interest created by the excellent accommoda- tion and better facilities afforded by the new premises. To make the arrangements more complete, a system of electric call bells connecting the Town Hall, Police Sta- tion, Mr. Lee's stables, with the men's Cottages will be necessary. The police, as in previous years, have ren- dered the brigade able service. At the end of the report is a tabulated statement which shows that in 1883 there were 14 fires,of which two were serious and the estimated amount of damage was £509 15s. The estimated amount of risk was £53,609. In 1889 there were 12 fires, damage 24,082 ; at risk £51,595 ; 1890, seven fires, damage ) £315 •, at risk £23,255; 1891, nine fires, damage £2,076 ; I at risk £221,700.

div.head: San. CANAL
div.p: THE San. CANAL
PASSENGERS ON CANALS.

The fact that earnings have already commenced on the Manchester Ship Canal—though not, it is true, on a very large scale—reminds " The Canal Journal "that the conveyance of passengers on canals is no novelty. It was regularly done before railways were made. Our contemporary, whose first number has just made its appearance, thinks it not unlikely that had canals been worked as vigorously as railways, passenger traffic might still have been carried on, in a limited way, for short journeys, where railways are not very near " When (it is added) you have time, travelling by canal is often pleasanter than being on dusty railroad ; and nowadays it is distinctly a novelty, and consequently attractive. This has been recognised in Manchester ; and a fleet of passenger steamers, placed on the Ship Canal, on the section from Eastham to the River Weaver was one of the attractions at Easter." DAMAGE DONE BY TRAMPS.

At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, nine tramps named John Flannery, John Ryan, William Redgreave, ' Thomas Stead, Peter Farrell, James Hayes, Thomas Tracy, George Johnson, and John Robinson were charged with sleeping in an outbuilding on the Canal Works, at Norton, on the previous night. P.C.'s Royle and Pettinger proved the case. They stated that shortly before midnight they were on duty with several other constables at Norton. Whilst passing along they I noticed flames issuing from the chimneys of several cabins, and on visiting them they found the defendants therein. They said they had no reason for being there. The cabins were broken into every night, and locks were taken off the tool boxes. The mea must have lighted the fires—Superintendent Atherton said that great damage had been done to the works. The men burnt coal and otherwise offended.—The prisoners were sent to gaol for 14 days with hard labour.

div.head: WEAVER POOL.
div.p: THE WEAVER POOL.

The advantage and facilities that the Manchester Ship Canal affords to trade received admirable illustra- tion on Sunday, when the steamship Dundonald, of Glasgow, commenced a 'voyage from the Weaver Pool to the North ot Scotland with a cargo of fishery salt. The vessel, which is owned by Mr. W. W. Christie- smith, arrived from Limerick " light," on Friday after- noon, to load salt from 'Messrs. Verdin's works at North- wich, and she was moored in the Pool. By Saturday evening 550 tons of salt had been lifted from flats into the hold, and she started on her voyage at eight o'clock on Sunday morning. This is the largest ship that has, up to the present been loaded so far up the canal from Eastham, and the success that has attended the tran- shipment of salt and the despatch of the ship marks a revolution in the salt trade of the Weaver. The neap tides are now on, and in ordinary circumstances, that is by using the Mersey, the vessel could not have started with such a large cargo until the 24th of the present month. The tide on Sunday morning was only lift. 4in., and yet a vesSei registered at 318 tons, carrying a cargo of 550 tons, and drawing 14ft. 6in., by using the ' Canal, experiences no difficulty in reaching the mouth of the River Weaver and returning to the sea. Mr. NV. Smith, the local traffic manager for the Ship Canal Company, superintended tbe loading of the vessel. On Thursday the steamship'Lucien arrived in the Pool, from Garston, and with the utmost despatch possible, a cargo of 570 tons of fishery salt will be placed in her. Her destination is Fraserburgh on the east coast of Scotland. Mr. W. H. Smith is superintending the load- ing operations.
As a cricket match was beitur play& at Silverdale, North Staffs, on Saturday, the Leek professional, named Rothera, was taken ill at the wicket, and died with in an hour.
CHILDREN TOSSED BY A MID COW AT ST. HELENS.

EXCITING SCENES. 19. bout half--past four o'clock,on Wednesday after non, some exciting scenes were witnessed in the neighbourkood of Duke-st., and the lower part of Cowley-hill, St. Helens, in consequence .f two children being tossed and seriously injuLl by a cow, a third child knocked down and hurt, and the kitchen •of a house being weecked by the infuriated animal- It appears that the animal belonged to Mr. Henry Turner, milk dealer and provision mer- chant, Peter-st., and on Wednesday he sent it to the Red Lion Rotel yard, and put it in Mr. W. Murray's sale. During the progress of business the animal by some means made its escape, and before it could be again captured it left the yard and got into the town. The cow dasked along Duke-street and arrived at the corner of Crab-street just as the infants were. leaving Lowe House Day Schools. Annie Rob- inson, aged five years, daughter of Joseph Robinson, engineman at Messrs. Pilkington's Top Glass- works, happened to be in the way, and the cow, making a rush, caught the chial in the side with its horns and tossed it over its head and back. The little girl was immediately picked up by a man and carried home man unconscious state. Other children, it is said, were knocked down, but fortunately escaped without serious injury, and the cow bounded along Oxford-street at a great speed. When it reached the butcher's shop of Mrs. Coop, at the corner of Halefield-street, it turned over the waste ground, and here two little fellows—Joseph Fenney, aged seven, son of an engine-winder at Groves's Colliery, and Joseph Birch, aged seven, of 92, Oxford- street—were playing marbles and chatting on their way home. The animal rushed at Fenney and tossed him in the air, inflicting serious injuries. Theboy Birch was also knocked down. Beth children were picked up and taken to their homes. The cow then crosssd over into Morley- st., and reached No. 64 just as Mrs. Clark, the wife of an engineman at Ale,ssrs. Pilkington's Glassworks, had entered carrying a child, she having been in the town. Just as she reached the table in the kitchen the cow struck her on the left side. The animal had come in with so much force that its momentum carried it for- ward and completely smasked the table into splinters. Mrs. Clark shouted for her mother,who was in the yard, not to come into the house; and she herself slipped back into the passage, and pulling the door to held the cow a prisoner, She hurried next door and told Mrs. Hun- ter, who went round to the back of the house. He took a stick and entered the kitchen, where he found the cow had made a complete wreck of the place in its frantic efforts to escape. The splintered table lay upside down with the fender and fire irons upon it. rhe sofa had two legs broken off. chairs were smashed, windows were broken, and on the stairs were large patches of blood from injuries which the animal had sustained. The back kitchen was also damaged and cooking utensils and dishes were strewn about. Mr. Hunter was at first perplexed as to how to deal with the animal. A good many children had con- gregated in front of the house, and to drive it out that way would have endangered their lives or limbs. Two ' other men came to his assistance and they beat the animal out into the garden and there secured it with ropes. It was then taken to Mr. Turner's shippon in Peter-st. But for this prompt action, the consequences, serious as they are, might have been more disastrous. The two children were on Wednesday night attended— Joseph Fenney, by Dr. Wyse ; and Annie Robinson, by Dr. Watson—who both regard the condition of their little patients as critical. The greatest excitement pre- vailed in thn neighbourhood up to a late hour, and many persons visited the wrecked kitchen of the Clarks.

div.head: TERRIBLE FIRE IN LONDON.
div.p: TERRIBLE FIRE IN LONDON.
FOUR LIVES LOST.

I fire broke out just before two o'clock on Monday morning on the premises of Messrs. Scott, a well-known (oyster bar and nulslic-house in Coventry-street, Picca- dilly. There were 13 persons sleeping on the premises, and the firemen, on being summoned, at once com- menced to play on the flames, and made a determined effort to rescue the inmates from what appeared to be certain death. The flames had obtained such a hold that entrance to the premises was impossible, and all that the firemen could do was to endeavour to prevent , the flames from spreading. This they succeeded in do- ing after two hours, and on entering the building they found in the rooms of the upper floor the bodies of four young men. Three of them were in bed, and they had apparently been suffocated in their sleep,while a fourth seemed to have made an attempt to escape, as his body lay close to a window. The screams of one person in the building are described as appalling, and were pro- bably those of this unfortunate youth in his fight for life. All the victims are Englishmen. The bodies have been identified as those of the young men Denning, Anstruther, Philips, and Barber, em- ployed at the restaurant. Though the premises retain the old name of" Scott's," the present proprietors are Messrs. Sinclair. They attribute the fire to the over- heating of a flue.

div.head: DEWSBURY TRAGEDY.
div.p: THE DEWSBURY TRAGEDY.
"WILFUL MURDER."

On Wednesday afternoon an inquest on the body of Sarah Ann Chapman, a native of Ashton-under-Lyne, Will was murdered at Saville Town, on Monday night, by being hurled over a bridge into the river, was opened at the Dewsbury Infirmary.—Tubal Gibson stated that he saw the woman and the pritoner (Harry Walker) on Saville Bridge. He heard Chapman scream, and a per- son shout, "He's thrown her over the bridge." He ran along the embankment and waded up to his neck in the water, but could not see her.—Dr. Watts, the Medical Officer ef Health for Dewsbury, described the results of the post-mortem examination of the body, which he had made. The cause of death was asphyxia by drowning Charles Humphreys, groom, said that an Monday even- ing he was driving his employer to Dewsbury. When. they were just on the bridge he saw a young man and a woman walking along. They appeared to be playing, for the woman ran away from the man, who overtook her, put his left arm around her, and threw her over the parapet into the river. He did not lift her fairly up, and she rolled, making a snatch either at the man's pocket or at the rail of the bridge. The man freed himself from her, and witness saw him pushing her off. Lie heard several people screaming. All the time the man stood still as though dazed, as if he did not know what to do. Then he walked two or three yards from the causeway on to the road, and subsequently he ran away in the direction of Saville Town. Wit- ness subsequently gave information to the police. After turther evidence had been given, the jury returned a verdict of wilful murder against Harry Walker. William Redfern, of Ashton-under-Lyne, brother of Sarah Ann Chapman, the Dewsbury victim, states that the deceased was 36 years of age, and was married to John Chapman at St. Mark's, Dukinfield, 12 years ago. 13-4 h gave way to intemperance, and soon after marriage separated. The husband is believed now to be dead. The deceased has three brothers and two married sisters living in Ashton-under-Lyne. fr3r many years the rela- tivas have not known deceased's whereabouts.

div.head: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.
div.p: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.

The monthly meeting was held at the Town Hall on Tuesday, Mr. F. H. Gossage presided and _there were present. Messrs. E. Curey,_4.,Brown, D. Wripht B. Cook, H. S. Timmins, G. I. NAO.- T 0603? Owen, J. Berch, J. Houghton, J. Mid wood, H. S. Oppenhiem (clerk), J. Craik (assistant clerk), S. Hoyle (accountant), J. S. Sinclair (surveyor), W. Lowe (nuisance inspector). _ _ _

OAR AND WATER COWEITTEE. AIR Committee reported that Mr. John-White, of War- rington, agent to Colonel Ireland Blackburne, had written aakmg for an extension of the water mains to Hale, and they had instructed the clerk and engineer to meet Mr. White and discuss the matter. Samples of water from Stockswell and bletherley had during the past month-1 been submitted to Dr. Campbell Brown for analysis, and that gentleman reported both to be of excellent quality and olear. The mean rainfall for the month had been 1.06 inches and the water in stock was 7,234,337 gallons. The illuminating power of the gas during the month had averaged 17.47 candles. The wages required for the next five weeks at the Gas and Water Works was I'llo. The clerk was instructed to express to the architects of the new engine-house at Netherley the dissatisfaction of the committee at the slow progress made and urging them to use their best endeavours to promote the speedy completion of the contraet.—The minutes were approved on the motion of Mr. Brown.

HIGHWAY ILATTER.S. The Highway Committee reported that the estimated wages for the next five weeks was ER 3s. Od. per week, including LIS per week for diversion of sewers, Water- loo-road. It was recommended that two crossings be laid in Birchfield-road, provided the owners would con- sent to pay half the cost : the footpaths also to be flagged. Railway Crossing near Pilkington's Works : 'Recommended that the question of the action of the Sheffield and Midland Co., in doing away with the small side gates at this level crossing, Ise referred to the clerk. Recommended that two watering barrels be purchased at the price of LIO each, for the districts of Halton View and Farnworth. Sulphuretted Hydrogen :—The Survey- or's report upon the state of the Board's sewers further considered. Recommended with a view to the ventila- tion of the West Bank sewer, that the Surveyor submit to this Committee suitable sites for the erection of ven- tilating shafts. Recommended that the Clerk write to the Hutchinson Trustees with regard to the discharge of mud by them into Marsh Brook and causing an obstruc- tion to the western outfall of the Board's sewers. Ann- street Sewer :—The Surveyor reported that the United Alkali Co., Ltd. had still failed to clean out the outfall to this sewer, and the clerk was instructed to interview Mr. Carey upon the matter. Mr. Sadler moved the adoption of these minutes, which were carried without discussion.

div.head: HEALTH OF THE TOWN.
div.p: HEALTH OF THE TOWN.

The minutes of the Health Committee contained the report of the Medical Officier for April, which stated that there were 94 births and 52 deaths, being at the respective rates of 36.3 and 2012.. Zymotic diseases caused one death. The Medical Officer attributed the high mortality to the inclement weather. The adminis- tration of the Hospitals is very satisfactory, and the treatment of the patients is all that could be desired. It is a pleasure to state that I have not found any cause to complain of the escape of noxious vapours, nor has any report been made to me during this month of any nuisance whatever.—Mr. Wright moved the confirma- tion of the minutes.

div.head: NUISANCE INSPECTOR AND HIS REMEDIES.
div.p: THE NUISANCE INSPECTOR AND HIS REMEDIES.

Mr. Sadler complained that the Nuisance Inspector in reporting nuisances to owners of property exceeded his duty by stipulating how the nuisances should be re- medied. He had known cases where the inspector's remedies had cost double the amount of money that the nuisance could have been obviated for.—Mr. Wright said if Mr. Sadler's statement were true, the Inspector had exceeded his duty. The Committee would inquire into the matter. THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT. A DECREASED RATE.

The accountant bad submitted to the Finance Com- mittee a statement showing the estimated and actual expenditure for the past year,also the estimated amount required for the year ending 25th larch, 1893. A penny in the £ was estimated to produce £465, and to raise the sum of £13,937 would require a rate of 2.5. 6d. in the £. The summary of the estimates was as follows : Estimate Expenditure Estimate March March March 1892. 1892. 1893. The Accountant reported with regard to the collection of accounts that " In the year 1881 the principal of allowing discount on gas and water accounts was adopted, on condition that the accounts were paid not later than the last day of the first month following the supply ; since this system was introduced the number of gas and water consumers has so largely increased that the staff cannot keep pace with the work under the pre- sent conditions, that the accounts be paid within a month. There are two ways in which this pressure of work may be dealt with, either by increasing the staff or by extending the time for the payment of the ac- counts. Rather than increase the staff, I would suggest that the conditions of payment be altered, and discount allowed on accounts paid not later than the last day of the second month following the supply.—Loans Having in view the present and prospective expenditure on capi- tal acconnt, I think it advisable that the Board advertise for loans. The expenditure on fire station and cottages having exceeded the amount brorowed by £5OO it will be necessary to make application to the Local Government Board for power to borrow that sum." It was recom- mended that the Clerk advertise for loans at 31 percent., and that application be made to the Local Government Board for permission to borrow the £5OO mentioned.— Mr. Midwood moved the adoption of the minutes.—Mr. Brown, dealing with the estimates, remarked that the Highway Committee bad spent nearly £BOO less than their estimate, and urged that they had no right to do this. This money had been taken from the ratepayers' , pockets, when it ought to have remained there. With regard to the Health Committee they proposed to spend almost double the amount of previous years in nightsoil work, and he thought, to say the least of it, that this was a gross waste of the public money.—Mr. Sadler replied that the inclement weather of the win- ter had prevented the Highway Committee from carrying out certain road improvements they had in- tended ; which accounted for the difference in the esti- mate and actual expendlture.—Mr. Wright, for the Health Committee, said the committee had the full con- fidence of the public, and he was quite prepared for the Board to go into committee and enquire into the esti- mates. The nightsoil question would speedily have to. be taken into consideration by the Board itself.—The niinutes were passed. _

div.head: PERRY APPROACH AND PROMENADE WALL.
div.p: THE PERRY APPROACH AND PROMENADE WALL.

The minutes of the General Purposes Committee stated that with regard to the Ferry approach the Clerk reported that, in accordance with the minate of the last meeting of this Committee, he had communicated with Messrs. Walters, Deverell, & Co., solicitors to the Marquis of Chohnondeley, but they had declined to afford him the information required.—Promenade The Clerk reported that he had written to the Manches- ter Ship Canal Company requesting them to carry out the necessary works of reinstating the wall, and offering (without prejudice) on behalf of the Local. Board to contribute £lOO towards the cost, and he submitted and read letter, 26th April, from the Company declining to agree to the proposal.— Recommended that the Clerk further negotiate with the Co. with reference to their original proposal, and that upon an arrangement satisfactory to him being arrived at, tenders be invited for the carrying out of the works. Bower's Brook :—Recommended that the Clerk write to the United Alkali Co. expressing the disappointment of the Board at the non-fulfilment of the agreement come to in February last, and insisting upon the immediate commencement of the works. Railsray Rates and Charges :—Letters from Sir J. J. Harwood (10th March) and Mr. J. W. Blackstock, town clerk's office, Manches- ter (28th April), with reference to the claim of £36 Bs. 9d. alleged to be due from the Board in respect of two contributions towards the expenses of the Lanca- shire and Cheshire Conference, read. Recommended that the Clerk reply thereto that the Board are unable to entertain the claim—Accident Ambulance :—Recom- mended that the Accident Ambulance be removed from the Police Station to the new fire engine station and placed under the control of the Board's officials. INCORPORATION REJOICINGS.

Mr. Midwood in moving VIP adoption of these minutes said the Charter of incorporation of Widnes was expected to arrive in the course of the next month. It the Chair- man of the Board intended to call a town's meeting, or to have a general holidny in the town, it was quite time that some steps should be taken in the matter.—The Chairman in reply, said any movement that took place in the town must come from outside and not from the Board. He could receive, but not give instructions.
TECHNICAL INSTRUCTION.

The sub-committee of the Technical instruction Com- mittee reported that they had made arrangements to continue the class for Dressmaking for another term of 10 lessons, commencing April Bth, the fee to be 3s. for the term ; and re-appointed Mrs. Dobson teacher at the renumeration of £1 2s. ed. per day inclusive. Arrange- ments had also been made to c.ontinue the French Class for another term of 101essons, and Mr. B. Meunier re- apuomted teacher at a salary of £7 7s. for the term. The minutes were passed.

div.head: FRIGIITFtTL COLLIERY EXP LOS lON.
div.p: FRIGIITFtTL COLLIERY EXP LOS lON.
GREAT LOSS OF LIFE,

SEATTLE, WEDNESDAY —A despatch received here from Roslyn, Washington, announces that a gas explosion , occurred on the slope of Mine 2 of the Northern Pacific Coal Company, at half-past one yesterday afternoon, just as two gangs were shifting. The exact nature of the explosion or the circumstances leading thereto will Probably never be known, as it is believed that every man in the two gangs perished. There were abort 45 men in the three levels affected by the explosion, and the only persons who escaped were two boys who were in a tunnel and a driver who had just come out of the shone when the explosion occured. The shock upset his car, knocked the driver and ,the mules down, and bruised a man standing 100 ft. away. The repo-t of the explosion was heard in the town a mile away, and in a short time the mouth of the slope was surrounded by men, women, and children. There were a number of negroes among the miners, and the lamen- tations of their relatives added to the horror of the scene. Rain was falling heavily, but the crowd took no heed of the downpour, as they waited anxiously for news of their friends and relatives in the mine. Up to half-past seven four bodies had been recovered terribly bruised, and death was probably instantaneous. These bodies were found quite near the opening of the pit, and some distance from the point where the explosion is supposed to have occurred, while most of the men were working 1,500 or 2,000 feet further in the slope. The, bodies, as they were recovered were carried to the City Hall, which was converted into a temporary morgue. A great proportion of the victims had large families, and, as they had not obtained over two days' work a week for a year, many of them were in straitened circumstances. The Northern Pacific Coal Company forwarded 40 coffins from Seattle at mid- night. The Roslvn mine is one of the largest in the State. and supplies coal to the western division of the Northern Union Pacific Railways. The mine has a capa- city of 20,000 tons per day. Seams, WEDNESDAY (LATER).—Great volumes ef afterdamp and smoke rolled from the entrance of the pit after the explosion, making any attempt at approach dangerous. As soon as it was possible to enter the mine a number of men set to work, and, as progress was made, the frightful havoc wrought by the explo- sion became manifest. The timber work supporting the galleries was torn out for a distance of 100 ft., and the whole of the interior was fearfully wrecked. It is thought that a fire has broken out in the lower level, and if this is so water will he again pumped into the mine. All men who are able are engaged in the work of rescue. Fourteen bodies had been recovered by mid-- night. The work of recovery is slovr on account of the large amount of gas in the workings. It is now be- lieved that the dead number 48.

div.head: LABOUR COMMISSION. WIDNES AND ST. HELENS CHEMICAL WITNESSES.
div.p: THE LABOUR COMMISSION. WIDNES AND ST. HELENS CHEMICAL WITNESSES.

Group C of the Royal Commission on Labour met again on Wednesday, at Westminster Rail, Mr. undella. M.P., presiding. Mr.tlealy, employed in the soda department of Messrs. Hutchinson s vitriol works, Widnes, was the first wit- ness. He said he attended on behalf of his fellow- workmen. The nsen worked on the piece and were ex- pected to turn out from 3 tons 3 cwts. to 3 tons 4 ewte. of soda per day, and this usually took them ten hours. Their wages varied from £2 to £3 7s. The saritary 'condition of the works was very bad, in some cases filthy. The men suffered greatly from gases, which- caused swelling of the stomach and vomiting. For three years and seven months witness worked as a salt- cake man. This occupation caused the men's teeth to drop out and their faces to be burned. If proper pre- cautions were taken by the employers much of this could be prevented. Owing to the nature of the work the men had to provide stimulants, usually rurn, which they had to provide themselves. The Chairman : Does this habit make the men in- temperate ?—Yes, in many cases. Some of the men suffer permanent injury to the chest. Is a medical man provided ?—Yes; but he is paid by funds subscribed by the men. Witness went on to say that the inspectors should be appointed from among the workmen, as he had never seen an inspector in the chemical yard. You want better inspection, bettet sanitation, and better ventilation ?—Yes.

Witness advocated three shifts of eight hours. In some works in Lancashire this was done, and although the men get less wages they had more comfort. Machinery should be properly guarded. Is it not the duty of the inspector to see to that?— Yes, but be does not do it. I have never seen an inspec- tor about machinery which I have worked myself fora considerable time.
Witness also said that the men thought the employers should not be allowed to serve on juries in cases of fatal - accidents.

Have you ever known a case where an employer has sat upon such a jury P—Yes the employer, manner, two foremen, and a clerk from the office had been present. Have they been on the jury P—The foreman and a man from the office were.

You don't contest their right to be present ?—Not if the men's representatives are also allowed to be present. Of course both sides should be represented P—lf they were the men would not have so much to complain of. Mr. Patrick Shiel, saltcake worker at Messrs. M'Bride's, St. Helens, Lancashire, said he generally agreed with the evidence of he last witness.

Mr. John Ca-rey, powder packer in the employ of Messrs. Curtis, St. Helens, also gave similar evidence. He gave a practical illustration of how the flannel TMIZZie is worn by the packers. The muzzle is composed of several folds of new flannel, which in time is destroyed by the powder. The men also wear "goggles" to pre- serve their eyes, and they cannot work for many minutes (continuously.

div.head: LORD SALISBURY AND THE EIGHT HOURS DAY.
div.p: LORD SALISBURY AND THE EIGHT HOURS DAY.

Lord Salisbury and Mr. Balfour, on Wednesday after- noon received at the Foreis,n Office a reptesentative depu- tation from the workmen's associations who are agitating for a legislative reetricbon of the working day to eight hours. Mr. George Shi pton introduced the speakers,who expressed an intention of making the legal eight hours day a test question at the general election Lord Salis- bury, in reply, said that although they were unanimous in their desire for an eight hours day, they did not appear agreed as to the means by which their object should be attained. The object was estimable, but the matter re- quired further discussion. No object obtained by violent methods could have permanent good results, and in warning them of disastrous results which might follow the legislative restriction of the hours of labour, he urged them to be careful of the fearful interests they controlled. Mr. Balfour expressed his concurrence in the views of the Premier, and designated as rash any endeavour to carry out the object aimed at by means of the great parliamentary machine.

div.head: CONGREGATIONAL UNION.
div.p: THE CONGREGATIONAL UNION.

The sixtieth annual meeting of the Congrerational ' Union of England and Wales oppened at the Memorial Hall, Farrinßdon-street, on Monday rught. The Rev. Herbert Evans presided, and the hall was crowded. The report, which states the total number of churches, branches, and missions in Great Britain and Ireland as , 4,888, and the income for the year at over £15,813, was carried. The Rev. Guinness Rogers character- ned the attack as a dastardly injustice.—Mr. Albert Spencer, who had been elected Chairman for the ensuing Year, seconded.—Dr. Parker moved that the assembly nominate a secretary by ballot, and declared that if the lest sermon had not. been written the second could not have been preached. They ought to be careful about fine distinctions between degrees of plagiarism—The amendment was lost by a large majority.—The election was carried unanimously, amid loud cheers and an enth- usiastic demonstration in Mr. Woods's favour. The 60th annual sleeting of the Congregational Union was continued at the City temple, Holborn Viaduct, on Tuesday. The Rev. With regard to Welsh Disestablishment, be asserted so far as argument was concerned, the 1. attle was won. Mr. Albert Spicer was elected chairman for next year

The Staffordshire and Worcester chain-makers have resolved to take a week's holiday on account of trade depression. and also with a view of restricting the out- put. In the fifth report of the Royal Commission on Vac- cination, the opinion is evpressed that persons impris- oned under the Vaccination Acts ought nst to he treated as criminals, and that it should no longer be possible to impose repeated penalties in respect to the non-vaccina- tion of the same child.

Preservation MAT is with us with its ,green. ,: of hedgerows and promise -of blo&,- Foctpathe. som,.and the thoughts of young, ' and old wholthow what is good for them, turn to, pleasant walks through the fields and woodo. The country is the poor man's park; the highways and, footpaths through it are the only land to-. which he can lay claim; and they ought to be carefully pre- served to him.. The highways may to a large extent be left,to the County Councils, or the High.. way Bosnia; but not so with footpaths. They require to.be specially traversed and guarded, or they have a tendency to disappear. Take a ease in point the other evening the writer pursued a pleasant walk within two miles of Warrington until he found the path obstructedlwith a wire fence. Disregarding this, he reached another point where the style was over-turned and fenced off, and the footpath ploughed up! This., looks very much like land-grabbing on the part either of the farmer or the landowner; and as to this it should, never be forgotten that land dedicated to the public is as, much the property of the public as land hold under title deeds by the private indivi- dual.. There ought to be an authority or organi- sation,for protecting the public in these cases. The National Footpath Preservation Society, say in their seventh Annual Report: "It would be much better it the preservation of footpaths were placed in the hands of a totally independent party, such as the Public Prosecutor or an Officer from the Board of Trade, perfectly unin- fluenced. The duties of each, official would be to hold a court of inquiry in every case, and inspect the locality whether appealed to or net, tor in many eases persons are afraid to oppose the closing or diversion of a footpath." Meantime, until something of the kind, is done, steps should be taken locally to preserve ancient rights of way—either by the formation of a branch of the National Society, or through a Cor- poration or other local authority. The latter course is to be preferred, and we are glad to sae that it is growing in favour. There are now no less than 36 Corporations affiliated to the National Footpath Preservation Society, as many as 18 having joined during the past year. The local authorities of this part of Lancashire and Cheshire- would i de well to follow suit. The annual cost s small, it ensures the best advice, and the fullest information ; and, what is of still greater moment, the knowledge that a local authority may take action often prevents the need of action being taken by operating as a cheek upon evil-doers. Other points which require watching are the use of barbed wire, dangerous stiles, and encroach- ments upon roads. It has been laid down by her Majesty's judges that "a man may not place at the side of the road, a fence which is dangerous to persons lawfully walking along the road." Yet fences of this kind are being continually placed.

It ought not, however,to be left to private duals to take proceedings in this case; it is the duty of public authores to protect the rights of the public. With regard to what is or what is not an encroachment, his Honour Judge MARTINBAII in deciding a case last year said :—" The general presumption was that all the space between hedge and hedge, whether metalled or not, was part ef the highway, and the burden was cast on anyone who attempted to take away land on sither side, of showing that what they took was not part of the highway." This clear and definite, and if the law were enforced it is not too much to say that thousands of acres would have to be' surrendered as land which bad is been "'nobbled" from the highways. div.head: PROPERTY SALES AT RUNCORN.
div.p: PROPERTY SALES AT RUNCORN.

Mr. Luke Holmes, on Monday evening, at South Bank Hotel, offered for sale by auction eight dwelling-houses and shops situate in Egerton-st., the total yearly rental of which was £l5l. No. 43, was disposed of to Mr. Vernon, No. 41 to the auctioneer, and No. 39 to Mr. Duckett, at the reserve price of £250 each. The double shop, Nos. 35 and 37, was sold to Mr. Kirkham for £490. The double shop, No. 33 and 31, was withdrawn at £450 and No. 2 Briscoe-st. at £.350. On the same evening at the same place Mr. S. Yarwood offered eight dwelling-houses in Waterloo-road, numbered from 23 to 27, in four lots. The bidding was far from brisk, and the whole of the lots were withdrawn on account of the reserve not being reached. Mr. Lake was the solicitor to the vendor in each instance. STONE THROWING AT TRAINS AT RUNCORN. . . .

The danger attending the mischievoui-P7a.c.tice of throwing stones and other missiles at moving railway trains was illustrated at Runcorn on Saturday. On the 9.45 an express from Liverpool to London arriving at Crewe, a lady, whose name has not transpired, com- plained of serious cuts about the face and head through being hit with a stone, which came through the carriage window when the train was passing the south end of Runcorn station. The lady joined the train at Mossley Rill, where it was stopped specially for her and she was on her way to Paris. Dr. Atkins, the railway com- panies' surgeon at Crewe attended to her injuries .after which she travelled to Manchester to consult a physician, instead of proceeding with her journey. The facts of the accident were telegraphed to Mr. Bethel, the acting stationmaster at Runcorn, who communicated with Superintendent Atherton, and the latter instructed In- spector Cooper and P.C. Worth to make inquiries. After an hour's search the officers found a boy who admitted having thrown a stone at the train, and it will be left to the railway company asto what proceedings should be taken against him. The train is estimated to have passed through Runcorn at the rate of 40 miles an hour.

STACK FIRE AT WESTON. On Sunday afternoon a haystack belonging to Mr. John Jeffs, farmer, Weston, became ignited from some unexplained cause, and as there was no water in the vicinity was totally consumed. The damage is put down at about £2O, and is not covered by insurance.

FUNERAL OF MR, RICHARD COLLIER, OF RUNCORN.

The mortal remains of Mr. Richard Collier, of Green- way-road, were committed to the grave in Runcorn Cemetery on Monday afternoon. The Rev. C. Finch was the officiating minister, and many members of the Primitive Methodist Chapel, with which the deceased was connected, and several tradesmen, were present. The deceased, who was 73 years of age, had amassed a competency in the grocery trade, and had led a retired life for the last 18 years.

At Widnes Police Court, on Monday, John McGee, of Lugsdale-road, was fined 53. and costs for being drunk and disorderly on Saturday and V. and costs for assault- ing P,C. THE SEAMEN'S INSTITUTE, RUNCORN.

The choir connected with this Mission, assisted by a few members 8f the Mill Brow Brass Band, on Monday evening, rendered the service of song " Bob the Shoe. black." PRIMITIVE METHODIST SUNDAY SCHOOL, RUNCORN. The anniversary of this school was celebrated in Greenway-road Chapel, on Sunday, when special servi- ces were held. The Rev. F. N. Shiminin, of Bolton, occupied the pulpit morning and evening, and the Rev. W. Arrowsmith (Wesleyan) was the preacher in the afternoon. Music specially selected for the occasion was rendered by the choir and scholars under the leader- ship of Mr. Hillidge, and Mr. W. Gittens junr. presided at the organ. The collections amounted to £32, an increase ot £5 on last year. There was a crowded con- gregation at each service.

PROPOSED NEW PRESBYTERIAN CHURCH AT RUNCORN. The members of the congregation worshipping at St. John's Presbyterian Church, Runcorn, have lately held a meeting to consider the advisability of providing a more commodious place of worship. It was stated that during the brief pastorate of the Rev. J. Pulford Wil- liams 46 members had been added to the church rolls, and there was an ever-increasing congregation, for the requirements of which the present church was far too small. It was unanimously decided to build a new church ; and a committee was appointed to select a site and ascertain the probable cost of the new church. Mr. E. Wynne Humphreys and Mr. James Richardson are co-secretaries to the committee; Mr. James Steele, treasurer; and Mr. James Pritchard, chairman. The committee consists of Messrs. Robinson, Leach, Harrop, J. H. Temperle3-, and F. Oliver. When in want of a chaste and elegant wedding or birthday present go to PRITCHARD'S, 51, High-st.—Advt.

ATTIIMPTHD.SubaomAT RUNCORN. At Runcorn Police Court, on Thursdaymorning, before Mr. James Handley, Mary &Donnel4 aged 50 years, of Back Mersey-street, was charged with attempting to commit suicide on the rath April by cutting her throat with a razor. The woman, who had that morning been brought from the Workhouse Hospital, appeared to be In a very weak state.—Patrick O'Donnell, the husband, said his wife had previously to the attempt on her life been very depressed and had constantly complained of pains in the head. He undertook to have her properly attended to, and os his entering into recognizances of 366 that his wife should be of good behaviour in future, he was allowed to take her away. WIDNRS AND DISTRICT TRADES COUNCIL. At the ordinary monthly meeting, on Monday night, a series of questions proposed to be put to the sitting members and candidates for the Widnes and Northwich divisions of Parliament came up for confirmation, and were unanimously adopted. The following resolution was also adopted : "'that this Council recom- mend all Trades Unionists to use moral suasion to get life assurance agents to become members of their trade organisation, and to refuse new business to non-Trade Union agents. The same to be signed by the president and secretary, and afterwards printed and circulated." The remainder of the business was of a formal eharae- I ter.

SUNDAY SCHOOL DEMONSTRATION FOR WIDNES. A meeting of the delegates from the various Sunday schools in the town was held on Monday evening, in Lacey-at., school, to further consider the question of holding a public demonstration of the Sunday schools of all denominations. Mr. F. Hartland occupied the chair, and there was a fair number of representatives present. After a long discussion, it was decided to hold the demonstration on Saturday afternoon, the 2nd of July, and that a general fund be formed to clear the expenses. Six gentlemen were appointed a Finance Committee, and Mr. T. Hughes was appointed treasurer. A hope was expressed that the superintendents and teachers would endeavour;to make the project a thorough success, the aim of the promoters of the scheme being to show the wonderful strength of Sunday schools at the present day, JOsEPE PEITCEAED keeps spectacles to suit all sights from • shilling • pair.—Advi RUNCORN CHURCH ARMY.

In aid of the funds of the Runcorn braneh of the Church Army, a Sale of Work was held in a tent adjoin- ing the Army House, on Tuesday and Wednesday, and was fairly well patronised. In the unavoidable absence of Mrs. Wood, her young son performed the opening ceremony. The Vicar, the Rev. Canon Wood, delivered an address, in which he said the Church Army work had a claim upon the sympathies of everyone in Runcorn, not because of what it had done but because of what it had left undone. The members, full of energy and zeal were one of the arms of the good old Church of England, and their work was to help spiritually and materially those who, through no fault of their own, had not re- ceived the cultivation and education which was happily becoming the property of all belonging to this country. They also did their best to reclaim those who had fallen in the scale of society. During the evening an entertainment was given by the band of the Seamen's Institute. The sum realised by the sale was £2O. JOSRPR PRlTCHLED,Watchmaker and Jeweller, 51, Higb- et., and 4, Bridge-at., Runcorn.—Advt. CONCERT AT LACEY-STREET, WIDNIN4

On Tuesday evening a successful concert was given in Lacey-street School, in aid of the new chapel scheme, in connection with Hutchinson-street Primitive Method- ists. Mr. S. Owen presided. The programme was opened with a " March" by Oakland-street band, who also gave three other selections. Mr. Branch was loudly applauded:for his "Powder Monkey" and "The little hero." Miss Lamb received a well-earned encore for her interpretation of " Tell me, my heart." Mr. Rimmer was re-called for " Keel Row." and "The Better Land," was sung by him in a feeling manner. " Every inch a soldier" was treated in fine style by Mr. Morris, who was also encored. Mr. Simkin contributed " Dolly's Revenge." Mr. J. R. Lea " Ho, ho, hear the wild winds blow," and " The last cf the boys." Mise Simkin was successful in " Alone on the raft." Mr. A. Evans amused the audience with his comic songs. The aecempanists were Messrs. J. T. Jones and Lancaster. DAMAGING TELEGRAPH WIRES AT RUNCORN. At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, Thos. Pownall, Alfred Dutton, and Herbert Lowe, youths ,were charged with having on the 2nd April, maliciously broken wire insulators, being part of a certain electric telegraph wire belonging to H.M.'s Postmaster General, doing damage to the extent of 13s. 9d.—Joseph Griffiths, of Halton-road, a singal man on the Ship Canal works, de- posed to seeing defendants throw stones at the insula- tors, and break two.—P.C. Benfield said the defendants tried to put the blame on each other's shoulders.—Mr. Walsh, divisional engineer, said the breaking of insula- tors in and about Runcorn had been very serious of late. They had replaced 20 within the past week between Percival-lane and Sutton. The insulators cost an aver- age of Is. each, in addition to the time and labour in fixing them, and in addition damage was done to the wires.—Mr. Brundrit informed the defendants that they had rendered themselves liable to two years imprison- ment without the option of a fine, and they.would thus see that it was a more serious offence than they thought. Any future offenders would be severely dealt with. Each defendant was fined ss. and costs.
If you wantyour watch repaired by skilful workmen. take it to PRITCIIID'S.—AIivt. TECHNICAL EDUCATION AT HALTON.

The session in connection with the agricultural class at Halton was concluded on Monday evening when Mr. Ford, of the gardens, Halton Grange, delivered a brief address. In the course of it, he warned them and their friends against being persuaded to lightly esteem the movement of technical education in agriculture. It had been more seriously and more generally considered in this country during the past year than at any previous time. He was very pleased to observe their class stood out before all others, as it was composed entirely of practical young men. In that, as in all movements for progress, there were many who would speak against the metheds adopted ; but meanwhile those who were wise would take advantage of the opportunities offered, and profit by them. Next session he should endeavour to give more extended illustrations in chemical experi- ments, and with specimens of manurial substances, food stuffs, seeds, grasses, &c. He trusted that the young men of the neighbourhood, who were alive to their`own interests would join together to increase the numbers in attendance. He certainly looked forward to the time (probably but a few years hence) when all who cultivated the soil would more or less understand those principles, and so bring into action an old proverb " Practice with science." ACTION AGAINST A RUNCORN SHIPOWNER.

In the City of London Court, oft Wednesday, Mr. Commissioner Kerr and two nautical assessors heard a case on the Admiralty side of the court, in which Mr. Greenway Millington, shipowner, Top Locks, Runcorn, was sued by Messrs. Dawson and Son, •Ospringe-road, Faversham, for damage done to the plaintiff's vessel, the Pioneer, by a schooner, the Lizzie,belonging to the defen- dant. Mr. Farnfield appeared for the plaintiffs, and Mr. Bowden Powell for the defence. Both the vessels were at anchor opposite the Greys Chalk Quarry Pier, in the Thames, on the 26th July, and it was alleged by plaintiff's witnesses that the Lizzie was so low in the water that she dragged her anchor, and came into con- tact with the Pioneer, carrying away her bowsprit and causing other damage, and the vessel was detained five days, damages for which would have to be determined by the court. The witnesses denied that the captain of the Lizzie called to the Pioneer to lengthen her chain, but the principal men on her had gone ashore, and the boy, who was the only person left, did not do so in time ' The defence was that the Pioneer took up a foul berth I too near the Lizzie, and had too short a chain out. I After hearing the evidence on both sides, the Commis- sioners said the assessors were of opinion that the plain- tiffs gave a foul berth.—Mr. Farnfied : Then it will be no use me contesting the case any further.—The Com- missioner: No. There will be judgment for the defen- dant, with costs.
SUCCESS OF A WIDNES MUSS BAND.

At a brass band contest, held at Skclmersdale, the Oakland-street Wesleyan Brass Band were successful in gaining the fourth prize, and defeated the noted" Wigan Rifles," who were placed fifth on the list. Thirteen bands competed.

THE RAILWAY COLLISION AT BOLD BRIDGE. The work of lifting the engine and shattered brakevan, and loading, up the debriB caused by the collision between two goods trains at Bold Bridge, near St. Helens, on the St. Helens and Widnes line was satisfactorily carried out on Sunday. The brakesman, William Collier, of 4, Peel House-lane, Appleton, near Widnes, who was injured internally appeared no better on Sunday.

On Wednesday, at Messrs. R. Evans and Co.'s Edgegreen Colliery, a man named Edward Jones, residing at Silcock-st., Golborne, was killed by, the fall of the roof of the section in which hs. was working after removing the props.

SUICIDE IN WALES OF A ST. ITELWAS WOMAN.

Miss Williams, who committed suicide under painful circumstances on Friday afternoon, at Llanrwst, was a native of St. Helena, and on Mon- day morning her remains were taken by first train from Llanrwst to St. Helens. Her father was engaged for years at a colliery in St. Helens, and still lives there, but has now retired from work.

BOYS' STEINS ON THE Si CANAL. A strike took place on Tuesday, in the Big Field Section of the Ship Canal, at Norton, near Run- corn. The boys employed in marking the points, So the number of about 70, struck for an advance of id. per hour. and made some demonstrations, in the district, but on the following day they ex- pressed their readiness to resume work on the old terms. New hands had, however, been pub en in their places.

div.head: SUDDEN DEATH AT NORTON.
div.p: SUDDEN DEATH AT NORTON.

Thomas Walsh, a navvy, of no fired abode, died suddenly at 47 Hut on the Ship Canal Works, at Norton, near Runcorn, on Thursday night. The de- seased told the occupants of the hut that he was and asked to be allowed to rest. After doing so a short time,he got up, and was in the act of putting on his boots,when he fell dead. The Coroner deems an inquest unnecessary. DEATH OF THE OLDEST MAN IN CROFT.

The death of Mr. James Waywell, sen., of Little- town-road, Croft, is reported, after a brief illness, at the advanced age of 87 years. The deceased was a retired hand-loom silk weaver, and was the oldest man in the parish. He was possessed of his usual faculties up to a short time before his death. He finished digging and planting his garden on the 23rd ult., but caught a cold, after which bronchitis set in, which was.the cause of death. The funeral of the deceased, who was much respected, took place at Winwick Church on Monday.

SAFETY BICYCLES.--J. S. Garland. 51, Bridge-et., War- rington. See advertisement on page 4. FOOT RACE IN ST. HELENS. On Saturday afternoon over 1,000 spectators were ' attracted to the Star Inn Race Ground, to witness the race between between George Cook, better known as " Shirt," and James Harrison, both of St. Helens. They met at Wigan some time ago, when Harrison just managed to win. The conditions on Saturday were to run 110 yards on level terms for a stake of .£5O. A good race was witnessed, Cook proving the winner by a yard and a quarter. Mr. Hugh, of Manchester, was the referee, and Mr. S. Kane, Salford the pistol firer.

div.head: RAILWAY ARBITRATION AT Si. HELENS.
div.p: RAILWAY ARBITRATION AT Si. HELENS.

The evidence in the arbitration between the Liverpool, St. Helens, and South Lancashire Railway Company and the United Alkali Union, to fix the price of certain lands and works required for the construction of the lines in St. Helens, was con- cluded at three o'clock on Saturday afternoon. The arbitrators, Mr. Sinclair, of St. Helens, and Mr. Doming, of Manchester, have sat three days and heard many witnesses, the umpire being Mr. S. B. Worthington, of Manchester. The award will be given in due course. DEATH OF A ST. HELENS TRADESMAN.

The death is announced of Mr. George Howarth, lime merchant, of Bickerstaff-st., St. Helens. Mr. Howarth. who was formerly a well known brick- linker, of Fartiworth, near Widnes, came to St. Helens ten years ago, and succeeded his brother as a lime and cement merchant. Last summer he was attacked with influenza, from which he never pro- perly recovered. About eight weeks ago he grew worse, and gradually sank, death taking place on Friday. Mr. Howarth was well known among S. Helens builders and tradesmen, and very much respected. Mn,. BRUNNER P AND ALDERMEN.

Mr. Btunner on Tuesday night withdrew the re- solution he intended to move on Wednesday, on the Liverpool Boundaries Bill, to the effect , that no charge in the existing law would be satisfactory which does not prevent aldermen voting in the election of aldermen, as a vote upon this resolution would have prevented the same question being raised again this session. Mr. Brunner intends in- stead at once to introduce a Bill to accomplish the purpose he has in view, and to extend its bearing to all municipalities.

UMBRELLAS RECOVERED.—S. and W. DUTTON, Sankey-it. Warrington.—Advt. THE SHIP CANAL.—WEAVER POOL. A correspondent writing on the subject of the recent voyage of a large steamer from Weaver Pool, to Scotland says There are not wanting indi- cations that Weaver Pool will be an extremely busy spot on the Shin Canal in a brief space of time. There is now in course of construction a jetty about 1,000 feet long capable of accommodating six vessels of large size. This jetty is situate just at the entrance to the canal from the Weaver Pool, and consists of a stage on the Frodsham Marsh side of the canal and an island jetty. The stage is now completed, and the first row of piles for the jetty have been driven, and the work is being pushed forward as rapidly as possible. The traffic will be worked in this manner. The flats and other small craft will lie on the inside of the island jetty, and the large vessels on the outside, and the cargoes will be transferred from one to the other by means of twelve power- ful cranes. The canal at this part is :extremely wide, and the jetty will in no way be a hindrance to the moving traffic. It is in con- templation to construct several other jetties, and the trade of the place may be expected to soon become very brisk.'

ALLEGED STABBING BY A SCHOOL BOY AT WIDNES. On Monday, at the Widnes Police Court, before Messrs. G. Pilkington and E. Mather, a boy named James Cullen, aged twelve, living at 30, Catherine- at., was brought up charged with unlawfully wounding another named Thomas M'Cormick, aged 13, residing at 88, Midwood-st. M'Cormick said he was waiting outside St. Mary's School, Margaret-st., with some other boys, about half-past eleven, on Friday morning last for the prisoner to come out of school to play with him. The prisoner came running out of the school waving his hand. When the prisoner got up to him he hit him on the left shoulder with something he had in his hand. He felt blood flowing down his back afterwards, and he became weak and fell to the ground. Someone carried him home. He attended the same school as the prisoner, and he saw prisoner with a knife the same morning in school. He and the prisoner had always been good friends, and they had had no quarrel. Witness gave his evidence very reticently, and contra- dicted his statements in several particulars, and at- tempted to give the Bench the impression that he had inflicted the wound himself.—The prisoner said he had the knife in his hand, and witness rushed at him, and they both tell down, and the knife ran into him.—Dr. O'Keeffe described the wound, and said the boy was very weak from loss of blood. The wound must have been caused by some sharp instrument, and could not have been caused accidentally, but by a deliberate stab. —Jas. Hayes, Alfred-st., and John Dempsey, Midwood- st., schoolboys, spoke to the prisoner having the knife in his hand.—P.C. Bamford said the prisoner stated when he was apprehended that he had not done it on purpose. He also said that he had thrown the knifa on the railway, but it could not be found.—The prisoner was committed to the Quarter Sessions for trial, and was liberated on bail.

div.head: MR. H. SETON KARR, M.P., AND RAILWAY SERVANTS.
div.p: MR. H. SETON KARR, M.P., AND RAILWAY SERVANTS.

Mr. H. Seton Karr, M.P. for St. Helens, has had • some correspondence with Mr. John Fowles, secre— tary of the S. Helens branch of the Amalgamated society of Railway Servants in reference to his views on lailway questions. Mr. Seton Kerr has written that he has long been of opinion that hours •of work of railway servants, as of miners, consti- tuted a special case, and should be regulated by Act of Parliament unless the railway companies them- selves are prepared to regulate the hours in a manner satisfactory to the public. Regarding the details of any proposed Bill on the subject, he could at present give no definite pledge, and before deciding upon the details it would be as well to wait for the report of the Select Committee now taking evidence on the subject. The proposal of a ten hours day seemed most reasonable, and he was inclined to support it. He considered proposals for Board of Trade inquiries in all cases of serious accident to employes, and for the com- pulsory provision of self-acting coupling appliances and more effective protection for platelayers, to be fair and reasonable. In reference to the suggested granting of certificates of competency to all engine drivers, he wrote that he had introduced a Bill on the subject last session, but it was blocked. His name, however, was now on the back of a similar measure introduced this session by Mr. Fenwick. He again promised his support to an Employers' Liability Act on the lines introduced by Mr. T. Burt, M.P., providing for "contracting out" to be made illegal,and the amount of cotnpeasation to be un- limited. He was opposed to the payment ef members of Parliament as unnecessary, and also tending to lower the tone of Parliamentary life. On the question of the payment of official election expenses by the State, he was not prepared, as yet, to give any definite pledge on the subject.

RUNCORN WESLEYAN CIRCUIT SUNDAY SCHOOL UNION. The annual meeting of this Union was held in Brunswick Vestry, Runcorn, on Monday evening. the Rev. T. Wilkes presided and there were present the Revs. W. Arrowsmith and J. Hanby, Messrs. E. Taylor, secretary; R. Posnett and A. R. Norman Visitors, and representatives from Brunswick Mill Btow, Camden, Nelson-street, Halton and Weston. The Secretary presented the statistical report, which stated that there were :—Teachers and officers in town schools, 154 ; average afternoon attendance, 92. Scho- lars in town schools, 1,766; average afternoon atten- dance, 1,069. Teachers in country schools, 69; average afternoon attendance, 43. Scholars in country schools, 630 ; average afternoon attendance, 380. Total teachers, 223 ; total scholars, 2,396. The visitors, who had twice inspected each school in the Union during the year, pre- sented an exhaustive report, after which there was an interesting and practical discussion. At the close the unanimous thanks of the large meeting were tendered to the visitors for their excellent services and for the faithful and honest report they had rendered. For the ensuing year Mr. A. R. Norman and Mr. E. Marshall were appointed visitors, and the secretaries were re. appointed. The proceedings concluded by the Pinging of the Doxology.

PROPERTY SALE.—On Tuesday evening, at the Bear's Paw Inn, Frodsham, Mr. C. J. Hughes offered for sale a water corn mill, situated in Bradley, together with several cottages with gardens adjoining, in Kingsley. The bidding not reaching the reserve, the property was withdrawn. The solicitors in the transactions were Messrs. A. and J. E. Fletcher. SERIOUS CHARGE AGAIRST PUBLICAN.—At the Prod- sham Police Court, before Mr. Thomas and Dr. Steele, a charge of assaulting his wife and P.S. Doyle was pre- ferred against Thomas Morris, holder of the license of the Volunteer Inn, Main-it., Frodsham, on the night of the sth inst. The evidence showed that on the night in question the prisoner was very violent,and it was neces- sary to call in the assistance of P.S. Doyle. That officer, in taking Morris into custody, received a somewhat serious injury to the face. Mrs. Morris was crying out murder.—A fine of 40s. and costs was imposed, and the prisoner agreed to sign a statement that he would leave the house within a fortnight.

div.head: LYMM.
div.p: LYMM.

WALKING DAY.—On Monday the children connected with the Wesleyan Sunday School held their annual walking day. They assembled at the schools at two o'clock, and proceeded through the village, and after- wards marched back to the schools, where they were entertained to tea. They then went to Mr. Winstanley's field, and spent an enjoyable time till dark.

WESLEYAN ANNIVERSARY.—The eighty-ninth anniver- sary in connection with the Lymm Wesley Sunday School was held on Sunday. The preacher both morning and evening, was the Rev. Thomas Champness, editor of "Joyful sews." There were good congregations. Special hymns were sung by the scholars, the conductor being Mr. F. 0. Moston. A sacred cantata, entitled " Emmanuel," was given by the scholars and friends in the afternoon, and the collections taken at all services were in aid of the school funds.

MARRIAGH.—The marriage of Miss Agnes Lillie, ' second daughter of Mr. George Warburton, to Mr. Joseph Dale, Lymm, took place at' Oughtrington on Saturday afternoon. Tha bride was given away by her brother, Mr. T. H. Warburton, and was attired in lavender custume with hat to match. The bridesmaids were Misses Maggie and Daisy Warburton, sisters of the bride, and the the Misses Sallie and Esther Hampson, of Sale. They each carried a beautiful bouquet presented by Mrs. Hampson.
