MISCELLANEOUS.—For being drunk fines were imposed upon Jas. Whittle. Nicholas Kelly, Ernest W. Holden, and John Black.—Henry Kirchin and Margaret Small were bound over to be of good behaviour for three months for creating a breach of the peace.—A fine of Is. and costs was imposed upon Michael Price for allow- ing the chimney of his dwelling-house to be on fire.—A number of parents were fined for the breach of the Edu- cation Act.

div.head: LONDON ANARCHISTS.
div.p: THE LONDON ANARCHISTS.

ALARMING DISCOVERY. Early yesterday mornidg a policeman discovered a a bombshell, loaded with gun cotton, and having a fuse attached, in the roadway near Highgate Archway. The bomb had been recently placed there, out the fuse had not been lighted. The shell was taken to Scotland-yard, I and the police are prosecuting inquiries.
THINGS HEARD AND SEEN
AT WARRINGTON.

A contemporary says While-the licensed houses are being reduced, .temperance reformers are over- looking the fact that the remaining houses are everywhere being, greatly enlarged, the facilities for drinking being, thus enormously increased yearly." The Lion Hotel in Warrington may be mentioned as a case in point. The conversion which it is undergoing will transform it into a huge drinking place. So far as means of getting in and out are concerned, it will be like a rabbit warren. The extension may indeed be regarded as an addi- tional public house,-; And the question which ought to be raised, and which will, I believe, be raised at next licensing sessions is whether all this is per- missible under the old license. The opening into Ship Yard ought certainly not to be allowed. It is going back to the bad state of things of twenty years ago.

Really, Dr. Rentoul is too bad ! One of the latest victims of his chronic inaccuracy—to put it mildly—is Mr. Caine. Speaking in Bradford the. day after he spoke at Warrington, Dr. Rentoul had the presumption to say that Mr. Caine had ex- pressed the opinion that the Nonconformist churches in England were mere shops or establish- ments whose whale power was spent in raising the salaries of their ministers. Mr. Caine has written to Dr.:Rentoul for his authority, and what does the care- ful Rentoul say? Here are his very words: " The article or letter to which 1 referred appeared some months ago, but 1 have not the slightest idea as to the periodical, in which it appeared." Doesn't even know whether it was an article or a letter. an d has altogether forgotten the periodical in which it ap- pealed. These are the kind of " fax " which Dr. Rentoul thinks good enough for Tory audiences. Perhaps they are; Dr. Rentoul has had a large ex- perience of Tory audiences.

It is indeed a reform that the Warrington Corpor- ation should at length have decided that those who attend the reading room at the Museum shall have the privilege of reading the daily papers there. That. they should have been denied this necessary mental aliment so long is a reproach to the ad- ministration of that body; and I am afraid that a fear cn the part of the Conservatives in the Coun- cil that readers might get too enlightened on politi- cal matters, has had something to do with the de- lay im taking this most considerate step. How- ever, the electioneering spirit seems to have made its presence telt in the bosoms of our municipal rulers ; and hence, though care has been taken to preserve a due balance between the two classes o f political literature, the daily papeis are at length to be admitted to the reading room.

It has struck me that the Cbuncil might with advantage adopt the plan of blacking out the sporting news in these papers. This step has been taken by public authorities in the case of other reading rooms ; and the resalt has been a consider- able diminution of the number of readers of the papers, amply justifyinßthe drastic course adopted. Perhaps if the Corporation follow the example it would be well to do so in a month or two, so that they might be able to estimate the difference in point of the number of readers of the daily papers that would be made by the obliteration of the sporting news in them. I believe sporting readers are to a large extent men who confine themselves to the perusal of items pertaining to the betting interest ; and I think it is hardly fair that those who read the papers through should have them unduly detained from them by individuals who care only to wade through their favourite horsey columns.

The proposal of the Clarke Aspinall Memorial Committee, to appoint a police court missionary, for Warrington, Newton, and Widnes, whose duty it would be to use his endeavours for the reclamation of police court criminals, is a very happy and com- mendable one. I am pleased to see that the com- mittee are following the example of the promoters of the memorial to Cardinal Manning in determining that it shall assume a philanthropic form. But it does strike me that could such a missionary have been appointed some six to eight months ago, the appointment would have been a mole timely one, though, of course, the Aspinall Committee could not have brought their proposal forward sooner, because Mr. Aspinall has only recently died. It is a remark- able fact that there has been a considerable decline of police-business, both in Warrington and in the adjacent districts for a number of raonths past ; the decline has been so continuous as to argue that there is really taking place a permanent reform amongst the communities of this part of Lancashire. Whether the change for the worse that has taken place in trade has much to do with this improvement 1 can- not say,but there have been periods in Warrington, I think I can safely say, of much worse trade and much more crime and drunkenness than exist at present in the town. The reform is taking place without the aid of the police court missionary; and this seems to me all the happier augury for the success of his work, should one be appointed.

The annual report which has been prepared by Mr. J. E. Warren, the hon. sec., shows that the War- rington Football Club is in as flourishing a position as ever. Mr. Warren mentions that though old members, who did yeoman service at the club in days, were dropping out of harness, their places were being filled by younger players of great pro- mise, and AO auceesaful bad they been in that res- pect that he ventures to predict that the first team will not show signs of deterioration for years to come at least. The finances of the club are on a thoroughly sound footing. The receipts at the matches of this season had been greater than on any previous season, though at the same time the expenditure has been considerable heavier in some departments. Lovers of sterling football will be glad to hear that home matches have been arranged with Runcorn and Salford for next season.

" The Cricket Field" is a new weekly journal, the objects of which are pretty fully indicated by the title. The information in the first number certainly covers the whole field of cricket. There is cricket intelligence from the Universities, the large public schools, the counties, and from Scotland and Ireland. Another department is devoted to " Club Cricket," and under the heading of " How's That" there is a page of readable " pars " about cricket and cricke- ters. One of these tells us that the latest additions to the ranks of cricketers is H.R.H. the Duke of Albany, who has joined the Esher Cricket Club. He is seven years old. This first number of "The Cricket Field "besides containing a great variety of miscellaneous information interesting to cricketers, has a splendid full-page likeness of W. G. Grace, and a biographical account of the great player. There is also a capital illustrated article on the " English Team in South Africa" by George Brann. By the way, Ni e are told that Mr. S. M. Crosfield, the popu- lar Warrington captain," is a conspicuous example of what may result from giving It man a really fair I trial when he shapes well, for it must be admitted ' that his earlier experiences were not altogether encouraging."

I understand that there has recently been some little friction between Messrs. Pearson, Knowles and Co., and the Trades Unionists on a question raised by the latter as to the wages paid to and the hours worked by certain of the labourers employed at Dallam Forge. The local branch of the navvies' and general labourers' union passed a resolution in consequence of which Mr. John Price, secretary of the branch, and Mr. A. Chiel of Eccles, district secretary to the union, waited as a deputation upon the manager of Dallam Forge, and asked that the labourers in question might have their present wage of 18s. per week increased to EL and that they should work no more hours than the labourers in other departments,or if they did, be paid 6d. per hour overtime. The manager has since, 1 understand, informed the men concerned, directly, and not through the union, that they can_ not have the concessions desired.

The ways of the bicycle thief ate devious and peculiar. Sometimes the unsuspecting wheelman leaves his machine by the roadside or in the streets while he makes a„call, and returns to find that it has been "lifted by some unscrupulous indivi- dual. At another time a bicycle or a tricycle is let out on hire and the hirer fails to turn up again. This has been the experience of the Burton Cycle Company, of Warrington. A short time ago a young fellow of prepossessing appearance and faultlessly attired, came to the company's works and hired a machine "just for the spin," but the " spin " was of rather long duration, i and nothing more was heard of the machine or ts, rider until a detective came upon the scene to maki a few inquiries. It then transpired that the machine had been taken to the establishment of Mr. Mason, in Renshaw-st., Liverpool, and there ' offered for saleVor .£B. Mr. Mason. suspecting that all was not right, called in a detective who detained the would-be seller of other people's property. The

result was that the Burton Cycle Company were more fortunate than some others in having their machine returned. It is stated that the young man who attempted the fraud held the position of a second mate on a Liverpool •vesseL.and would have sailed the next morning had not his little schema miscarried. He is said to have been well connected, and we do not hear that he has been prosecuted.

The note of alarm has been sounded in the New-- ton Division. There•is uneasiness in the Conserva- tive camp, and energetic preparations are conse— quently in progress. The biggest fight on record,in this division is predicted, and !dr. Legh is now fairly on his mettle. It is evidently very surpris— ing to him that he is not. to be allowed to walk. over, and it is felt on all hands, that no stone must. be left unturned, nor any opportunity allowed to pass of adding to the chances of victory. Ttie• Liberals are working quietly; there is no flourish of trumpets, but nevertheless when the battle- note is sounded, every lover of the cause will be found at the post of duty.
MERLIN.

div.head: DISCOVERY _OF HUMAN REMAINS. IN
div.p: DISCOVERY _OF HUMAN REMAINS. IN
FRIAR'S GREEN.

In the course of excavations at present going on In a passage on Friar's Green, Warrington, between Burgess's chandlery and the cottages close by, for the laying of a- sewer through Friar's Green, large quantities Jf human bones and skulls, and in one case an almost complete skeleton, were found yester- day. The spot in question is where in 1886 the foundations of St. Austen's Priory were discovered. This priory was founded in the thirteenth century, and was demolished along with other religious houses by Henry VIII. Numerous relics of the priory have been discovered at intervals since 1886. The skeleton was found in a strong oak ccffi.n of an inch thick, and of about seven feet in length, the wood of which was in good preservation. The remains, which were discovered at the depth of about 11 feet, were subsequently re-buried.

div.head: ST. PETER'S CHURCH NEWTON.
div.p: ST. PETER'S CHURCH NEWTON.

FOUNDATION STONE, LAYING. Beautiful weather favoured the ceremony of lay- ing the-foundation stone of the proposed extension of St. Peter's Church, Newton, on Tuesday. For some time past now it has been, seen that some alter- ation was necessary in the church, in order to give I more accommodation for worshippers, and also with I an. ultimate view of entirely restoring and enlarging the church. For the present however it is only pro- posed to erect a new chancel, organ chamber, south choir aisle, vestry and heating chamber. It is also proposed to take down the east end of the church, and by enlarging it at both sides, provide accommo- dation for 800 persons, the present seating being for 600. The contractors for the work are Messrs. Win- nard, of Wigan; and the architects Al essrs,Demaine and Brierley, of York and Westminster; and the estimated cost is about £2,500, the greater portion of which has already, been collected. The proceedings on Tuesday comprised a proces- sion of school children, several of whom carried banners, from the school to the church, service in the church, the laying of the stone, and an address by the Bishop of Liverpool. A file of volunteers from thelocal Company of the 6th V.R., K. L. R., accompanied by the band of the regiment, was present, and took up a position round the site, under the command of Sergeant-Major Parks, There was a short service in the church after which a procession to the site was formed, consisting of the choir, clergy and building committee, the con- gregation bringing up the rear. Around the stone were gathered the Bishop of Liverpool, Rev. H. Monk, Canen Whitley, Canon Penrhyn, T. R. Mat- thews, T. W. Johnson and several other clergymen, besides a large number of ladies and gentlemen. After another short service,, the Rev. 11. Monk addressing Col. McCorquodale, said on behalf of the Building Committee he offered for his acceptance a trowel, which with the mallet and square presented by Mr. Winnard, the contractor, he should use to place that corner stone, which he now requested him to do.

In the cavity beneath the stone was then placed a bottle containing silver coins of the realm, a "Church Guardian, and a programme of the cere- mony that day. Colonel McCorquodale then proceeded to lay the stone. The trowel which was of silver with ivory handle bore the following inscription—" Presented to Colonel McCorquodale, in honour of the laying of the foundation stone of St. Peter's Church, New- ton. May 10, 1892." On the square, which also was of silver, beautifully chased was the similiar inscription. The mallet which was of ivory was presented by the builder and was also inscribed. The Bishop then delivered an address. He said he should not like to allow that occasion to pass without saying a few suitable words to those who had assem- bled that day. He considered it was a high honour and a great privilege to be allowed to be present at such a ceremony. He took a great interest in the question of the increase in the number of churches, and also in their enlargement and improvement. During the twelve years he had had the honour of being the bishop of the diocese he had been present at the consecration of no fewer than 30 new churches, in addition to the present one. When be came into the diocese he found only 170 churches for twelve hundred thousand people, and he had lived to see the day when 30 more churches had been added to the number, and at least five more were being built, and one more about to be greatly improved, as in the case of that church, the foundation stone of the chancel of which had been laid that day. Why there were so few churches in the South-West of Lancashire he could not pretend to say. There was only one incumbent to at least 6,000 people, and making every allowance for the large number of Roman Catholics, who worshipped God according to their own views, and the Noncon- formists, who preferred their own forms of worship, that left an immense number of persons who had been debarred up to the present time from the grace which the Church of England ought to provide for all her children. He came from a diocese in which there were 950 incumbents, and a proportionate number of parish churches, and yet the population did not exceed half of what he had in his own diocese that day. He had al- ways considered it to be his duty to promote in every way he could the building of more churches, in order Ls provide the inhabitants of the diocese with the means of obtaining the grace according to the blessed mode and ritual of the Church of England. He thanked God for what had been done by the help of the laity, and liberal men, whom God had stirred up to build churches. Be hoped, if his life was spared, to see more churches conse- crated. One church was about to be consecrated few miles from that place—he alluded to Haydock—and he trusted that on that occasion. the 25th June, many clergymen would be present. He could not refrain from saying that that church was not exactly what a church ought to be. They knew that churches were somewhat differently built to what they used tobe, and during the last 300 or 400 years many churches had been built which were very little credit to the architects, or to the blessed services of the Church of England. When one looked at the grand cathedrals which were built by their forefathers hundreds of years ago, they had every reason to be ashamed of themselves for not having followed in their footsteps. Referring to St. Peter's, he said that it would be very much improved with the addition of the chancel. He expressed a hope that it would often be filled with spiritual communicants. He believed that many had been turned away in the past owing to the insufficiency of accommodation, and he hoped that the present extension wo..ild meet require- ments. Although bricks and mortar did not make Christians, yet he thought that if they built churches in which to worship God, they ought to erect the finest edifices. The Bishop expressed an opinims that a tower to the church would be a desirable addition, and in con- clusion said that he always felt a deep interest in Newton ; for in the days gone by, when the only building of any importance was the Railway Hotel, all church movements of any importance were discussed there. The Benediction was shortly after pronounced and the gathering dispersed. The Volunteers were afterwards entertained t) dinner at the Pied Bull Hotel, and the workmen employed on the building were similarly regaled at the Blue Bell Hotel, by the Building Committee.

div.head: IHE ANCOATS SCUTTLING CASE.
div.p: IHE ANCOATS SCUTTLING CASE.
VERDICT OF WILFUL MURDER.

The Manchester coroner on Thursday morning re- sumed the inquiry into the death of Peter Kennedy. aged 16, who met his death at the at the hands of the Ancoates scuttlers. Three young men named Allan, Fleming' and Davidson, were arrested by the police for causing Kennedy's death. Evidence was given to the effect that the prisoners said they had " dosed " de- ceased,and the jury returned a verdict of wilful murder against all three.

div.head: PA.RNELL- -WOOD CASE.
div.p: THE PA.RNELL- -WOOD CASE.

In the London Appeal Court, on Thursday, the appeal by one of the parties to the Parnell v. Wood probate suit against two orders made on a compromise in the probate action which came before Mr. Justice Jeune, was dismissed, the parties being ordered to pay their own costs.

div.head: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.
div.p: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.-MONDAY.

The Speaker took the chair at 3 p.m. PETITION. —Petitions were presented by Mr. T. C. Edwards-Mpss, from the Temperance Mission Lodge, Warrington, to prohibit the sale of intoxicating liquor to children under 16. Watsisi NOMENCLATURE.—Mr. THOMAS ELLIS asked the President of the Board of Agriculture whether he was awar:, of the dissatisfaction existing among Welsh scholar., geologists, and others with the inaccuracy and incompluteness of the place names in the Ordnance Sur- vey may, of Wales, and whether he would take steps to secure tlt aid and co-operation of Welsh scholars to secure W./racy in the nomenclature of these maps. Mr. CHAPLIN : 1 was not aware of the dissatisfaction to which the hon. member refers. I think the question might with advantage be considered by the Departmental Committee that has Just been appointed, and I will bring the matter under their notice. Maras in Paison.—The HOME SECRETARY, replying to Mr. P. O'Brien, said he knew of no sufficient reason why the prison rules should be altered so as to permit the removal of all female prisoners to a public hospital during confinement. VOLUNTEERS AND POLITICAL CLUBS.—Mr. MATTHEWS informed Sir W. Lawson that when Volunteers were ' made honorary members of political clubs and supplied with intoxicants there was no violation of the laws regulating the sale of intoxicating liquors. The BUSINESS OF THE Flonse.—Mr. T. Ellis and Mr. Morton asked whether Supply was going to be taken this Session, and in reply Mr. BALFOUR said that he could give no answer until they had got on with the business of which he (the first Lord) had given notice. Tan SMALL HOLDINGS BILL.—The House then went into committee on the Small Agricnitural Holdings Bill, when a number of amendments were disposed of. HOUSE OF LORDS. —TUESDAY. The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack at katf-past five o'clock. The Liverpool Overhead Railway Bill was read a third time, and passed. A bill to amend the law relating to Joint Stock Companies was read a fitst time. The House adjouined at 5.40. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TIIESDAT.
motion.

The Speaker took the chair at two o'clock. PETlTlONS.—Petitions in favour of the Bill to prevent the sale of drink to children under 18 were presented by Mr. Brunner from temperance societies and others in Runcorn, Winsford, and Halton, and by Sir W. Houlds- worth from the Manchester Guardians and the Lanca- shire and Cheshire Band of Hope Union. RAILWAY RATES.—Mr. Fereesss, on the consideration of the Eastern Railway Rates Bill as amended, moved an amendment for reckoning timber by "measurement weight" as well as "machine weight." On a division, the amendment was defeated by 148 to 135. The Bill was then read a third time. ACCIDENTS FROM FIREARMS.—The Home SECRETARY, answering Sir J. Bain as to the numerous accidents and cases of murder and suicide caused by revolvers, said a license for a revolver was already required by law, and the Government did not propose to introduce any fur- ther legislation dealing with the carrying of such fire- arms. tiOVERNSIENT BUSINESS.—Mr. BALFOUR informed Dr. Tanner that a vote on account would be taken before Whitsuntide, but it would not be necessary for more than three weeks. Supply would not be dealt with. SMALL HOLDINGS BILL.—The House again went into tommittee on the Small Agricultural Holdings Bill, when several clauses were, after discussiou, agreed to. EVENING srrrlNG. The Speaker again took the chair at nine o'clock. Mr. CALDWELL called attention to the working of the Crofters' Holdings (Scotland) Act, and moved, " That, in the opinion of this House, the Crolderh' Holdings Act ought to be extended and amended in the following respects, namely, that the provisions of the .4c1., be extended to small leaseholders ; that all improvements made by the tenant or his predel%essors in the same family, and not paid for by the landlard, be expressly exempted from the payment of rent ; that adewiate powers be given to the commissioners to enlarge present holdings, and that to this end an inquiry be instituted with the view of ascertaining authoritatively the amount of land suitable and available for that purpost." Dr. CLARK seconded, and Mr. SHAW STEWART MOVCd as an amendment ;-- " That while, in the opinion of this House, it is important that all improvements made by a crofter or his predecessors in title should be fully pro- tected, the main improvement on the system of land tenure in the Highlands is to be sought in the extension of the principle of land purchase to that part of the country." Considerable debate followed, in the course of which the LORD ADVOCATE declined to assent to Mr. Caldwell's motion, but accepted the amendment. HOUSE OF COMMONS. —WEDNESDAY. - EDNESDAY. The Speaker took the chair at a quarter past twelve o'clock, but a house was not made, through the :medium of a count, until twenty-five minutes to one o'clock. MUNICIPAL CORPORATIONS ACT (1882) AmExn- MENT BILL. Mr. MATTINSON moved the second readinr; of the Municipal Corporations Act (1882) Amen,lmmt Bill, the object of which, he said, was to removo dielentrics that had arisen in readjusting municipal bouadaries to meet the shifting of population and its increase in particular districts. He pointed to the circumstances of various boroughs, and especially to that of Liverpool, to justify an amendment of the hw. Fle proposed that a simple majority of the Town Council, or in default of their' action a certain num tr-r of electors, should initiate proceedings by petitioning the Privy Council. Mr. NEVILLE moved that tile Bill be read a second time that day six months, and said it was really a measure to " gerrymander " the wards of Liverpool, in order to enable the Tories of Liverpool to maintain their long-continued, but now threatened, ascendency in that place. Mr. Picton seconded the amendment. Mr. Forwood, Mr. Willox and Mr. W. 11. Cross defended the measure, while Mr Picton and Mr. T. P. O'Connor described it as designed to serve Tory ends. Mr. Neville'a amendment was re- jected by a majority of 83, and the bill was read a second time. Mr. Healy moved that the bill should be referred to a Select Committee, and Mr. Mattinson ob- jected, the debate consequently standing adjourned at a quarter to six.

Miscetr-axxotrs.—Bills to amend the Married Women's Property Act (1882) and to amend the law in regard to stamping of documents were read a first time, and on the motion of Mr. Jasper More a Select Committee on corn sales was appointed. The House adjourned at six o'clock. HOUSE OF LORDS.—THIIRSDAY.
- - --- The Lord Chancellor took his seat at :quarter-past

four. THE LAW OF PROPERTY.—On consideration of the report of amendments to the Conveyancing and Law of Property Act., 1881 Amendment Bill.—Lord HURSCRELL moved the insertion of a new sub-section.—The Marquis of SALISBURY opposed the amendment, mainly on the ground that the court had the power to give or refuse relief on the motion of the lessee.—The Earl of Krona- mix supported the amendment.—The motion was nega- tived without a division. The Bill passed through its report stage, and the, .Bouse adjourned at 5.15. HOUSE OF COMMONS.--THURSDAY. The Speaker took the chair at three o'clock. CHK&P TRAINS FOR WORKING PEOPLE.—On the order for the consideration of the Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire Railway (Extension to London, &C.) Bill, Mr. Pictersgill moved to insert a new clause in the bill requiring the Company to run cheap trains for working people between London and all stations within a dis- tance of ten miles, such trains to arrive at the London terminus up to eight o'clock in the morning. It was pointed out that special terms for workmen had already been offered by the Company, and Mr. Pickersgill, hav- ing regard to this concession, withdrew his amendment, and the bill was ordered for third reading. SWEETS AND BEER.—Mr. JOHNSTON asked the Home Secretary if his attention had been called to a handbill issued by a publican at Stepney statiqg tha.t a. present

would be given to every child purchasing beer on Saturday May 7, and whether such an offer could leg- ally be prohibited. Mr. Conyebeare asked whether the right hon. gentleman was aware of the extent to which this practice prevailed both in London and in the pro- vinces, and whether he would do his best to bring the offenders to justice. Mr. MATTHEWS said he was ad- vised that such handbills were not illegal, but any case which was brought to the attention of the police would be referred to the licensing authorities. QuksTioss.—ln reply to Mr. GULLY, Mr. A. J. BArsotra said it would be useless to introduce the District Councils Bill unless there was some hope of its passing into law in the present session. He did not think it likely that the bill would be introduced before Whitsuntide. The right hon. gentleman informed Mr. FOWLER that he had no objection to the question of Civil Service superannuation being investigated by a Select Committee provided there was no undue delay. In answer to Mr. F. EVANS, Mr. J. W. LOWTHER said Her Majesty's Government had declined to assent to the Convention between the United States Government and the Government of Newfound- land, having been unable to depart from the position that the negotiation of a convention between the United States and Newfoundland must proceed pari passa with the negotiation of an arrangement between Canada and the United States. SMALL HOLDINGS BILL &c.—The House again went into Committee on the Small Agricultural Holdings Bill. Afterwards the Chancellor of the Exchequer moved the appointment of a Select Committee to consider the financial relations between England, Scotland, and Ireland. Mr. S. EVANS moved an amendment to include Wales in the inquiry. The CHANCILLOR of the EXCHE- QUER said it was impossible to constitute Wales a separ- -,te financial entity, and on that ground he resisted the The debate was adjourned at midnight.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.

SAVED " BUT 1J NCLEGSNBRA.TB Sarah Morton. a girl of fourteen, was charged at the Warrington Police Court, on Saturday, with having stolen sixpence from Rose Higgins, aged nine. It appeared that on Friday Mrs. Higgins sent her daughter Rose, to redeem a pair of boots at Mrs. Tunstall's shop, and while the girl was counting her money in the shop. the defendant, who was also there, snatched sixpence and ran away with it. Information was given to the police, and Detective Sergeant Monaghan went to Morton's house and saw the defendant. She at first denied having stolen the sixpence, and said" I was saved the other night in the army. You do not think I would steal it after being saved, do,you, Mr. Monaghan ?" On being told she would have to go to the police-station she admitted the theft, and having spent the money in sweets and chip potatoes.—Defendant's father, a respect- able man, said he remembered his daughter coming home one night and saying that she had been at the army and had been saved. He was afraid, however, that it had not got very deep into her heart.—The bench dismissed defendant with a caution.

ACCOSTING THE CHIEF CONSTABLE.—A man named Charles McNasby was charged with wandering at large in Church-st., on the previous afternoon.—The Chief Cons-able (Mr. Hunt) was proceeding down Church-st., when the prisoner who was walking behind him, began to use bad language. He accused Mr. Hunt of being the man who had given him three months at Liverpool ; and acted in such a strange manner that a large crowd gathered round. A constable made his appearance, and the prisoner was brought to the Police Station.—The Bench now remanded the case in order that an examin- ation as to the state of the man's mind might be made by a medical man. THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MAY 14, 1892.

The state ot affairs in Afghanistan is said to be assum ing a critical aspect. The rumours of intrigues by th- Ameer's agents among the Afridis and other tribes have been confirmed, and it is stated that the Indian Govern° ment has warned the Ameer. - -

----- -- According to information that has reached Berlin from Zanzibar, Emin Pasha has become totally blind. Justices Day and Charles held on Tuesday that pub- licans were bound to accommodate whatever uutnber of menthe military authorities might please to billet upon them.

Each of the three daughters of the late William Astor will receive 2,000,000 dols., and when the other bequests are deducted there will be in the neighbourhood of 60,000,000 dols. to be handed over to John Jacob his son. The widow will receive an annual income while she lives of 500,000 dols. A youth named Kennedy died at Manchester Infirm- ary, on Sunday night, having been stabbed in the left aide in Ancoats, a low quarter of the city. Two youths are in custody. The Scotch steel-warkers' strike terminated on Thursday, a 10 per cent, reduction having been accepted. Twenty thousand pounds has been bequeathed by Mr. John Henry Fox, of Norton, near Stockton-on-Tees for the purpose of building arid endowing almshouses in the village, on condition that the land on which to build them is given. While practising gun drill on shore at Malta, a seaman, named John Church, on bcard H.M.S. Collingwooa, was killed. A young man, named Arch, was sentenced to death at Glasgow on Monday, for the murder of his cousin, Annie Campbell, by cutting her throat. By the fall of a roof in Manvers Main Colliery, Mexborough, South Yorkshire, a miner, named Albert Johnson, and James Wood, a boy, were killed on Monday. In accordance with the agreement of matters last week, the cotton mills in the Ashton-under-Lyne district re-commenced work on Monday. The operatives at the Stalybridge Spinning Company still remain out, owing to dissatisfaction with the list of persons chosen for employment. In connection with proceedings arising out of the affairs of the late Mr. H. S. Whalley, solicitor, of Black- burn and Southport, it transpired at the Chancery Court, St. George's Hall, Liverpool, on Monday, that the liabilities were £147,096, in addition to three other claims not yet adjudicated upon. Following the example of Mr. M'Carthy, Mr. Sexton has placed upon the motion paper a motion for the re- jection of the Irish Local Government Bill. Mr. John Corbett, M.P., has presented the Hill estate, comprising 30 acres and a mansion-house, with money for alterations and endowment, amounting in all to £10,500, for a hospital for the Stourbridge district. The Anarchist Meineau, who was arrested at Liege a few days ago, has confessed that he was the author of an attempt to blow up the house of Councillor Renson, who presided over the proceedings against the Anarchists at the Assize Court.

In the House of Commons on Thursday the Manches- ter, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire Railway (Extension to Loudon) Bill was ordered for the third reading. At Welshpool, on Wednesday night, Griffith Jones, a gnarl on the Cambrian railway, was killed by falling between the platform and a train.

The opening match of the Warrington season took place on Saturday, when the locals met Leyland. The' weather, although fine. was marred by coldness, which rendered matters anything but agreeable to the large crowd that bad assembled. The demands made by the Lancashire executive for the Colt's match at Werneth put the sides on an equal footing, and Captain Manson winning the tess, of course elected to bat on a capital wicket. The opening essays were indeed promising, for Smith, treating Nash lightly, runs came at a rapid pace, and 52 runs had beea chronicled before J. J. Crosfield was bowled by Hill, the latter having relieved Nash at 32. Smith's career came to an end a run later, he hav- ing made 44 in clinking style. Lee was bowled after making five, but Captain Manson and Clarke treated the spectators to some fine hitting. The fielders were spread-eagled, but to no purpose,and boundary hits were common. With 86 runs totalled, Clarke was bowled by Tongue, and in 2 overs, R. Bell, W. Podmore, and Clarke were all dismissed, the latter with two successive deliveries. Captain Manson had a useful partner in W. Dutton, and at 123 Nash resumed at his old end, and thel last‘comer was caught at 130. With only three runs on Jefferson was bowled by Tongue, and Captain Manson preferring to hit out at the close, succumbed to an easy catch, and the venture closed for 139. Included in Cap- tain Manson's score were seven fours. On Leyland going in to bat, B. Kershaw and Padgett were the first pair, R. Smith and J. J. Crosfield opening the attack. Only seven runs were on the board when Kershaw drove one over the bowler's head, and Dutton effectod a neat catch. Padgett and Gerrard raised the hopes of their admirers for a time, but Smith, sending down an extra fast one, Padgett was sent back, having made 10. Pyke had but a short stay, whilst Hill w,as bowled with- outscoring. Wickets continued to fall at short inter- vals, but trouble coming from Gerrard and Brown, Captain Manson relieved -Smith. His third ball proved fatal to Gerrard, and Baxendale joined Brown. At 67 Bell took the ball from Crosfield, but the change proved expensive, as his two overs cost 15 runs, so the original bowler again took up the attack. A separation was brought about at 88, Podmore accounting for Brown, whilst a capital catch by Captain Manson at short slip dismissed Baxendale, with no addition to the , score. div.head: SHAMEFUL CONDUCT TO
div.p: SHAMEFUL CONDUCT TO

CHILDREN. At the Warrington Borough Magistrates' Court, on Tuesday, before Mr. R. Garnett, James Hunter, general labourer, of Lovely-lane, was charged with indecently, insulting conduct in that thoroughfare, towards Margaret Handles, wife of John Bandies, 54, Lovely-lane, on the 17th ult., and on the 9th inst. towards a little girl named Taylor. The evi- dence disclosed the most cool and revolting shame- lessness on the part of the prisoner, and he was sen- tenced to three months' imprisonment with hard labour. At the same Court, on Tuesday, Richard Lambert, who had been lodging for two years at Old-road,Latch- ford, was charged with indecently assaulting, on the iron bridge, Arpley, about a quarter to five o'clock on Monday afternoon, a little girl, aged 61 years, named Marguerite Wheeler, daughter of George Wheeler, labourer, 2, Stanley-street. From the evidence it appeared that a young man named Francis Quinn, of Latchford, and two men named Michael Bro- derick and John Duffy, were having a walk, and in crossing the iron bridge, came upon the prisoner in the act of committing the offence, he being quite sober. Quinn,who knew him, said, "You are a coward, Dick," and Broderick said, " I have a good mind to punch your head—to do a trick like that." The prisoner replied, "You had better get it done," and got up, and I then he and Broderick had a fight, Lambert getting the worst of it. Then he pulled out a knife, and they let him go. They proceeded on their walk and sat down, and presently they saw the prisoner coming with a stick towards them in a threatening manner. Broderick took off his coat, and he and his companions prepared for another fight. The prisoner rushed at Broderick,aiming a blow at him with the stick, threatening he would slaughter them. Broderick ran at him and got him on the ground, and with the assistance of a crowd that had collected, got his stick from him. Broderick also hit him a number of blows with it. They were carrying him to the Police Station, when some constables came up, and he was given into custody.—The prisoner, in answer to the charge, said, "I never meddled with the girl, to my knowledge.—He was committed for trial to the Assizes.

div.head: ECLIPSE OF THE MOON.
div.p: THE ECLIPSE OF THE MOON.

Astronomers, in England, at all events, had on Wednesday night a most favourable opportunity for observing the eclipse of the moon. For the greater part of the evening the aky was perfectly clear, and the progress of the eclipse could for some hours be uninterruptedly noted, Towards the end of the eclipse there was for a time a change in the conditions, which may have been highly unwelcome to scientific men, but greatly added to the beauty of the scene in the eyes of unscientific observers. A bank of light clouds floated between the spectators and the moon, and produced a second partial eclipse, with lovely and swiftly varying effects. These clouds, with all their beauty, promised to be very tantalising at half-past twelve, when most people wished to note the actual emer- gence of tke moon from the earth's true shadow ; but nothing could well have been prettier and more interesting than what actuary happened. Just as if they were consciously answering to the wishes of the impatient spectators, the clouds cleared off from the face of the moon a minute or two before ' the cessation of the eclipse, and left a clear view of the lunar globe graduallSt resuming its proper shape. Then there was seen the brigotening of the moon's rim in token that the penumbra was also 1 moving away, and the whole of this secondary 1 clearing of shadow from the face of the moon was I plainly and beautifully visible. The eclipse was almost a total one, nineteen- twentieths of the disc being obscured. The first contract with the penumbra occurred at four min- utes to eight, but it was not until ten minutes past nine that any trace of the shadow became discernible. The eclipse was at the greatest at fifty-three minu- tes past ten, and the last contact with the shadow occurred at thirty-six minutes after midnight. At nine minutes to two in the morning the moon was again clear of the penumbra. The progress of the eclipse was watched with great interest by u largo number of people.

div.head: CONVICTION OF DEEHING.
div.p: THE CONVICTION OF DEEHING.
A LYING CONFESSION.

The " Melbourne Argus " states that Deeming, or, as I he is better knswn there, Williams, has confessed to the Rev. Mr. Scott, the prison chaplain, that he made four attempts to murder his wife, Emily Mather—nameiy, ' once in London. shortly after their marriage ; once at the Federal Coffee Palace, Melbourne, and twice in Andrew- street, Windsor. He took the house in Windsor, he said, on December 18 last, and slept that night on a mattress. Oa the night of the 18th, in obedience to the commands of his mother's spirit, he made an attempt to cut his wife's throat, but she suddenly awoke, and he was thus prevented from carrying out his design. The following night he awoke at two o'clock and found a candle burn- ing beside his wife, who was sitting up in bed peeling an 1 apple with a large clasp knife. He wrenched the knife from her hand and cut her throat. He then rushed out out of the house much terrified at what he had done, and at daybreak found himself on the pier at St. Kilda. Fla there saw a man fishing, and gave him £lO to bury ' the body. Deeming declares that he knew nothing of how the murdered woman was buried until he heard it in Western Australia. He cannot account for his pur- chase of the cement beforehand, because he said he was not himself. He cannot accounts for the wounds on kis wife's head. He repeated the story of the man he calls Old Ben, at Rainhill, and to whom he alleges he gave £5O to secure the disappearance of his first wife. Emily Mather, he declared, committed the Rainhill murders. A knife has been found among his luggage which agrees with the prisoner's description of the one used by him at Windsor. The prisoner's demeanour has altered a good deal during the last day or two, as is shown by the attention which he is now paying to the religious preparations for his approaching end. The other day he asked the gaol authorities to let him have the large Bible which was found amongst his luggage when lie was arrested in Western Australia. The request was complied with ,but despite his improved demeanour he positively refuses to see the prison chaplain, the Rev. Mr. Scot. ALLEGED BREACH OF GAOL REGULATIONS. Deeming's solicitor, Mr. Marshall Lyle, has written to the Sheriff, calling his attention to the breach of the gaol regulations committed by Messrs. Scott and Whitton in divulging the particulars of the confessions made to them by the condemned man. Their want of reticence may, he states, possibly result in the collapse , of the proposed appeal to the Privy Council. Deeming, it is stated, is desirous of bequeathing 'llls head to the medical faculty with a view to a thorough examination being made of the condition of his brain No petition has yet been lodged by Deeming, nor his 1 representatives, for leave to appeal against the sentence of death passed on him in Australia. The Judges are quite prepared to consider at once any appeal of this nature that may be presented to them.

?Letter to the elittor.
TORY ESTIMATES OF TORY CAPACITY.
sir,—Recent political outpouring has convinced me, if
indeed it needed further proof, of the very low—not to
say contemptuous—estimate the men of " light and leading" of the Primrose persuasion have given of the understanding of the rank and file of the party. Both

locally and generally is this the case; from the Premier to a Pierpoint they are offering their followers the most unmitigated " pobs "—political pabulum -which it would be an insult to offer to mere robust intelligences. Dr. Houston having been photographed in his Q.C. gown, Mr. R. Pierpoint is jealous, and gives us to understand, with many significant nods, that he could be" photoed" in an M.A. habit. Ali ! now then ! And if that is not sufficiently " taking " he could pose as a Warrington 'Volunteer. What a pity he could not add—and a Cheshire cabbage-cutter! In the name of good sense—if any change of raiment will improve a Tory candidate,let the change be .Ifected. Such sartorial silliness ought to be beneath usitia by one aspiring to legislate for his country. As a maa:l political education such stuff as this is distinctly stet calculated to raise anybody's political intelligence. And this is a sample of the rest. The Tory leaders treat the working-man rather as tools to be worked with than as national beings to be reasoned with. Hence that instrument of political enveighnent the Primrose Leauge which is designed to pander to the innate fiunkyism of those willing to sell their political birth- right for a temporary and latently contemptuous social notice from their" betters." But the climax of political absurdity—and worse---is reached when we find the responsible head of the Government vapouring as to what will be done if the country—by its elective voice—decides in favour of Home Rule. "some Rule was not a message of peace, but it was a message of civil religious war.' How like in colour the Orange and the Primrose League ! This means that if Ulster cannot get or cannot keep what it has no right to have,, it will show its loyalty to the Crown by exhibiting its disloyalty to the people. If its legislative wishes are disregarded it will resort to arms. Well if Ulster does attempt to flourish its dagger of lath and line the ditches—it will very soon find itself forming the inside lining of a goal, as now those who utter such foolishness should of a lunatic asylum. But if Home Rule was accepted by the country— He did not believe it would be a final verdict, and this strange and anomalous condition of things fully justifies those precautions which the constitution had happily taken against hasty or subversive decisions." So! If the country, by its representatives in Commons decides in favour of giving Ireland •Home Rule—Ulster and the House of Lords will say no ! In that case I think both will find they are kicking against the pricks. In all this there is much material for reflection, especially where Primrose Leagueism finds a "local habitation and a name."—Yours, &c., Penketh, May 9, 1892.
JOAN PEERS.
MINING ROYALTIES AND LABOUR REFORMS. VARY OBTRCTIONS. .

Sir,—Of all the labour questions now demanding sound and urgent reform that of mining royalties is the most vital to us a mining nation. Yet such Tory M.P.'s as Dr. Rentoul, and such Tory candidates as Mr. R. Pier- point, who claim supreme fitness for ruling the nation are so shamefully ignorant an shamelessly brazen-faced, that when the vital question was submitted to them at the public meeting held on April 25th, the farmer shallow statesman gloried in publicly declaring that he "did not understand mining royalties : " he "had never made a study of the matter; he was not a Radical." He neither knows nor care that mine rents and mineral royalties are ruining our English trade, and starving thousands of my fellow working-men, their wives, and helpless children, all in order to foster the Shylock greed of great landlords and that, as Lord R. Churchill confesses in his letter just written to Mr. Arnold White, Liberal Unionist candidate for the Tyne- side Division of Northumberland, "Our land laws were framed by the landed interest for the advantage o the landed interest (invariably Tories), and foreign policy was directed by that interest to the same end. Political Power passed very considerably from the landed interest to the manufacturing capitalist interest." "And," he adds, "our whole fiscal state revenue system was shaped by this latter power to its own advantage, foreign policy being also made to coincide." Then there is the cursed strong drink revenue—the revenue of blood, crime, poverty, immorality and death. Its dire effects infinitely exceed all other .known evils eombined i--Oppression with its groans,. sighs, hunger, and tears ; war, with all its ghastly panics ; pestilence, with its sickening blight ; famine, with its keen teeth gnawing away the vitals of life. What man with a mind and line, fit for the social duties of ordinary citizenship, to say nothing of the nobler qualities essential to a Ruler of the British Empire,would be as dumb on these matters as Mr. Pierpoint was on April 25th? It is evident that he has not the fitness for taking upon himself such duties as involve the destinies of our nation, or he most assuredly would not have utterly •failed as he did upon such vital questions. He was thoughtless, therefore speechless, on such matters. For as the Bible says "Out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaketh." It is high time that all labouring men especially, opened their eyes to the painful fact that both Tories and Liberals have too long and too often used us for their own ends and interest. Let us in future vote on all occasions for such men as know our sufferings and just requirements, and pledge themselves to secure our social, commercial, and moral rights. It is to place every passible hiadrance to prevent us securing such right that Mr. Pierpoint, and others with his political views, object to payment of M.P.'s and to the Eight Hours system en which matters questions were sent him. Alas ! says Lawyer Rentoul, he had never made a study of " how to remove Mining Royalties," content with ths present state of things. £10,000,000 plundered annually by landlords as Royalties on mines! The returns for 1891 show that the total production of pig iron is between 24,500,000, and 24,750,000 tons, while out of this weight Great Britian made 1,059,174 tons less than was made in the United States. Compared to the world's total pro. suction of pig iron, in 1891 England has only made ,bout one third, though in 1854 she (says Mr. C. M. -ercy one of the oldest living authorities on the subject) sroduced as much iron as all the other countries of the world combined. The so-called Royalties are a commer- cial curse and an immoral scourge to Great Britain. How can ministers, justices of the peace, sabbath school teachers, !sc., side with this ruinous and unjust state of things, with the classes oppressing and misleading many poor uncultured thoughtless suffering working-men, to vote, to put a man in Parliament, who is on the side of oppression, and strong drink, in which is infinitely worse than wasted about £141,000,000, or more, as was the case last year? Ministers and rulers !whom God has not ordained, fill places in ,the Church and State. Of such Rulers and Ministers the truth must be declared "'ye cat the fat, and ye clothe you with the wool, ye. kill the fatting§ but ye feed not the sheep!, The diseased have ye not strengthened. neither have ye bound up that seti.lch was broken, neither have ye brought again that which was driven away, neither have sought that which was lost, but with force and with vigour base ye ruled oveythensa Ez. 34 c., 2, 3,4 and sv. The poor have no wish to deal with the , rich as they have dealt witn by them, but justice I demands that the toilers who create the nation's wealth be better paid, bean-fed, better housed,bettereducated ; have fewer temptations to entice them to drinking and immorality ; fewer hours of labour, and more leisure for high and pure culture, end education made free alike to every British subject,so that he,or she,whom the Supreme Being has endowed with the requisite gifts of mind, and heart, may fill the respective positions, in the empire, of rulers, subjects, teachers, and manual toilers, in love, not force, goodwill, not hate, for the joy, peane, and. happi- ness of all concerned and the glory of God.—Faithfully yours, Warrington. May 6th, 1892.

div.head: PROPOSED NEW PUBLIC HALL
div.p: THE PROPOSED NEW PUBLIC HALL
FOR WARRINGTON.
THE CORPORATION ASKED TO BUILD A HALL

With regard to the proposal to erect a new Public Hall in Warrington, a deputation, consisting of Mr. John Rylands, Mr. T. Giazebrook Rylands, Mr. J. C. Parr, Mr. James !damn, Mr. John White, Mr. L. W. Reynolds, Mr. Robert Garnett, and Mr. Rupert Crossley, waited upon the General Purposes Committee, on Monday afternoon, in the Mayor's Parlour at the Town Hell, to ask them to consider the advisability of providing a public assembly 'room or concert hall for the inhabitants of the town at the cost of the ratepayers. The Mayor presided over the Committee. The meeting wcs private, but we understand that Mr. Joni: RYLANDS, who was the first speaker, gave a detailed description of the events which led to the building of thepresent Public Hall, and said it was built by a company, because there was no other way known in those days in which the work could be carried out. The present Public Hall had been made ' available for theatrical purposes, and as it was now too small for public hall purposes, the company agreed to sell it. The deputation to some extent represented the inhabitants of the town, and they came to the Corpora- tion to ask them if they could see their way, in erecting new buildings, as he assumed they were about to do at the Town Hall, to erect also a large hall similar to what many other towns possessed in connection with their Town Hall. Mr. Rylands pointed out that the Corpora- tion could borrow money at a very low rate of interest. —Mr. J. C. Pang corroborated what Mr. Rylands had said, and remarked that they all felt the necessity for the erection of a good hall in iWarrington. If towns like Crewe and C,ongleton could have a large public hall Wilt by their respective Corporations, he did not see why Warrington should not act in a similar manner. He hoped the General Purposes Committee would take the matter into their earnest consideration.— Mr. T. G. RYLANDS said he well remembered the diffi- culty which existed in connection with the erection of the first publ' hall. Be was Mayor at the time, and he I thought it highly improbable that any company could be got together now to do what was done at that time. The hall was quite inadequate to the requirements of the town, and he hoped, therefore, that another build- ing would be erected which would be capable of accom- modating from 2,000 to 3,000 people, with better acous- tic properties. It seemed to him that the Corporation were the people who should take the matter in hand, for the good of the whole town,and not for any particular class. —Mr. Joan WHITE said the first point was, had the Cor- poration power to erect the hall'? He had been told not, but if other towns could do it, he supposed Warrington could also get the necessary powers. Then came the second point, were they willing.? He apprehended they would be willing if it could be shawn them there would be no loss, and this could be proved from figures. He believed that not only would there be sufficient income to pay 3 per cent, upon an outlay of say £6,000 but also a surplus for a sinking fund. The princial outgoings were ground rent (what the Corporation would not have to pay), hallkeeper, which, if the* Corporation built the hall, would not be necessary, rates, from-most of which Corporation property would be free, and gas, which the Corporatima could supply for nothing. He estimated that the annual expenditure would be 70 per cent less to the Corporation than if the halt was built by a com- pany.—After the deputation had explained their views, the General Purposes Committee promised to carefully sonsider the matter and communicate with the deputa- tion at as early a date as possible.
WHAT HAS BEEN SUGGESTED, AND WHAT CAN BE DONE.

The need for a new Public Hall or place of as- sembly, adequate to the growing ,population and requirements of Warrington, has been pretty gene- rally admitted for some years past. In April of last year the subject was dealt with 'pretty exhaus- tively in our columns by the late Mr. Gen. Woods. An idea which he touched upon was that of provi- viding an Assembly Hall in connection with the Gymnasium, which was not built at that time, but that idea could not be carried out because the Charity Commissioners, who had some command over part of the building fund of the Gymna- sium, would not sanction such a scheme. Mr. Woods, however, argued strongly in favour of a proposal to build a spacious assembly hall over the new baths which would provide seating accommodation for 1,000 persons, and an orchestra capable of holding 250 performers. In order to do this he calculated that it would be necessary for the Corporation to borrow an additional £B,OOO. "The nece&ry £8,000," he said, could be obtained at 34 per cent., which would mean £2lO per annum interest on capital ; and the cost of " hall keeper "and " gas " would be charged against those using the hall. No secretary would be required; in all such cases applications for the hall are made either to the Borough Treasurer or the Town Clerk. It is self-evident, that, with proper arrangement, the in- come derived from " letting "the hall would cover the interest on the capital, and probably there might be some profit. But the latter is not the main argument. It is not necessary to say, however, that the project was not taken up by the Corporation, and, as yet., we have neither new baths nor assembly hall. Mr. Woods took a good deal of trouble in gathering information as to what was done in other towns with regard to the provision of places of assembly for the Inhabitants. He had, he said, "from a reliable source of information, made a list of the towns of England each of which has a Town Hall, and the owners of which are 'The Corporation.' There are 50. I have not included the city of London nor any part of it under the control of the County Council. There are 21 which possess halls capable of seating 500 to 900 persons. 24 towns, etc. 1,000 to 2,000 persons,

„ „ 2,000 and upwards. There are several towns with a population of 30,000 and less which have Halls capable of seating 1,000 persons. St. Helens, population, 57,000 • Rochdale, 88,000 ; I cherley, 20,000; Congleton, 12,400 ' • Luton, 30,000; Dover, 28,000 ; Barrow-in-Furness, 47,000: these have Corporation Assembly Rooms capable of seating over 1,000 people.”

div.head: WHY NOT UTILISE THE MARKET HALL?
div.p: WHY NOT UTILISE THE MARKET HALL?

It will be seen from the above that in a large num- ber of towns the Corporations have considered it part of their duty to provide a suitable assembly room for the inhabitants. In most cases, and, indeed, probably in almost every case, the Assembly Room is in connection with the Town Hall, and it is in this respect that War- rington differs from most other places. Our Town Hall having originally been a private residence, contains no room anything like large enough for the purposes— even if we leave out of account many other objec- tions which might be urged—ef public assem- blies, and, it is not easy to see how one could be I provided in connection with the hall without an outlay I very much larger than the Town Council is likely to I sanction. Turning in another direction however, we find that there is another building in the hands of the Corporation which, alike as to situation, size, and pro- bable cost of conversion, is eminently suitable for ad- aptation to the uses of an Assembly Hall—and that is the 'Market Hall. Councillor Blackhurst, the deputy chair- man of the Markets Committee, has been kind enough to furnish us with a number of particulars as to this Hall, which, in view of the present movement in favour of a new Public Hall, will no doubt be of interest to our readers, We may mention that Councillor Blackhurst is himself strongly of opinion that, if the Corporation does undertake to provide an Assembly Hall, there is no other way by which it can do it so effectively and econo- mically as by making use of the Market Hall for the pur- pose. First, with regard to accommodation,we find that the area within the four walls of the Market Hall is 85ft, 10 in. by 59ft. 10in. The area of the present Public Hall is 54ft. by 50ft., that of the Assembly Room at Birkenhead Town Hall, eOft. by 50ft., and that of St. I Helens 96ft. by 441 t. From this it will be seen that the , Market Hall gives more ample seating space than any ' of the other places mentioned, and, with galleries, sitting am:in:iodation could be found for well on to 2,000 per- sons. The scheme to which We are alluding does not necessarily involve the disuse of the Hall as a mar- ket. What is suggested is that the walls of should be raised as many feet as may be considered desirable; and, if need be, the present floor of the building could be lowered, by encroaching upon the cellar space beneath, to the level of the ground outside. By these means there would be a sufficient height of wall to permit of the ground floor still being used for market purposes, while the floor above would be the assembly room. The main entrance would be from that side of the Hall behind the shop of Mr. P. Leigh, Horsernarket-at., and access to the Hall would be obtainable by a wide staircase of easy ascent. It may also be pointed out that anterooms could be provided on a line with the Hall above the entrance and the market offices which at present occupy that end of the Hall ; and these anterooms could be formed with- out encroaching upon the dimensions of tke Hall given above. The advantages of this scheme for providing an Assembly Hall that is equal to the needs of the town are obvious. One advantage, and certainly one of the most important, is the situation it would occupy, being as near the centre of the town as it could well be, and of easy access from many directions. In the next place, the site and the building are already in the hands of the Corporation, so that there would be ne preliminary outlay in acqiring these, nor any subse- queet payment of heavy ground rents. It should be noted, too, that the Market Hall, as at present used, is of comparatively little profit to the Corporation. The total annual income from it is about £2BO, but the un- avoidable expenses against it are so heavy as to have probably not more than £lOO a year in the treasury of the borough after these are met. Whatever is done, should, it need hardly be said, be done with a view to meeting the requirements of Warrington to-day, and for the next twenty years. The matter, is one, therefore, 4 which should be well considered on all sides.

confroan-oux HERE TO CANADA. Having been out here two years myself. I guess I ought to pretty near know the run of the country by this time, especially Manitoba, and would like to inform my friends in Warrington that this coun- try is not 80 good as it is represented by agents for the Dominion. I should like to give particulars from the beginning, and say that any man who wishes to come out here, I would advise him to get all the information he can from experienced persons that he can rely upon, and consider what part to go to that would suit him best for his busi- ness. lam referring to working-men and I think I can give a few facts that might be of some use to the emigrant. I would advise him in the first place to go intermediate or second cabin if he . can afford it on any of the steamship lines, and, if he cannot afford to come otherwise than by steerage, to get some eatsbles.that he thinks he would fancy in case of sea sickness and take them with him. I have tried it myself three times, twice on the Dominion Line and once on the Allan Line(per Par- isian) and I must say I prefer the Allen Line for comfort, cleanliness, and everything. There is one thing I should like to mention to the passenger coming out here, and that is that he should provide himself with

A VACCINA.TION CERTIFICATE. It would save him a little trouble, as it would not be necessary for him to be vaccinated on hoard ship which I myself just escaped. Not one of the passengers knew anytbing in regard to being vac- cinated until we were about six days oat at sea, when we received word from the stewards of the ship that any person who could not show a certifi- cate of vaccination would have to submit to being vaccinated by the ship's surgeon, and any one who' had any objections to it would be delayed in quar- antine. The steerage passengers were in an uproar, in a short time, and every one had objections and wanted to know why they were not informed of. this before they embarked, but they could not get any definite answer and declared they wouldn't be vaccinated, but they all submitted, as they did not care about being put in 'quarantine. Having a ticket from the surgeon of the Oregon, I showed it to the surgeon of the Parisian (the ticket stated' that I was protected) and he passed me and gave me another ticket, and so I escaped the perform- ance, much to the surprise of my fellow passengers* as I was the only one out of eight hundred steerage passengers who was not re-vaccinated, and I was not sorry either. I think they ought to make it known that persons would have to be vaccinated who couldn't show their certificate, and not take advantage of them when they get on board. It is but natural that people who have an idea they would like to come out to Manitoba would apply to the agents for papers, circulars, etc., in the country. but I would tell them right straight one half of it is not true. It describes the place as a perfect Paradise—to mislead a man of course. The average man believes it, and the odds are if he don't repent ever taking any notice of them. The Dominion Agents don't care so that they make their money i and get the people into the country, and when you get there they want to keep you there. I will

°WS MANITOBA ITS DUE for it is certainly a tine country for farming; land is cheap and of good quality, and anyone who would give their mind to it would make a success of it. I am surprised at farm labourers for stopping in the old country for little wages when they could get a great deal bigger wages here and their board as well, besides a homestead if they desired to go in for themselves. It has its drawbacks; you have got to run the risk of getting frozen out, or a hail- storm come up and clearing you right out,or even a wet fall and spoiling your grain, but it pays in the long run. If a farmer only got two crops out of his farm I think it would pay him. This country is a fine one for single young men, but he must turn his hand to anything, and be in no way particular what he does. He must keep his eyes open, taking the first chance he gets until he sees a better show, and he will get along all right. This is a poor country for manufactories, for there are hardly any at all, and what there are are on a very small scale. If the country had a few large factories it would be a great improvement and a benefit to the people. There is one business that I am sure would pay well here in Winnipeg, and that is a wire works on the same principle as the wire firms in Warrington. It is true they have two small firms here who make barbed wire, but one firm have to send for their wire from Montreal and the other have started to make their own wire on a small scale; but it is not anyways near being up to the mark in galvanizing. The 3 now have a chance of turning out good wire, as a friend of mine has come out to Winnipeg whom I had informed that they wanted a competent man. He is now working for them, and is most likely to make a great improve- ment in their wire. There is always a great de- mand for wire here among the farmers, as there is so much fencing to do. The greatest drawback to this country is

THE LONG WINTERS we have, which last on an average of at least six months. This winter has been a very hard one, the worst that has been experienced for ten years. It commenced freezing last fall in the latter part of September, and we have not done with it yet, for even as I am writing this we are , having a snow storm. We are haring hail,rain, and snow in one day. I often used to read that this country never had any blizzards, but I must say such is the case, for we have ex- perienced some pretty bad blizzards. We had one last December, which lasted about four days and nights without ceasing. Several others we experienced this last winter. The streets were all I blocked up and nobody could stir, and snow was banked up where ice had drifted to the height of eight and ten feet. All the trains were stopped, and some were snowed up. A great many reports were coming in of people getting lost, or frozen to death on the prairies. The thermometer kept about 40 degrees below zero for six weeks. Several times I have known it to reach fifty degrees below, and yet they try to bluff a person in the old country that they don't experience very cold weather here ;it don't appear like it anyway. The country is boom- ing this year, as settlers are coming in from Ontario to settle in Manitoba. Nearly all of them are far- mers, and I have known them to come up as many as 800 on one train. I know it is a better country than Ontario. A man out here must work hard in summer, and get as much as he can to keep him through the winter, for there is hardly anything to be done in winter, except he works in the bush, or goes on a farm for his board or for little wages. lie might drop across a job in the city for small wages, Ibut the chances are few and far between.

IN SUMMER. THERE IS LOTS OF WORK, men cannot be got, especially this summer, as half the thrashing was left over until this spring. The farmers are offering big wages but cannot get men. Labourers here get on an average of 1-50 to 2 dollars per day this year, and there are lots of men in Winnipeg to-day digging sewers, who are getting their 20 cents, per hour. I would advise any man to consider these things well before he comes out here to make a home. I think it best for a married man to leave his wife and family at home until he gets settled down, for he could then find out which is the best place for himself and then send out for his family. It costs too much money to run about this country; and look what a fix he would be in if he had his family with him, if he preferred the old country, and wanted to go back. He must bear in and it will cost him very near as rauch again to get back to the old country as it did to come out. Any man who is a tradesman, and has a permanent situation in England, is certainly better off there than here. I come across old countrymen here very often who have only been out about a month and have left good homes. They are disappointed in the country and curse it for everything. They think they are going to find money in the street, and think they are going to have a slick time of it, buttheyll get left,and don't you forget it,for he has got to work if he wants to make his dollars, and I can lay this that any man who is willing to work

I don't consider myself .01- cient in writing letters for newspapers, but I thought I would try anyhow. RUNCORN BURIAL BOARD.

The monthly meeting was held at the Cemetery Office, on Wednesday afternoon. Mr. H. Coleburn presided, and there were present Messrs. -W. Whit- taker, E. 'lmis on, T. Handley, Rev. Dr. Oastaldi and W. F. &Ikeld (sec.) The Secretary reported that for the month ended ApriL2sth,the interments were 49; last year 34, increase 15. The fees received during the same period were £53 9s. Ed., last year £33 25., increase £2o7s. Bd.—The Finance Committee recommended the payment of accounts amounting to £4 10s. 9d. An application had been received from the Runcorn Com- missioners for the balance of making Victoria-road. The total amount was R,534 35., and there had been paid _£36o.
