div.head: WORD . ABOUT THE CANADIANS.
div.p: A WORD . ABOUT THE CANADIANS.

They are a friendly, good-natured, and civil kind of people, more so than they are in my own country, for they consider one another as equals, or, as I might say," Jack is every bit as good as his master." I notice also there are more religious and temper- ance people here in Winnipeg,than any place I ever was in yet, for it is very seldom you would see a man intoxicated. We are expecting soon to have total Prohibition in the province of Manitoba, which I hope we shall have,and so do a great many in Canada. I think with the rest it will be a bless- ing to the country and to every man. I wish to say this that I don't advise anyone to come out here. I say every man must please himself, then he will have no one to blame, but if there is anyone in Warrington who is thinking of coming out to Canada, and would likb any information regarding the country, if it is in my power to give it I will only be too glad to oblige them, if they will write to my address as below. lam afraid, Mr. Editor, I am taking too much space in your paper, if you publish this letter which, I hope you will. 539, 6th Avenue N. Winnipeg, Canada, BRIMSTOOIN AN' TRAYCLE. {MIXED.) Br Tust Dicic o' Bon's.

There's one class ow offence on th' increase as wants lookin' to an' stoppin,' an' thad is railway eawtrages. Aw should think aw read o' tour or dye a' last weeks poppers, mi own opinion bein' as one iv nod two on 'em were trumpt up cases for th' sake o' freetenin' brass eawt o' th' chaps concerned, or else to ged some chep notoriety. Iv aw were a, Judge aw'd be varra heavy on cases o' this sort, becose they're booath planned eawt afoorehand: Th' chaps calculate on th' trains between certain stations bein' so long on th' rooad, an' th' wi amen on th' chaps payin' p I preference to bein' med into a target for th' ncospapers an' th' public to chuck mud at. 0' as aw con say is as th' waistrel as teks advantage ov a woman thad way owt to ha' th' cat—an' plenty on id, beside a long term o' imprisonment—live year at leeast ; an aw'd be just as generous wi wimmen o' proved bad charac- ter as browt a charge o' thad soort ageean a respect- able chap. Id seems to me as iv th' railway com- panies 'll hey to hey different lots o' carriages, labelled " Men only," an' " Women only"—yigh, an' " Married couples only;" and they'll hey to be varra strict, an' hey intelligent poorters to examine th' marriage lines o' th' last lot aw mentioned. Aw darsay they could add a carriage or two for "En- gaged Couples," an' soon spare other fooak th' sad spectacle o' their silly carryin'•on. As far as aw'm concerned a* olez ged into a carriage wheere there's a lot o' chaps—an' aw olez shall do ; an' my advice to other chaps wod be for 'em to gooa an do th' same. Th. wimmen wod be better in a carriage wheere there's a lot moore wimmen; but on no ackeawnt wed aw advise 'em to ged in a compartment full o' men, becose they play " nap," an' use bad langwige when they loyse. an' they will smook iv id isn'd a smookha' carriage. Abeawt this Orme. Nod Little Orme, nor Great Orme—nowt so little as them, ail grand as they are. Nor th' Mrs. Orme as deed Cottler day., becose hoo wor but connected wi' literary chaps, like Ruskin, an' Rossetti, an' Svvinburne, an' professor this, thad, an. Vother.; 800 d th' noospappers wod'nd waste their vallyable space on fooak as nobbut knew a tooathri chaps they were inclined to laugh at. Orme's nowt ; Orme's snot so common as owt intellectual ; it's a race-boss.: Th' peppers hes quarried Deeming for o' he's wo'th, an' th' same wi' Mrs. Montagu, an' th' date o'th general lection : it's too owd a game to tawk abeawt th' sees-serpent, an' too soon on i'th' year for mammoth mushrooms, an' big gooseberries— sooa welcome Orme. We've hed at leeast a fortnit o' Orme, an' aw fancy mony a theawsand on us does'nd keer a—ne'er mind wod—whether th' hose hes bin pizeued, or whether it's bed th' toothwerch bad. _ . _
'oAtd

Five theawsand ipeawnd reward isn'd so dusty, when yo' come to consider as we seldom offer more nor fifty for a mortherer—but yo' mon excuse me for forgeddin' an' bein' so silly as to compare human life wi' thad ov a hoes, an' a race-hoes, to boot ; one the hp his '

aunderdth is abeawt th' vally. A mon or woman's life is'nd wo'th so mich. even iv it's weel insured an' yore lucky enough to ged th' brass ; but wi' a race- hoss—well, yo' con lay one shillin' or a quid to sixty on id an' win—happen wont i' five hundred times. Wod abeawt loysin' t'other four hundred an ninety nine times? An' th' suicides through dooin' soot ? Losses is never ceawnted, an' as for th' suicides—ax me summat eeasier. To tell yo' th truth, th whol truth, an' nowt nobbut th' truth, aw hey'nd a bit o' sympathy wi' his Grace, nor wi' them as sympathises wi' him, for aw think bettin' on bosses 'hes bin th' mekkin' o' moore clam'd wimmen an' childer nor owt else, includin' drink; an' th' cause o' moore suicides nor th' tables at Monte Carlo.

- • Thinkin' o' th' good use five theawsand peawnd could be put to reminds me o' th' fifty-nine Brad- ford fooak as landed at Liverpool last Tuesda' fro' Rio de Janeiro. Moore nor a year sin' welly six hunderd men, wimmen, an' childer went to Brazil under th' impression as id were a land flowin' wi' milk an' honey, iv th' streets worn'd paved wi' gowd. They bed pamphlets gi'n 'em bi a emigra- tion agency as towd 'em as werkin' men an' their families could save sixty peawnd a year, as they'd hey a free grant o' land, a boss, a keaw, an' some poultry. Th' English government denies hevin' owt to do wi' this bit o' fiction, an aw believe id; sooa does th' Brazilian government, an' aw dorn'd believe id. Soon after these fooak went letters reycht Bradford o' th' state they were in; a com- mittee were formed, subscriptions gotten in—varra slowly—an' a Bradford chap sent eawt wi' th' brass to collect th emigrants an' bring 'em booam. When he landed be fun as they were slavin' on' th' coffee plantations, or i' th' cotton factories, fro' foss thing th' mornin' to sunset, in a boilin' hot sun, wi' nowt to eyt but rice an' black beeans; they hed to live i' mud huts, wi' no windows to keep th' rain or th' heeat eawt, an' they geet no wages. Just th' opposite, for they were towd as they were i' debt for their booard an' lodgins ! That's saturant like bein' a British sowjer, isn'd id ? As far as th' food an' heawsin' an' wages gooa aw meean. An' one eawt o' every three as went are dead ; some on 'em were robbed o' their clooath in an' o' on 'em were werkt herd an' clam'd. Mother's wi' childer at their breasts dropt deawn bi th' rooad side, an' lay theere till they rotted. Dorn'd yo' forged th' name o' this hell-hoyle. B-R-A-Z-I-L ; that's th' way its spelled. * * *

Everything's bin so grand this week i' th' o' weather, an' th' trees, an' fleawers, an' birds, till aw r'ally meant to be leet-hearted ; but this news abeawt th' poor Bradford fooak's acted on my spirits sum- mat like rain or sweeat acts on sterched things. Aw dorn'd feel as iv aw could laugti heawever mich th' provocation, but aw hooap we con o' httv a smile together as soon as th' general lection's o'er. ugh, we'll smile a forty hoss-peawer smile.
THE HON. P. NUGENT SENT TO PRISON.

At the London Sessions, on Thursday, before Sir Peter Edlin, the Hon. Patrick Greville Nugent was indicted for improperly assaulting Miss Marion Price on the London, Brighton, and South Coast Railway, on Easter Monday. Accused, who was very carefully dressed, , said, on being charged, that he emphatically denied committing an indecent assault, but pleaded guilty to a common assault. Mr. Cluer, for the prosecu- tion, said he thought justice would be met if his lordship accepted this plea. He would not offer any evidence. Counsel added that no attempt had been ' made to compromise or arrange the matter. Sir Charles Russell, for the defence, said, according to the evidence, the prisoner was in drink. He was not in a position to deny that he did misconduct himself ; but he was prepared to resist the more serious charge. Sir Peter Edlin directed the jury to return a verdict of not guilty on the more serious count, and, in addressing the jury on the second count, said they had to regard not only the prisoner's actual conduct in the train, but also his subsequent statements accusing Miss Price of , attempted blackmail. The jury found poisoner guilty of a common assault, he was sentenced to six calendar 1 months' imprisonment with hard labour, and ordered to pay the costs of the prosecution. Sir Charles Russell asked that the prisoner's wife might be allowed: to see him, and the request was granted.
A telegram from Buenos Ayres records a shocking dis- aster there. A skating rink collapsed whilst crowded with people, thirty of whom were killed and a number injured.

div.head: DARESBURY HIGHWAY BOARD.
div.p: DARESBURY HIGHWAY BOARD.
.A meeting of this-Board was held in the Sessions Boom, Daresbury, on Thursday afternoon. Mr. J. ' C. Parr presided, and there was a full attendance 11. of 'members.

ELECTION OF CHAIRMAN AND VICE-CHAIRMAN.—On the motion of Mr. James Parr, seconded by Mr. T. S. Bur- gess, Mr. J. C. Parr was re•elected chairman for the en- suing year.—On the motion of the Chailman, Mr. Cliffe was re-elected vice-chairman. A QUESTION OF LEGALITY.—Mr. John Darbyshire questioned the legality of the last meeting of the Board, which was held on the '7th April. He said the Act of Parliament prescribed that the meeting dealing with the estimates should be held between the 7th and the 14th April. He contended that if the meeting had been held according to Act of Parliament the results might have been very considerably modified.—The Clerk said they had always been in the halsit of holding the meeting on a Thursday, and they could not hold it on a Thursday without its being held on the 7th or 14th.—Mr. Darby- shite thought the highway rate could not be legally laid under the circumstances, but the Clerk replied that the rate would be perfectly legal.—The minutes of the pre- vious ,meeting were confirmed. TTLETATAL ACCIDENT AT RUNCORN.—A letter was read from Mr. E. J. Worsley, coroner, calling attention to the ,dangerous condition of the Big Pool at Runcorn, owing to the defective fencing, a fatal accident having recently happened there, by which a perambulator tan into the pool and one of the occupants,an infant, was drowned.— The Chairman said the accident was a very deplorable one,and he thought the Board ought to improve the fence if it was within their power.—The Surveyor said the Ship Canal Co. might possibly be .doing some work at the Big Pool. Hacalculated that an additional iron bar could be placed along the fence at a cost of £6 10s. or was decided that the Surveyor should write to the Ship Canal Company to ascertain what were their intentions with regard to the Pool, and also that be should take such steps as he thought proper to prevent similar a•cidentsin.the future.

div.head: – – ST. ALBA34'S SCHOOL ANNIVERSARY AT WARRINC, TON.
div.p: - - ST. ALBA34'S SCHOOL ANNIVERSARY AT WARRINC, TON.

There were large congregations at St. Alban's Roman Catholic Church, on Sunday, when the school anniversary was held. 'ln the morning at eleven o'clock solemn High Mass was celebrated. The morning preacher was the Very Rev. Dr. , Sanders, 0.5.8.,,wh0 took his text from the fourth ' Chapter of Galatians. The sermon,was an eloquent plea for the education of the young, and he pointed out that the lack of education was one of the greatest carses that could fall upon the rising generation. In the evening, an exceillent discourse was also preached by the Rev. Dr. Larkin, 0.5.8., of St. Augustine's, Liverpool wh• took for his text the words" The image of Gcsar, or the image of God ? Is it lawful to give tribute to Cresar P Render unto Cresar the things that are Cre3ar's, and unto God the things that are Gores." There, he said, in one sentence, with all the depth and yet simplicity of divine wisdom, our Blessed Lord stated and solved the great preblem of to- day, the great problerh of Education. Education was undoubtedly one of the great difficulties of to-day, and he purposed to consider that evening, by the light of the text, what was said must be the Christian answer to it. Now, there never was a time, perhaps, in all the world's history,when people were so fully persuaded that knowledge was power, and seemed so determined to spread knowledge by every means at their com- mand. England was simply over-laid with schools of every size, grade, and character. The great gates of knowledge were flung widely open to their many millions, and they were compelled to enter, for elementary education, at least, was compulsory. The civil power had stepped on the scene, and had I begun to assume to a ,very great extent the control 1 and supervision of education. But what about religion? How was the State to teach the knowledge of God, the nature of the soul, the moral duties of man, and the mysteries of the world ? People were not agreed on the question of religion, to begin with, and they would not take it from the State, even if they were, and so the civil power halted, and that ended by a com- promise. It could not please everybody, and so perforce it pleased nobody. It could not teach all the religions, and so it resolved to teach none. It secularized educa- tion, as they called it, or, in plainer words, made it prac- tically atheistic. And what had they to saw to that ? They could not, they dare not accept it. They must fight it to the death, for the system was false to its very core. Education without religious instruction was no true education. Even if it were education it would be productive of the most deplorable results, both to the soul of the child, to those who educated it, and to human society at large. Education was a state of the mind. To be truly educated, a man must not merely know the things, but he must know them in their proper order, in their true light, in their- real dependence upon and relation to each other. Could they banish God from a school and still call it a school ? Could they exclude Him altogether from a scheme of Education, and fancy that it was education in any real sense of the word ? God really existed, and had revealed Himself to man. That they all believed. Therefore He was a legitimate object of their knowledge, and as such the knowledge of God should be taught. God was the centre, the spring, the secret of all existence, and, therefore, the knowledge of God ought to be the centre and support of all their knowledge.

div.head: LUNATIC IN A CATHOLIC CHAPEL. EXCITING SCENE AT NEWTON.
div.p: A LUNATIC IN A CATHOLIC CHAPEL. EXCITING SCENE AT NEWTON.

Worshippers at the early morning service in the , church of St. Mary and St. John, Newton, were witnesses of an unusual and exciting scene, which ' took place in the chapel on Tuesday morning. To digress a little, on Monday about mid-day a strange man appeared at the entrance to the chapel, and walking up the aisle, proceeded to the chancel, where he divested himself of his clogs and coat, but on being requested by a domestic in the employ of Father Lennon, he quietly left the chapel. Nothing further was thought of the incident, until Tuesday morning, when it was unpleasantly revived. About eight o'clock, just as the service had concluded, and before the worshippers had left the chapel, a man, who was subsequently identified as the one who behaved so strangely the preceding day, rushed up the aisle in an excited state, towards the chancel, shouting the while in an unintelligible manner. Ile entered the chancel, and at once divested himself of his clogs and coat,which he placed within the altar rails, whilst his cap he threw upon the altar table. He then faced the people in the church, and began to expose his breast, shouting at the top of his voice that he would show the people what he hed suffered. Father Lennon, who had been officiating, was much concerned at such unseemly behaviour, but Father Holmes, of Preston, who was present in the church, set about ejecting the unwelcome visitor. Whilst doing so, the man attempted to strike the reverend gentleman, but the latter suceeded in putting him out- side. When be got to the door, he said he was going that day to shoot Lord Gerrard. Father Lennon, having to leave home, gave orders for the church doors and the doors of his house to be kept locked,and he sent word to Sergeant Longworth inform- ing him of what had occurred and asking him to keep a watch for the man, who he considered was dangerous. The individual, however, eluded the vigilance of the police, and made his appearance again at the church, but finding the doors locked, he went away. On inquiry it was found that the offender was a col- lier named Mark Jones, living at Railway View, Burton. wood. He is a married man, but has for some time been separated from his wife. About five months ago it was noticed that he was rather strange in his manner, and he has gradually become worse, until it has been considered unsafe for him to be at large. After his escapade at Newton, he appears to have returned to Burtonwood, where it is said he threw a brick at a man, but missing its mark, it struck his own brother and injured him. He then entered a shop in the village, and seizing a large knife, flourished it in such a threatening manner as to cause the occupants to seek safety in the street. On Wednesday morning he made his way to Collins Green Colliery, and seeing a can, he drank the contents. The owner of the can remonstrated, but the lunatic seiz- ing a large iron wrench,struck at the man's head, though fortunately he evaded the blow. The man was then seized and bound hand and foot, and P. C. Grundy was sent for, on whose arrival the colliery people provided a conveyance and Jones was taken to Newton. On arrival at the Town Hall, he was examined by Dr. Watkins, who certified that he was of unsound mind, and Mr. T. Peare.cn ordered his committal to an asylum, Mr. Bowes, relieving officer, then took charge of him and conveyed him to Rainkill Asylum.

The bodies of tw o women were found in a pond at Highgate on Thursday morning. They were still warm when extricated, but efforts to restore life failed. There is every appearance that it is a case of double suicide, heavy atones being found in each woman's pocket,
CRICKET. Cambridge University second innings closed for 368. THE GOLF CHAMPION.
At Sandwitch yesterday afternoon the amateur golf club championship was won by Mr. John Ball, jun.
SIR ARTHUR SULLIVAN.
Sir Arthur Sullivan completed his fiftieth year yester- day. We are glad that Sir Arthur's condition continues to improve.
A MANAGER'S SUICIDE.

Yesterday morning, Mr. Peter Thomas, manager of the Cambourne Posting Company, hanged himself in the company's stables. CABINET COUNCIL. A Cabinet Council was held at the Foreign Office yes- terday morning, all the Ministers being present except Mr. Stanhope, who is on the Continent for the benefit of his health.

THE DATE OF THE DISSOLUTION. A West Hartlepool telegram states that the "Northern Guardian" publishes a letter received by a north coun- try politician from a prominent Conservative member of Parliament, stating that the dissolution is now prac- tically fixed for the 7th or Bth of July.

BILLED ON THE SPOT. A Guernsey correspondent telegraphs :—Whilst Mr. Gerald Dejersey, aged 18,lieutenant in the Royal Guern- sey Militia Artillery, was seeking for gull's eggs, on Thursday evening, on the cliffs at Plienraont, which is the most westerly point of the island, he fell from a height 9f about a hundred feet to the rocks below, and was killed on the spot.

div.head: STRIKE AT DURHAM.-AN ABORTIVE CONFERENCE.
div.p: THE STRIKE AT DURHAM.-AN ABORTIVE CONFERENCE.

At yesterday's Conference of Durham Coal Owners and Miners, the latter offered to accept a reduction of seven and a half per cent, or thirty-five per cent, above standard wages, but the owners would take nothing less than 10 per cent, on the whole. Neither side would give way, and the '..3onference broke up without any proposals for further negotiations.

SHIP CANAL WORKMAN DROWNED IN SALFORD. At one o'clock yesterday morning a sad fatality oc- curred at the Ship Canal works, Trafford-road, Salford. A bridge is in course of erection over the river Irwell, and men are at work night and day. At the time above stated oneof the workmen, named Henry Smith, aged 28, who resided at 8, Crofton-at., Ordsal Lane, was at work Oa the bridge, when he missed his footing and fell into the river. He was drowned before he could be rescued.
THE CONVICT DEEMING.
PROSPECTS OF AN APPEAL.

MELBOURNE, THURSDAY.—There does not seem much prospect of an appeal being made to the Privy Covncil on behalf of Deeming. The convict states that he is perfectly resigned to his fate, and declares that he is the happiest man in the world. He expresses the be- lief that he must have been insane when he committed the Windsor murder. The local branch of the British Medical Association have decided to ask the authorities to permit them to make an examination of Deeming's brain after his execution. THE CONGREGATtONAL UNICN.

The Rev. Herber Evans presided yesterday at the resumed assembly of the Congregational Union, in the Memorial Hall, Farringdon-street, London. The Rev. Alexander Frances, minister of the British and American Church in St. Petersburg, made an appeal on behalf of the anti-famine campaign in Russia. On the motion of Mr. Carvell Williams, it was resolved to endeavour al the next election to secure the return of representatives who would romote temperance, peace, social purity, and an improvement in the condition of the masses. A discussion on village congregational churches fol- lowed.

div.head: YESTERD,kY'S PARLIAMENT.
div.p: YESTERD,kY'S PARLIAMENT.
HOUSE OF LORDS.

The House met at quarter past four. The EARL Oi DEVON took the oath and his seat on suc- ceeding to the title. Numerous Railway rates and Charter order Bills were read a second .time. The Statue Law Revision Bill was referred to a Joint Committee of both Houses. The House adjourned at quarter to five. HOUSE OF COMMONS.

[ The Speaker took the chair at five minutes past two. ' SUBSIDENCES IN CHESHIRE.-011 the motion of Mr. LONG, a bill was introduced to confirm a provincial order made by the Local Government Board for the formation of the Northwich and Winsford Compensation District. ALIEN IMMIGRATION.—Mr. JAMES LOWTHER asked the first Lord of the Treasury whether he was in a position to fix a day on which the Government would place the House in possession of the results of their consideration of the question of alien immigration into this country.— Mr. BALFOUR said the bill :was in charge of the Home Secretary, and would, he hoped, be introduced WOO. THE EIGHT 1101712 S BILL.—Mr. BALFOUR, answering Mr. Cunninghame Graham, said it was hardly possible for the Government to find time for a discussion on the Eight Hours Bill. COLONISINU BRITISH COLUMBIA.—The Chancellor of the Exchequer, answering Mr. Seton-Karr, said the Imperial Government had arranged to advance £150,000 to the Government of British Columbia for the purpose of colonisation in that country. The repayment would be spread over a period of 25 years. The details would be settled with a representative of the Government of British Columbia. It was hoped that some families , would be sent out soon.

- - SMALL HOLDINGS.—The House then went into Com- mittee on the Small Holdings Bill. On clause 7, discus- sion was resumed on the amendment of Mr... 1. COLLINGS to secure that land specifically taken for agricultural purposes should be permanently dedicated to those pur- poses. After some discussion the amendment was with- drawn, Mr. Chaplin promising to consider the question of altering the clause or of introducing a new clause. Other amendments were then debated.

One that was accepted by the Minister of Agriculture prohibited the erection of any house for the sale of in- toxicating drinks upon a holding. Mr. Chaplin agreed to consider a suggestion made by Mr. Chamberlain that any land to be re-sold by the County Council should be offered first to the original holder. Mr. HOBEIOUSE'S amendment providing that money bor rowed under the Act should not be reckoned part Of the total debt of the county was agreed to, and the remain- ing clauses were agreed to. Mr. CHAPLIN'S new clause for Registration of the title to small holdings was added to the dill.

div.head: POLITICAL SPEECHES.
div.p: POLITICAL SPEECHES.
MR. BALFOUR.

Mr. A. J. Balfour, M.P., First Lord of the Treasury, visited Manchester, on Saturday, and fulfilled a series of engagements. In the afternoon he addressed a great meeting of his constituents in East Manchester, at Belle Vue Gardens. Ile believed that judged by their Irish policy, so far from their prospects being more gloomy than they were five years ago, they were infinitely and incomparably brighter,and that they could look forward with absolute confidence to whatever controversies might be in store for them upon the batter government of Ireland. After the Belle Vue meeting Mr. Balfour was present at a banquet in the Manchester Conser- vative Club in honour of the Conservative and Libe- ral Unionist members and candidates for the city.

div.head: SIR W. HARCOURT.
div.p: SIR W. HARCOURT.

Sir William Harcourt, addressing a public meeting at Bristol on Tuesday night, sail Lord Salisbury's recent speech showed his policy to be one of class domination and everlasting strife. He would not say that Ulster was not a promising field for an artist in sedition like the Prime Minister. Liberals refused to regard Ireland as a hostile island on eur flank. Their policy was to treat it as a friendly island by our side. He had always declared against Fenian Home Rule. He was equally against Fenian Unionism. Liberals looked with confid- ence to the election close at hand.

THE DUKE OF DEVONSHIRE. The Duke of Devonsire addressing, the annual meet- ing of the Women's Liberal Unionist Association on Wednesdaf, said he did not attach so much importance as Si! Villiam Harcourt to a majority at the polls. M. eking further reference to Sir William Harcourt, he insisted that Liberals were rank deserters. After urging that it would be impossible for Mr. Gladstone to present a Home Rule Bill differing essentially from the last, he illustrated his opinion of Liberal promises by reference to cheap jacks, puffing prospectuses, and sham finaacia enterprises. LORD ROS RBERR Y. Lord Roseberry was presented on Thursday night with an address by the Liberals of the City and County of Edinbugh on the occasion of his returning to political life. In acknowledging the address he said that the Irish question was practically settled, but the questions uf the new democracy- and a new Trade Unionism had

Gentlemen,—l have now had your Marsh's Patent Smoke- oonsuming Stove for 18 months in constant use, and the longer we use it the better we like it, and for cleanliness and comfort it is a great contrast to the open Sr.. I was rather sceptical in regard to its not requiring the chimney sweep- ing. but haying watched it very carefulty for over 12 months, lam now satisfied that it does all that your advertisement says it will do. for I have not had the chimney swept since It was put in. and it keeps its draught ; and so I find that not only does it save fuel. but the dirt, cost, and inconvenience of the sweep.—Yours truly, JOHN A. THISTLETHWAITE. -- 322, Leeds Road, Bradford, January 15, 1292. Gentlemen,--I have two of your Marsh's Patent Smoke. consuming and Fuel-economising Fires at work continuously in my establishment. One fire has been fixed for fourteen ' months, working two large ovens (one heavy east iron and one sheet iron), and the other is applied to a complete bakers I range, with large ovens, side boiler, and hot plate, and they have both given every satisfaction. After getting the fires well started with nuts, we use practically nothing but smudge on the two-decker, and nuts and smudge on the range, for the remainder of the day. The heat obtained from this inferior coal with this Patent fire is really marvellous ; indeed, one can hardly realise tile fact of being able to bake bread and pastry with common smudge. Previous to having these Fires we had to sweep the chimney every two months, but it Is now fourteen months since we had it swept, and so far as I can judge, there will never be any necessity to sweep it again.—Yours truly, E. NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS. FOOTBALL. R. Lockwood, the popular little international, has a splendid record as captain for the Heckmondwike Club. During the past season he crossed his opponents' lines no less than twenty times, dropped three goals, and placed above a score of goals. -- During the past season Hunslet (the Yorkshire Cup- holders) have played 40 matches' won 27 of them, lost eight, and drawn five, scoring 441 points against 113 made by their opponents. Leeds, who were defeated in the final for the cup by Hunslet, played 39 matches, won 31, lost six, and drawn two, and scored 498 points against 163. Taking all in all, there is not much to choose in the figures, and both clubs may justly feel proud of them. The past season has been the most successful, finan- cially and otherwise, that the Sunderland Club has ever had, and when the annual meeting is held the members will see on the balance sheet a balance on the right side of £l,OOO on the year's working. Last season closed with a debit balance of £750, but that was spent in alterations which have not been necessary since. CRICKET. If one may judge from what is practically his initial appearance in first-class cricket, Parris, the new Sussex bowler, has a brilliant career before him. To take twelve Marylebone wickets for 48 runs is a performance of which anyone may be proud, and it is doubly so when the wickets are those of such famous cricketers as A. N. Hornby, Chatterton (twice), Barnes, C. W. Wright, Flowers, Hearne (twice), Martin (twice), Leatham, and Foley. -- Parris, who hails from Rmgmer, a small village near Lewes, is a stout-built young fellow about 22 years of age. He may be described as a medium right-handed bowler, but varies his pace considerably, and occasion- ally sends down a eery fast ball, and keeps a capital length. He should make his mark in county cricket, and prove a rare acquisition to Sussex, who are sadly in want of a good bowler. He is not much of a batsman, and in this department he is left-handed. There are plenty of men who bowl left and bat right handed, but it is a very rare occurrence in first-class cricket when the reverse is the case. It is, says the" Athletic News," a hit rough on Ley- land having to tackle such a club as Warrington without two such trusty men as Albert Ward and Alf. Tinsley. Their batting was sadly wanted, Warrington winning by 34 runs? Captain Manson and Reginald Smith col- lared the Leyland bowling, each scoring 44, but nobody else could do anything against Nash and Tonge. Still, the" wirepullers " came off conquerors, so that they were quite satisfied. The Earl of Sheffield brings home with him a memento of the decisive victory which was achieved over the Australian Eleven in the match concluded at Adelaide. The ball which the Australians pursued so zealously until it had been sent to all parts of the field for runs has been presented, suitably inscribed, to the Earl by Mr. Blackham, the captain of the vanquished eleven. Lancashire were severely defeated at the beginning of the week in their encounter with Marylebone and Ground. In their first innings the Marylebone team compiled a score of 238, the only individual efforts be- ing those of Chatterton who was not out for 109, and Gunn's 46. Lancashire first innings resulted in 155, in- cluding 33 by A. N. Hornby, 28 by A. Ward, 25 by S. M. Crosfield, and 22 by Balser. In the second innings, which added another 110, Albert Ward figured most prominently with 64. The combined score of Lanca- shire left their opponents with only 28 to get, and these were soon knocked without the loss of a wicket. Lan- cashire were therefore defeated by ten wickets. MISCELLANEOUS. At the Manchester Central Athletic Club sports on Saturday, J. Whitfield, of the Warrington Harriers, carried off the first prize in the three miles handicap, starting at the 355 yards mark. S. Phillips, East Manchester' was second with 286 yards start, S. Cooper, ' jun., of the Adelphi Lads' Club, coming in third from the 300 yards mai Ir. Whitfield won easily, his time being 1 15 minutes, 50 seconds. On Saturday afternoon a main of bowls, in aid of a member who has been ill for some time, was commenced on the Bank Quay Bowling Green. The weather was rather cool, a strong wind blowing, but nevertheless , there was a good muster of bowlers. The entries were very numerous, and the close of the day's sport found the first round completed. The competition will be con- tinued to-day (Saturday.) Conneff, owing to an "[affection of the heart" having failed to meet Morton, of the Salford Harriers, in the five miles raze at Dublin, on Saturday, Morton determined to attempt to lower the existing Irish record, held byl Conneff, of 25 minutes 24 seconds. Although the" gate" suffered very considerably by Conneff's absence, the • spectators present witnessed a magnificent performance, ; which places W. H. Morton far ahead of any of his com- peers, and conclusively proves that he is the finest long- distance runner living. The last lap only occupied 69 seconds, the full time being 25 minutes 3 seconds, which is 4 4-5 seconds faster than the previous English record held by Mr. W. G. George. Morton was accorded a grand ovation for his marvellous performance, the sport- loving Irishmen being delighted that such a record has been made on the Balls Bridge track.
